chunks.title: Architecture
chunks.heading: Caching layers (hot path)
chunks.text:
Key resolution traverses exactly two caches. Postgres is never read on the hot path:

```
Request with Bearer token (or x-api-key)
  → moka (in-process, TTL=5min, cap=100k keys)  ← fastest, no network
  → Redis  (sub-ms, shared across pods)          ← fast, network
  → miss on both = 401
  → Redis error or timeout = 503
```

A Redis error or timeout during key lookup returns `503 authentication backend unavailable`, never `401`: a transient Redis failure does not read as an unknown key.

Redis is populated from Postgres at gateway startup and on every config write. The gateway also re-pushes keys, models, and MCP servers to Redis every `OBLETH_REDIS_REWARM_SECS` (default `300`) and after every pub/sub reconnect, pruning entries that no longer exist in Postgres, so a restarted or flushed Redis heals on its own. `POST /api/v1/resync` (the dashboard's **Reconcile cache** action under Settings → Data) runs the same rebuild on demand.

chunks.title: Architecture
chunks.heading: ClickHouse: usage and cost ledger
chunks.text: Append-only. Every completed request inserts one row asynchronously via a bounded channel and a 1-second flush loop. Never blocks a request. The gateway boots without ClickHouse: if the ledger is unreachable at startup or later, rows spill to a local write-ahead log and replay once it recovers.

chunks.title: Architecture
chunks.heading: Data plane  `:8080`
chunks.text:
Handles all inference traffic. Every request runs the full pipeline:

```
auth → parse + resolve model → boons enrich → cache check → fairshare admit → budget reserve → upstream proxy → reconcile → telemetry
```

This is the OpenAI-compatible surface. The Responses API (`POST /v1/responses`) and the Anthropic Messages API (`POST /v1/messages`) are translated to chat requests and run down the same pipeline, so admission, budgets, boons, and billing apply identically. The Verdicts API (`POST /v1/verdicts`) and the MCP gateway (`/mcp/:server`) are native handlers that share the same authentication and tenant gate. The same listener answers model discovery: `GET /v1/models` merges the catalogs of the upstreams behind registered models and rewrites recognized entries onto their registered names, and `GET /model/info` is served from the gateway's own registry. Client keys (`sk_...`) authenticate here; when OIDC issuers are configured (`OBLETH_JWT_ISSUERS`), short-lived identity-provider JWTs are accepted alongside them. The full route list is in [Data Plane Routes](/docs/reference/data-plane-routes).

The boons-enrichment stage is where gateway-granted [model boons](/docs/guides/model-boons) rewrite the request before anything downstream sees it: vision description, knowledge (RAG) retrieval, compression, guardrails input scanning, tool injection for the gateway tool loop, the `generate_image` tool, structured output, and speculation. chunks.title: Architecture
chunks.heading: Management API  `:9180`
chunks.text:
The versioned config and analytics surface. Authenticated separately with an admin bearer token. The Next.js dashboard and any CLI or automation consume this API exclusively — nothing touches the datastores directly.

All config writes follow a single path: **Postgres → Redis → pub/sub invalidate**. Every gateway pod's in-process cache is invalidated as soon as a key is created, deleted, or weight-changed.

chunks.title: Architecture
chunks.heading: Overview
chunks.text: obleth is a single Rust binary (`obleth`) that boots three listeners and connects to Postgres, Redis, and ClickHouse at startup.

chunks.title: Architecture
chunks.heading: Postgres: configuration source of truth
chunks.text: Holds tenants, API keys, model routes, MCP server registrations, fairshare groups, quotas, knowledge-base collections, settings, and the full audit log. The dashboard's own sign-in tables live in the same database. OLTP workload. Never on the request hot path, and required at boot: the gateway applies its migrations on startup.

chunks.title: Architecture
chunks.heading: Prometheus metrics  `:9091`
chunks.text: Always-on `/metrics` endpoint. Low-cardinality labels only (admission class, status class). Per-tenant breakdowns live in ClickHouse, not Prometheus, to avoid label explosion.

chunks.title: Architecture
chunks.heading: Redis: hot cache + atomic budgets
chunks.text:
The data plane reads *only* Redis:
- **Key resolution**: `obleth:key:{sha256_hex}` → `ResolvedKey` JSON (tenant, key, weights, quotas, group)
- **Model resolution**: `obleth:model:{name}` → `ResolvedModel` JSON, stored under the canonical name and every alias
- **Token budgets**: `obleth:budget:{tenant_id}` and the term-budget hashes → Lua-atomic reserve and reconcile
- **Response cache**: `obleth:cache:{sha256_hex}` → cached response, keyed per tenant
- **Pub/sub**: `obleth:invalidate` channel triggers in-process cache eviction on every pod

Redis requires a password. The full key layout is in [Redis Layout](/docs/reference/redis-layout).

chunks.title: Architecture
chunks.heading: The data plane pipeline
chunks.text: See [Request Lifecycle](/docs/concepts/request-lifecycle) for a step-by-step walkthrough.

chunks.title: Architecture
chunks.heading: The fairshare scheduler
chunks.text: A single Tokio async task owns all admission state — no lock races, deterministic order. Each model has its own pool inside that task, sized by the model's `max_in_flight` or `OBLETH_DEFAULT_MODEL_MAX_IN_FLIGHT`, under a total ceiling of `OBLETH_GLOBAL_MAX_IN_FLIGHT`. See [Fairshare Engine](/docs/concepts/fairshare-engine) for how the scheduler works.

chunks.title: Architecture
chunks.heading: Write path discipline
chunks.text:
All configuration mutations follow one path:

```
Management API handler
  → write to Postgres (durable, audited)
  → sync to Redis (cache)
  → publish to obleth:invalidate (invalidate moka on all pods)
```

This ensures there is exactly one validated code path mutating configuration. A delete or disable whose Redis eviction fails returns `502` instead of leaving the old entry serving; `POST /api/v1/resync` repairs the cache.

chunks.title: Capacity Provider
chunks.heading: Extension seam
chunks.text: `CapacityProvider` is the only interface between the scheduler and the ceiling. An implementation that derives the ceiling from live backend signals (queue depth, KV-cache utilization) replaces only the `CapacityProvider` binding; the fairshare scheduler and the rest of the pipeline are unchanged. obleth ships `StaticCapacity` only.

chunks.title: Capacity Provider
chunks.heading: Horizontal scaling note
chunks.text:
Each obleth pod has its own `StaticCapacity` instance, and its own set of per-model pools. If you run three pods each with `OBLETH_GLOBAL_MAX_IN_FLIGHT=1024`, the effective ceiling across the deployment is 3072 concurrent requests — and the same multiplication applies to every pool, so three pods each running a 32-slot pool for a model can admit 96 requests to it at once. HAProxy (or your ingress) distributes incoming requests across pods, so per-pod limits add up naturally.

Because of that, the Helm chart defaults to a **single** gateway replica (`obleth.replicas: 1`, `hpa.enabled: false`) so the numbers you configure are the numbers that reach your upstream. For redundancy, run N replicas and size `globalMaxInFlight` and the pools you care about so that N × those numbers stays within what your upstream can absorb; replicas cannot lend each other idle capacity, so a quiet pod's share goes unused.

See [Scaling](/docs/operations/scaling) for more.

chunks.title: Capacity Provider
chunks.heading: Overview
chunks.text: The `CapacityProvider` trait is the seam between the fairshare scheduler and the cluster's actual capacity. It answers one question: **how many requests may be in flight right now, across every model's pool?**

chunks.title: Capacity Provider
chunks.heading: Per-model max_in_flight
chunks.text:
Each model route can carry an optional `max_in_flight` slot cap; the pool for
that model is sized to it, or to `OBLETH_DEFAULT_MODEL_MAX_IN_FLIGHT` when unset.
This is the primary capacity control per backend. Tenant, group, and key limits
are enforced by fairshare *within* that pool, and the global `CapacityProvider`
ceiling caps the sum across every pool on top of all of it.

Set slots manually:

```bash
curl -X PUT http://localhost:9180/api/v1/models/$MODEL_ID/capacity \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"max_in_flight": 32}'
```

For self-hosted chat and embedding backends, use the **auto-tune ramp probe** to
find the upstream knee instead of guessing. The probe is recommend-only; apply
the result with `POST …/autotune/apply` or the control-plane **Auto-tune** panel.
Cloud models should stay on `capacity_mode: static` with a conservative manual cap.
See [Capacity Auto-tune](/docs/guides/capacity-autotune).

chunks.title: Capacity Provider
chunks.heading: Sizing the limit
chunks.text:
The ceiling from this trait is not the lever for matching a single backend's real concurrency — the **per-model pool**, below, is. Size the `max_in_flight` of each model (or the shared default) to approximately match the number of concurrent requests its inference backend can serve without queuing. Practical starting points:

| Backend | Suggested starting point |
| --- | --- |
| Single vLLM instance (A100, bf16, 7B model) | 32–64 |
| Aibrix cluster, 4 replicas, 70B model | 16–32 per obleth pod |
| Benchmark fixture backend (dev/demo) | 64–256 |

Then keep `CapacityProvider`'s ceiling (`OBLETH_GLOBAL_MAX_IN_FLIGHT`) **above the sum** of the pool sizes you expect concurrently active — it exists to cap aggregate memory/connection pressure on the gateway process, not to shape traffic to any one backend. A ceiling sized at or below that sum binds before the pools it's supposed to sit above, and pools fall back to round-robin instead of fairshare.

If you see high `obleth_queue_depth` and a growing share of `queued` admissions on a model, its pool is too small for the offered load. If requests are rarely queued but GPU utilization is low, you may have room to increase that model's `max_in_flight`.

chunks.title: Capacity Provider
chunks.heading: StaticCapacity
chunks.text:
The shipped implementation is a fixed limit backed by an atomic integer:

```rust
pub struct StaticCapacity {
    max: AtomicUsize,
}

impl StaticCapacity {
    pub fn set(&self, max: usize) { ... }  // runtime-tunable
}
```

Set it at startup:

```bash
OBLETH_GLOBAL_MAX_IN_FLIGHT=1024   # default; keep above the sum of the pool sizes you expect
```

Or tune it live without restarting:

```bash
curl -X PUT http://localhost:9180/api/v1/capacity \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"max_in_flight": 300}'
```

Read the current value:

```bash
curl http://localhost:9180/api/v1/capacity \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN"
# {"max_in_flight": 300}
```

A value set through the API applies to the gateway process that served the call and is recorded in the audit log. It is not persisted: on restart the process returns to `OBLETH_GLOBAL_MAX_IN_FLIGHT`, and with several replicas each one must be set separately.
