have already tested on your cluster. The header carries the routing metadata
obleth needs — engine, model name, port — and the body is submitted to Slurm
verbatim. Recipes are the practical way to create a
[Slurm-managed model](/docs/guides/slurm-provisioning): you keep the script you
know works, and obleth handles registration, replicas, and health.

Recipes are admin-authored. Anyone who can write one can run arbitrary commands
on your cluster as the Slurm user, so treat the recipe directory as trusted
operator territory.

chunks.title: Deployment Recipes
chunks.heading: The script body
chunks.text:
Everything after the closing `---` is submitted verbatim as the job's
`script_body`. Its `#SBATCH` directives are parsed and lifted into the JSON
fields of the submission, because slurmrestd ignores `#SBATCH` comments in a
submitted script.

Bind the server to `$OBLETH_SERVING_PORT`, not to a hardcoded port. The
provisioner injects a probe block after the shebang that walks the port window
and exports the first free port, so several replicas can share a node without
colliding.

```bash
---
name: Deploy Ollama
description: "Serve any Ollama model from an Apptainer image."
engine: ollama
model_type: chat
api_model_name: qwen2.5:0.5b
port: 8000
health_path: /api/tags
target_replicas: 1
max_job_failures: 0
---
#!/bin/bash -l
#SBATCH --nodes=1
#SBATCH --output=logs/qwen2.5-0.5b-%j.out
apptainer exec --nv /path/to/ollama.sif \
  sh -c "OLLAMA_HOST=0.0.0.0:${OBLETH_SERVING_PORT} ollama serve & \
         sleep 5 && OLLAMA_HOST=0.0.0.0:${OBLETH_SERVING_PORT} ollama pull qwen2.5:0.5b && wait"
```

Keep the engine's own model alias equal to `api_model_name`. Deploying a recipe
sets `upstream_model` from `api_model_name`, so a mismatch means the gateway asks
the server for a model id it does not serve.

chunks.title: Deployment Recipes
chunks.heading: Variables
chunks.text:
A recipe can declare substitution variables so one file covers several models or
paths. Declare them in the header and reference them as `{{name}}` in the body.

```yaml
variables:
  - name: model_path
    label: "Path to the GGUF file"
    required: true
  - name: ctx_size
    default: "8192"
```

Variable names must start with a letter or underscore. At deploy time each
declared variable takes the value you supply, falling back to its `default`. A
required variable with no value fails the deploy; an optional one that is left
unset keeps its `{{token}}` in the script rather than expanding to nothing.

chunks.title: Energy & Carbon Accounting
chunks.heading: Choosing a power query
chunks.text:
obleth only ever computes `sum()` and `count()` over your expression, so any
exporter that exposes a per-device or per-node power gauge works:

| Exporter | Example query |
| --- | --- |
| Habana / Intel Gaudi | `habana_device_power_watts` |
| NVIDIA DCGM | `DCGM_FI_DEV_POWER_USAGE` |
| IPMI / node-level | `ipmi_dcmi_power_consumption_watts` |

If the metric is per-accelerator rather than per-node, either aggregate it
yourself (`sum by (node) (...)`) or declare slots per *device* consistently —
the math only needs `cluster_watts / node_count` to mean "average power of the
unit you declared slots against." Filter with label selectors
(`habana_device_power_watts{cluster="prod"}`) to scope mixed clusters.

chunks.title: Energy & Carbon Accounting
chunks.heading: Enable it
chunks.text:
Open **Settings → Energy** in the [dashboard](/docs/guides/control-plane) (or
use the [Management API](#management-api)):

| Field | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| Enabled | Master switch |
| Prometheus URL | Base URL of the Prometheus that scrapes your power metrics |
| Power query | PromQL returning one power sample (in watts) per node or device |
| Poll interval | How often the gateway refreshes the reading (seconds, default 60; the dashboard accepts 10 or more, and the gateway never polls faster than every 5 seconds whatever is stored) |
| Energy cost ($/kWh) | Your electricity rate |
| Carbon intensity (gCO₂/kWh) | Your grid's emission factor (`0` disables CO₂) |
| PUE | Facility overhead multiplier ≥ 1.0 (default `1.0`) |

Use the **Test query** button before enabling: it runs the query once against
Prometheus and shows a live *"X kW across N nodes"*. On failure it surfaces the
raw Prometheus error string verbatim — that's your debugging tool for a bad URL
or expression.

The Prometheus URL must be reachable **from the gateway process**. In the
Docker Compose stack that means the in-network name
(`http://prometheus:9090`), not `localhost:9090` — inside the gateway
container, `localhost` is the gateway itself, and a wrong URL produces silent
zeros plus a poll-failure alert rather than an error at save time.

The Prometheus URL is checked against the gateway's upstream destination policy
both when you test a query and when you save it, so an address the gateway is
not allowed

chunks.title: Energy & Carbon Accounting
chunks.heading: Failure behavior
chunks.text:
The module's contract is **fail-open**: energy accounting can never delay or
fail a request. Requests record all-zero energy whenever any input is missing —
the feature is disabled or incompletely configured, the model's
`energy_slots_per_node` is `0`, no power reading has arrived yet, or the query
returned no nodes or non-positive watts. A computed value that is not a finite
number (for example, a `NaN` reading) is stored as `0` rather than written into
the ledger, where it would poison every rollup.

If a poll fails, the gateway keeps using the **last good reading** and raises a
deduplicated [alert](/docs/operations/alerting) (key
`energy_power_poll_failed`) instead of zeroing live traffic. The poller runs
continuously — while the feature is inactive it just rechecks settings every
15 seconds, which is why enabling it needs no restart.

chunks.title: Energy & Carbon Accounting
chunks.heading: Frozen at completion
chunks.text:
Energy follows the same immutability rule as [`cost_usd`](/docs/reference/clickhouse-usage):
computed **once** when the request completes, from the settings, power reading,
and slot count in effect at that moment, then stored. Editing rates, PUE, slots,
or the query later changes only future requests — history is never rewritten,
and there is no backfill. Rows written before the feature existed read as `0`.

chunks.title: Energy & Carbon Accounting
chunks.heading: How attribution works
chunks.text:
obleth uses **amortized slot-share with declared saturation**. You state, per
model, how many concurrent requests saturate one node
(`energy_slots_per_node`). A request is then charged its wall-time share of one
slot at the cluster's average per-node power:

```
serving_ms     = total_ms − queue_wait_ms          (queued time holds no slot)
watts_per_slot = cluster_watts / node_count / energy_slots_per_node × PUE
energy_wh      = watts_per_slot × serving_ms / 3,600,000
energy_cost    = energy_wh / 1000 × energy_cost_per_kwh
co2_g          = energy_wh / 1000 × carbon_g_per_kwh
```

`cluster_watts` and `node_count` come from your Prometheus power query (below),
refreshed on a poll interval. **PUE** (Power Usage Effectiveness) is an optional
facility-overhead multiplier for cooling and power delivery — `1.0` (default)
charges bare device power; typical data centers run 1.1–1.6.

A worked example: a query reporting **44,800 W across 64 nodes** is 700 W per
node. A model declared at **8 slots per node** gives 87.5 W per slot, or 105 W
after a PUE of 1.2. A request that spends 2.4 s being served is charged
`105 × 2400 / 3,600,000 = 0.07 Wh` — at $0.12/kWh and 400 gCO₂/kWh, that's
$0.0000084 and 0.028 g of CO₂.

chunks.title: Energy & Carbon Accounting
chunks.heading: Management API
chunks.text:
| Method | Path | Description |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `GET` | `/api/v1/settings/energy` | Current energy accounting settings |
| `PUT` | `/api/v1/settings/energy` | Update energy settings (applies live) |
| `POST` | `/api/v1/settings/energy/test` | Run a power query once against Prometheus |

```bash
# Configure and enable
curl -X PUT http://localhost:9180/api/v1/settings/energy \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{
    "enabled": true,
    "prometheus_url": "http://prometheus:9090",
    "power_query": "habana_device_power_watts",
    "poll_interval_secs": 60,
    "energy_cost_per_kwh": 0.12,
    "carbon_g_per_kwh": 400.0,
    "pue": 1.2
  }'

# Dry-run a query without saving anything
curl -X POST http://localhost:9180/api/v1/settings/energy/test \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"prometheus_url": "http://prometheus:9090", "power_query": "habana_device_power_watts"}'
```

`POST /settings/energy/test` returns the reading or the raw Prometheus error:

```json
{ "cluster_watts": 44800.0, "node_count": 64 }
```

Set a model's slot count on create or update alongside its other fields:

```bash
curl -X PUT http://localhost:9180/api/v1/models/$MODEL_ID \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{ "energy_slots_per_node": 8 }'
```

chunks.title: Energy & Carbon Accounting
chunks.heading: Overview
chunks.text:
When you self-host, you own the power bill — and no cloud gateway can tell you
what a request actually cost in electricity. obleth can, because it runs next to
your cluster: it reads real power draw from your Prometheus, attributes each
completed request its share, and freezes three values into the usage ledger
alongside `cost_usd`:

| Field | Unit | Meaning |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `energy_wh` | watt-hours | Electrical energy attributed to the request |
| `energy_cost_usd` | USD | That energy priced at your configured $/kWh |
| `co2_g` | grams | That energy at your configured grid carbon intensity |

The numbers roll up everywhere cost does — per request, per tenant, per model,
per day — so questions like *"this course consumed 4.2 kWh this term"* are
answered with the same fidelity as spend reporting.

Everything is **off by default** and fails open: until you configure it, and for
any model that doesn't opt in, the three fields are simply `0`.

chunks.title: Energy & Carbon Accounting
chunks.heading: Per-model energy slots
chunks.text:
Each model carries an `energy_slots_per_node` count (model form in the
dashboard, or the models API): how many of this model's requests one node can
serve at once when fully loaded — replicas per node × concurrent sequences per
replica. For example, 2 vLLM instances per node each serving 4 concurrent
sequences declares `8`.

`0` (the default) opts the model out entirely — its requests record zeros. Leave
external API-backed models at `0`: their energy isn't yours to meter.

chunks.title: Energy & Carbon Accounting
chunks.heading: Troubleshooting zeros
chunks.text:
Work down this list — every zero is one of these by design:

1. **Settings incomplete** — active means enabled *and* a Prometheus URL *and* a
   non-empty power query. An empty query silently disables the whole feature.
2. **Model opted out** — `energy_slots_per_node` is `0` for the model that
   served the request.
3. **No reading yet** — the first poll hasn't completed; wait one poll interval.
4. **Prometheus unreachable from the gateway** — check for the
   `energy_power_poll_failed` alert and remember the container-reachability
   note above. The **Test query** button reproduces the poller's view exactly.
5. **Query returns nothing** — `sum()`/`count()` over your expression came back
   empty or non-positive.

Old rows from before the feature (or before a model opted in) are permanently
`0` — frozen history is never backfilled.

chunks.title: Energy & Carbon Accounting
chunks.heading: What the numbers deliberately leave out
chunks.text:
The model is designed to **never over-attribute** past physical draw, at the
cost of understating:

- **Idle power is unattributed.** Nodes burning watts while serving nothing are
  nobody's requests. Totals therefore understate the utility bill — never
  overstate it.
- **Cluster averaging smears busy and idle nodes.** A request on a hot node and
  one on a cold node are charged the same average rate.
- **Queue time is free.** A request waiting in admission holds no serving slot,
  so only its serving time is charged. (`serving_ms` includes a small amount of
  gateway overhead.)
- **Helper calls record zero energy.** Vision descriptions, repairs, tool-loop
  turns, drafts, and other boon helper calls are ledger rows of their own with
  `energy_wh = 0`; the hardware time they use falls inside the main request's
  serving time, which is where it is charged.

Energy is charged for the slot time a request actually held, on **every**
outcome. A request that fails upstream without producing anything billable
records zero tokens and zero `cost_usd`, but its serving time still records
energy, because the hardware drew power regardless.

Treat the results as a defensible lower bound suitable for showback and
sustainability reporting, not a metered invoice.

chunks.title: Energy & Carbon Accounting
chunks.heading: Where the numbers appear
chunks.text:
- **Request Logs** — an **Energy** column (Wh) per request; the detail view adds
  **Energy cost** and **CO₂**.
- **Reports** — an Energy KPI (kWh) and CO₂ KPI over the selected range, plus
  optional **Energy (kWh)** / **CO₂ (g)** / **Energy cost (USD)** columns in the
  breakdown table by day, tenant, key, or model. **Export CSV** includes them.
- **Management API** — energy/carbon sums ride beside `cost_usd` in
  [`/usage`, breakdowns, series, and `/usage/daily`](/docs/reference/management-api).
- **ClickHouse** — raw columns on `usage` and summed columns on the permanent
  `usage_daily` rollup; see [ClickHouse Usage](/docs/reference/clickhouse-usage).

chunks.title: Guardrails
chunks.heading: Actions
chunks.text:
The policy `action` decides what happens when a scanner flags content:

- **`block`** — reject with `400`. An input match returns `request blocked by
  content policy` before admission, so the model is never called and nothing is
  billed. An output match returns `response blocked by content policy`; the
  upstream already generated the answer, so the request settles with its real
  usage and releases its fairshare permit before the error is returned.
- **`redact`** — mask the matched spans (e.g. PII) and let the request proceed
  with the sanitized content.
- **`log_only`** — never block or modify; raise an operator alert so you can
  monitor what *would* have been caught. Output-side `log_only` scanning runs asynchronously
  after the response has streamed, so it adds no latency. See
  [Streaming output monitoring](#streaming-output-monitoring).

Output scanning under `block` or `redact` needs the whole completion, so the
gateway requests a non-streaming upstream response and, for a client that asked
for `stream: true`, re-emits the scanned result as server-sent events. It also
disables the [response cache](/docs/guides/response-cache) for the request, so a
cached entry can never bypass the scan.

Two scanners are not redactable, so under `redact` they still **block**:
`prompt_injection` (there is nothing meaningful to mask in an injection attempt)
and the tier-2 `harm` classification. `pii` and `ban_keywords` are the scanners
`redact` actually sanitizes in place. Under `lo

chunks.title: Guardrails
chunks.heading: Fail-open vs fail-closed
chunks.text:
By default (`fail_open: true`) a scanner error — including a guard-model timeout
or outage — passes the content through unchanged, so a flaky scanner never takes
down a tenant. Set `fail_open: false` to **fail closed**: if a scanner can't run,
the request is rejected with `503 content policy scanner unavailable`.

chunks.title: Guardrails
chunks.heading: From the dashboard
chunks.text:
Open a tenant and use the **Guardrails** tab. Start from a preset and tune from
there:

- **FERPA / PII redaction** — redact PII (`pii`) on both requests and responses;
  passes through on scanner error.
- **Prompt-injection defense** — block (`prompt_injection`) on the request before
  it reaches the model or the tool loop.
- **Monitor only** — log an alert when PII appears, never block or modify.
- **Custom** — hand-pick the action, scanners, keyword list, and guard model.

chunks.title: Guardrails
chunks.heading: How it works
chunks.text:
Guardrails differ from the [model boons](/docs/guides/model-boons) in one key
way: there is **no global master switch and no per-model `boons` grant**. A
tenant's guardrails are **on whenever that tenant has a policy set**, and off
when it doesn't. You configure them entirely through the per-tenant policy.

- **Per-tenant.** Each tenant carries an optional `guardrails_policy`. Set one to
  enable scanning for that tenant; clear it to disable.
- **Two tiers of scanner.** Tier-1 scanners (`prompt_injection`, `pii`,
  `ban_keywords`) are deterministic and run in-process with no model call. The
  tier-2 `harm` scanner asks a configured **guard model** a one-token yes/no
  question and reads the verdict from the first-token log-probabilities
  (`logprobs`, `top_logprobs: 20`), flagging content when p(unsafe) exceeds 0.5.
  A reply that puts almost no probability on either answer counts as a scanner
  error, so a prose refusal cannot clear content. The guard model's backend must
  return logprobs.
- **Input and output.** `input_scanners` run on the incoming request; optional
  `output_scanners` run on the model's completion.
- **Internal keys are exempt.** Gateway-owned probe keys are never scanned.

chunks.title: Guardrails
chunks.heading: Observability and billing
chunks.text:
- **Spans.** When tracing is enabled, guardrails record `boon:guardrails_input`
  and `boon:guardrails_output` spans (see
  [Observability](/docs/operations/observability)).
- **Billing.** Tier-2 `harm` classifications are helper-model calls, metered
  against the tenant as a `guardrails_boon` usage record. Tier-1 scanners make no
  model call and aren't billed.
- **Alerts.** `log_only` matches raise operator alerts through the channels in
  **Settings → Alerts**, keyed `guardrails_input_<tenant_id>` and
  `guardrails_output_<tenant_id>`, plus `guardrails_input_harm_<tenant_id>` and
  `guardrails_output_harm_<tenant_id>` for a `harm` verdict. Blocked requests
  appear in the request log with status `400`. See
  [Alerting](/docs/operations/alerting).

chunks.title: Guardrails
chunks.heading: Overview
chunks.text:
**Guardrails** are obleth's per-tenant content-safety policy. When a tenant has a
guardrails policy, the gateway scans that tenant's request (and, optionally,
response) content and **blocks**, **redacts**, or **logs** matches — prompt
injection, PII, banned keywords, and harmful content — before the request reaches
a model or the response reaches the client.

Like the other capabilities it sits beside in `boons/`, guardrails is
**fail-open by default** and runs entirely at the gateway, so it protects every
client of a tenant with no client-side changes.

chunks.title: Guardrails
chunks.heading: Relationship to model boons
chunks.text:
Guardrails live in the same gateway engine as the [model boons](/docs/guides/model-boons)
and share their fail-open posture, but they are enabled per **tenant** (by setting
a policy), not per **model** (via the `boons` list). A model never needs to opt
in — a tenant's guardrails apply to whatever models that tenant calls.

chunks.title: Guardrails
chunks.heading: Scanners
chunks.text:
| Scanner | Tier | Runs on | What it catches |
|---|---|---|---|
| `prompt_injection` | 1 (deterministic) | input | Prompt-injection / jailbreak patterns |
| `pii` | 1 (deterministic) | input, output | Personal info — SSN, email, phone, card numbers |
| `ban_keywords` | 1 (deterministic) | input, output | A tenant-supplied keyword list (`ban_keywords`) |
| `harm` | 2 (guard model) | input, output | Harmful content, classified by the configured `guard_model` |

chunks.title: Guardrails
chunks.heading: Streaming output monitoring
chunks.text:
A `log_only` policy with `output_scanners` set monitors **streamed** successful
responses as well as buffered ones. As the gateway forwards each chunk to the
client it also feeds a copy to a decoder; the client's stream is never delayed,
buffered to completion, or rewritten, and the scan runs once the stream has
drained.

- **Decoding spans chunk boundaries.** Server-sent events are reassembled
  incrementally, so a partial event split across two network chunks — or a match
  split across two tokens — is still seen whole. Multi-line `data:` fields,
  `\r\n` line endings, comment lines, and the terminating `[DONE]` sentinel are
  handled; the response is scanned as the client would read it, not chunk by
  chunk.
- **Reasoning is decoded too.** Content deltas and reasoning deltas
  (`reasoning_content`, `reasoning`, and the provider-specific reasoning field)
  each accumulate on their own channel. Deltas within a channel are joined with
  no separator, so a keyword split across two tokens is still matched; the
  channels themselves stay apart until the scan, so interleaved reasoning and
  content can neither manufacture a match that was not in the output nor hide
  one that was.
- **Streamed tool-loop responses are covered.** A response driven by the
  [gateway tool loop](/docs/guides/model-boons#the-gateway-tool-loop) in
  streaming mode passes through the same decoder, so the model text produced
  across all of its turns is monitored, not just the first.
- **Buffers are bound

chunks.title: Guardrails
chunks.heading: Via the Management API
chunks.text:
Set or clear a tenant's policy with `PATCH /api/v1/tenants/{id}/guardrails`. Send
`{"policy": null}` to remove it (disables guardrails for the tenant).

```bash
curl -X PATCH http://localhost:9180/api/v1/tenants/$ID/guardrails \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{
    "policy": {
      "action": "redact",
      "input_scanners": ["pii", "prompt_injection"],
      "output_scanners": ["pii"],
      "guard_model": "qwen3-235b",
      "ban_keywords": [],
      "fail_open": true
    }
  }'
```

| Field | Type | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| `action` | string | `block`, `redact`, or `log_only` |
| `input_scanners` | string[] | Any of `prompt_injection`, `pii`, `ban_keywords`, `harm` |
| `output_scanners` | string[] | Any of `pii`, `ban_keywords`, `harm` |
| `guard_model` | string \| null | `model_name` for the tier-2 `harm` scanner (required if `harm` is used) |
| `ban_keywords` | string[] | Tenant keyword list for the `ban_keywords` scanner |
| `fail_open` | boolean | `true` (default) passes through on scanner error; `false` rejects with `503` |

> The tier-2 `harm` scanner only runs when `guard_model` is set and that model is
> registered. Tier-1 scanners need no model.

chunks.title: Identity Tokens
chunks.heading: 1. Generate a signing keypair
chunks.text:
ES256 (P-256) keys are small and fast to verify. Generate one **once**, offline:

```bash
openssl ecparam -name prime256v1 -genkey -noout -out signing-key.pem
openssl ec -in signing-key.pem -pubout -out signing-key.pub.pem
```

The private key goes into your provider's secret storage — an environment
variable, a Kubernetes Secret, a KMS entry. It is never sent to the gateway, and
the gateway has no setting to receive it. The public key is published in the next
step.

Nothing in this step contacts obleth. Key generation is purely local: the
gateway learns about the key only when it fetches your JWKS document, and only
trusts it because you named that document in `OBLETH_JWT_ISSUERS`.

chunks.title: Identity Tokens
chunks.heading: 2. Publish the public key as a JWKS document

chunks.title: Identity Tokens
chunks.heading: 3. Mint a token
chunks.text:
After authenticating the user, sign a token whose claims match the issuer entry
exactly. Keep `exp` short — minutes to hours — since expiry, not revocation, is
the primary bound on a leaked token.

```js
import { SignJWT, importPKCS8 } from "jose";

const key = await importPKCS8(process.env.SIGNING_KEY_PEM, "ES256");

const token = await new SignJWT({ device_id: deviceId, uid: user.id })
  .setProtectedHeader({ alg: "ES256", kid: "2026-09-a" })
  .setIssuer("https://idp.example.com")   // must equal `issuer`
  .setAudience("obleth")                   // must equal `audience`
  .setSubject(user.id)                     // read from `subject_claim`
  .setIssuedAt()
  .setExpirationTime("1h")
  .sign(key);
```

`iss`, `aud`, `sub`, and `exp` are mandatory. `device_id` and `uid` here are the
claims named by `device_claim` and `identity_claims` in the example
configuration — rename them to whatever your provider already emits, then point
the gateway config at those names rather than changing the provider.

chunks.title: Identity Tokens
chunks.heading: 4. Verify end to end
chunks.text:
```bash
curl -sS https://gateway.example.com/v1/chat/completions \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"model":"my-model","messages":[{"role":"user","content":"ping"}]}'
```

A `200` means the token verified and an identity key exists or was just created
— check the **API Keys** page for a new `identity` badge. A `401` carries no detail by
design; read the reason from [Troubleshooting](#troubleshooting) below.

chunks.title: Identity Tokens
chunks.heading: Apply the configuration
chunks.text:
`OBLETH_JWT_ISSUERS` is read once, at startup. Editing it has no effect until
the gateway restarts.

```bash
# Compose: set it in deploy/docker/.env, then recreate the gateway
docker compose -f deploy/docker/docker-compose.yml up -d obleth
```

On Kubernetes, set `obleth.jwtIssuers` in your values; the chart rolls the
pods when its rendered Secret changes. With `obleth.existingSecret`, the JSON
goes under the `OBLETH_JWT_ISSUERS` key of that Secret instead, and because
editing an externally managed Secret does not restart pods, roll the
deployment afterwards. See [Helm Values](/docs/reference/helm-values).

Two log lines confirm the feature came up:

```
INFO obleth: jwks loaded issuer=https://idp.example.com
INFO obleth: jwt bearer auth enabled issuers=1
```

If neither appears, the variable is empty or unset and every bearer credential
is treated as an API key. A `jwks not loaded at boot` warning instead means the
key document could not be fetched; the issuer's tokens are rejected until a
refresh succeeds.

chunks.title: Identity Tokens
chunks.heading: Configure an issuer
chunks.text:
Set `OBLETH_JWT_ISSUERS` on the gateway to a JSON array. One entry per trusted issuer:

```json
[
  {
    "issuer": "https://idp.example.com",
    "jwks_url": "https://idp.example.com/.well-known/jwks.json",
    "audience": "obleth",
    "algorithms": ["ES256"],
    "subject_claim": "sub",
    "device_claim": "device_id",
    "identity_claims": ["uid"],
    "tenant": "cli-users",
    "jit_provision": true
  }
]
```

| Field | Required | Default | Meaning |
|---|---|---|---|
| `issuer` | yes | — | Must equal the token's `iss` exactly. |
| `jwks_url` | no | discovery | Signing-key document. When omitted, `jwks_uri` is read from `<issuer>/.well-known/openid-configuration` at boot. |
| `audience` | yes | — | Must appear in the token's `aud`. |
| `algorithms` | no | `["RS256","ES256"]` | Allowed signature algorithms. Asymmetric only; `HS*` is refused at boot. |
| `subject_claim` | no | `sub` | Claim that identifies the user. |
| `device_claim` | no | — | Claim recorded as `device_id` on usage rows (letters, digits, `_`, `-`; at most 64 characters). |
| `identity_claims` | no | `[]` | Extra claims stored on the identity key at creation, e.g. an immutable user id. |
| `tenant` | yes | — | Tenant that identity keys are created under. Must match the tenant your account system already uses. |
| `jit_provision` | no | `true` | Create the identity key on first sight. When `false`, unknown identities receive 401. |

An invalid configuration stops the gateway from starting. The JWKS URL is

chunks.title: Identity Tokens
chunks.heading: How the trust works
chunks.text:
Three parties are involved, and trust is granted in exactly one of them.

| Party | Holds | Role |
|---|---|---|
| Identity provider | The **private** signing key | Authenticates the user, then signs a short-lived token naming them |
| Its JWKS endpoint | The **public** key, published | Lets anyone verify a signature without calling the issuer per request |
| obleth gateway | `OBLETH_JWT_ISSUERS` | Trusts the issuers named there, and no others |

End to end:

1. A user authenticates to your identity provider by whatever means it already uses.
2. The provider signs a JWT carrying that user's subject, an `aud` naming the gateway, and a short `exp`. The private key never leaves the provider.
3. The gateway fetches the provider's JWKS at boot and caches the public keys by `kid`, refreshing every 15 minutes.
4. The user sends the token as `Authorization: Bearer …` (or in `x-api-key`, which is how Anthropic clients send `ANTHROPIC_API_KEY`). The gateway selects the issuer by `iss`, verifies the signature against the cached public key, and checks `aud`, `exp`, `nbf`, and `iat` — all offline.
5. The subject claim resolves to an identity key, and the request proceeds under that key's tenant and budgets.

chunks.title: Identity Tokens
chunks.heading: Identity keys
chunks.text:
Identity keys appear on the **API Keys** page with an `identity` badge, the subject, and the issuer host. They have no secret, so there is nothing to copy or rotate. Disabling one blocks that user's token traffic immediately, ahead of the token's own expiry. Deleting one removes it; the next verified token recreates it with fresh budgets. Disable, not delete, is the revocation control for identity keys.

The Management API returns `kind`, `identity_issuer`, `identity_subject`, and `identity_claims` on each key. `identity_subject` is the field external account systems should join on.

chunks.title: Identity Tokens
chunks.heading: Issuing tokens
chunks.text:
This half runs on your identity provider, not on the gateway. If your provider
is a full OIDC server (Keycloak, Okta, Entra, Auth0, Dex), it already does all
of it — create a client whose audience is the value you configured, and skip to
[Apply the configuration](#apply-the-configuration). The steps below are for
minting tokens from an application you control, such as a portal that hands
short-lived credentials to a CLI.

chunks.title: Identity Tokens
chunks.heading: Key handling
chunks.text:
- Signing keys are cached and refreshed every 15 minutes. If a refresh fails, the previous keys keep verifying; only new logins depend on the issuer being reachable. An unknown key id triggers one immediate refresh per minute.
- Every verification failure returns `401` with `invalid token`; a verified identity whose key cannot be created returns `503` `identity provisioning unavailable`. The reason is exported as `obleth_jwt_verify_total{result}`.

chunks.title: Identity Tokens
chunks.heading: Overview
chunks.text:
The data plane accepts two kinds of credential, sent as `Authorization: Bearer …` or in the `x-api-key` header:

- an **API key** (`sk_…`), minted from the dashboard or Management API, and
- an **identity token**: a short-lived JWT access token minted by an OIDC identity provider you trust.

A token is verified offline against the issuer's published signing keys (JWKS). A verified `(issuer, subject)` pair maps to an **identity key** — a real key row of kind `identity` under a tenant you name — created on first use. From that point the request is handled exactly like one made with an API key: tenant status, schedules, budgets, model allowlists, guardrails, and disable all apply.

chunks.title: Identity Tokens
chunks.heading: Rotating the signing key
chunks.text:
Rotation is additive, and the order matters because the gateway caches keys for
up to 15 minutes:

1. Generate a second keypair with a new `kid`.
2. Publish **both** public keys in the JWKS document. Wait for the gateway to
   pick it up — a token bearing an unknown `kid` also triggers one immediate
   refetch per minute, so this is usually quick.
3. Switch the provider to signing with the new key.
4. Keep the old public key published until every token signed with it has
   expired, then remove it.

Skipping step 2 rejects live traffic: tokens arrive carrying a `kid` the gateway
has never seen. Removing the old key too early rejects tokens that are still
inside their validity window.

chunks.title: Identity Tokens
chunks.heading: Tenant mismatch
chunks.text: If the `tenant` named for an issuer does not exist, it is created with default policy and an alert is raised. In a deployment where your account system already manages that tenant, treat the alert as a configuration error: token traffic has landed in a new tenant instead of the intended one.

chunks.title: Identity Tokens
chunks.heading: Troubleshooting
chunks.text:
Rejections are deliberately indistinguishable to the caller, so read the reason
from metrics:

```bash
curl -s http://127.0.0.1:9091/metrics | grep obleth_jwt
```

| `result` | Cause |
|---|---|
| `ok` | Verified. |
| `unknown_issuer` | The token's `iss` matches no configured issuer. Compare both strings exactly, including any trailing slash. |
| `bad_alg` | The header's `alg` is not in this issuer's `algorithms`. |
| `unknown_kid` | The header has no `kid`, or no loaded key carries it. Check the JWKS document loaded and that its keys have `kid` values. |
| `bad_signature` | A key with that `kid` was found and did not verify the token. |
| `expired` / `not_yet_valid` | Outside the `exp` / `nbf` window. Check clock drift on both sides. |
| `bad_audience` | `aud` is absent or does not contain the configured audience. |
| `bad_subject` | The subject claim is missing, empty, or not a string. |
| `malformed` | Not a parseable JWT, or larger than 8,192 bytes. |
| `not_provisioned` | Verified, but the identity is unknown and `jit_provision` is `false`. |
| `provision_failed` | Verified, but the identity key could not be created. Returns `503`, and raises an alert. |

`not_provisioned` and `provision_failed` are counted in addition to `ok`, so the
rejection count is the total minus `ok`, not the sum of the other labels.

If no counter moves at all, the credential never reached the verifier: either
the feature is off, or the value does not look like a compact JWS.

`obleth_jwks_refres

chunks.title: Identity Tokens
chunks.heading: Usage
chunks.text: The request log and `GET /api/v1/usage/logs` include `device_id` for identity-key traffic, and accept `device_id` as a filter.

chunks.title: Identity Tokens
chunks.heading: What the token must carry
chunks.text:
The gateway treats a credential as a token only when it is a compact JWS: three
base64url segments starting with `eyJ`, at most 8,192 bytes. Anything else is
looked up as an API key.

The header must name an algorithm from the issuer's `algorithms` list and a
`kid`. Key lookup is by `kid` alone, so a token without one is rejected and a
JWKS entry without one is skipped when the document is loaded. See
[Rotating the signing key](#rotating-the-signing-key) for the order to publish
and retire keys in.

Claims: `iss` and `aud` must match the issuer entry, the subject claim must be a
non-empty string, and `exp` is required. `nbf` and `iat` are enforced when
present, with 60 seconds of clock skew; an `iat` in the future beyond that skew
is rejected.

chunks.title: Identity Tokens
chunks.heading: Why a token cannot be forged
chunks.text:
Generating a keypair is free and offline — anyone can do it. What an attacker cannot do is get their public key into your provider's JWKS document, and the gateway never fetches any other one. A token signed with a self-generated key therefore fails verification: `unknown_kid` if no published key carries its `kid`, `bad_signature` if one does. Both return `401`.

Forging a token requires the issuer's private key, write access to the JWKS response, or environment access on the gateway to add an issuer of your own — each of which already implies control of the system. Two common downgrade attacks are closed structurally: symmetric (`HS*`) algorithms are refused at boot, so the published public key can never be replayed as an HMAC secret, and `none` is not an accepted algorithm.

The signing key is a tenant-wide credential. Anyone holding it can mint a valid
token for **any** subject, and with `jit_provision` enabled the gateway will
create an identity key for that subject on first use. Protect it like the admin
token: secret storage, no source control, rotate on exposure.

chunks.title: Import Models from a Provider
chunks.heading: 1. Connect
chunks.text:
Enter the provider's **API base URL** and an optional **API key**.

- The base URL must be `http` or `https` and is the OpenAI-style base: obleth
  fetches `GET {base}/models`. If you get *"No /models endpoint here (HTTP
  404)"*, check whether the base should include or drop the `/v1` suffix.
- The key, if the provider needs one, is sent as a bearer token on the
  server-side catalog request only. A `401` or `403` is reported as a rejected
  key.
- The request times out after 5 seconds.
- Redirects are not followed. A provider that answers with a redirect is
  reported with its status; enter the final base URL instead.
- A base URL whose host resolves to a link-local or cloud-metadata address is
  refused.

obleth accepts the OpenAI `{ "object": "list", "data": [...] }` shape or a
bare JSON array, keeps entries with a non-empty `id`, and dedupes and sorts
them.

chunks.title: Import Models from a Provider
chunks.heading: 2. Select
chunks.text:
Every model the provider returned is listed and classified:

- **new**: no route of yours matches it. Selected by default.
- **existing**: already registered. Hidden until you choose **Show N already
  imported**, and never offered for import.

A model counts as **existing** when one of your routes matches it **by
normalized model name** (with or without its format suffix), *or* by the
**same provider base URL and upstream id** together. That dual check is what
makes a re-run surface only genuinely new models, even if you renamed a route
after importing it.

Each discovered id is turned into a suggested route:

- The name is normalized to obleth's naming rules: lowercase, with spaces,
  underscores, slashes, and other characters outside `a-z 0-9 . -` replaced by
  dashes.
- A trailing serving-format token (`fp8`, `bf16`, `fp16`, `mxfp4`, `nvfp4`,
  `int8`, `int4`, `awq`, `gptq`, `gguf`) is lifted out of the name into the
  route's [`quantization`](/docs/guides/model-registry#quantization) field, and
  the full normalized name is added as an
  [alias](/docs/guides/model-registry#aliases), so clients that call the
  provider's spelling keep working. For example, `Qwen3-8B-FP8` becomes
  `qwen3-8b` with `quantization: fp8` and the alias `qwen3-8b-fp8`, and
  `Qwen/Qwen3-8B-FP8` becomes `qwen-qwen3-8b` with the alias
  `qwen-qwen3-8b-fp8`. Only a trailing token is lifted, and only when a name
  is left over: a model named just `fp8`, or `fp8-tuned`, keeps its name.
- The route's

chunks.title: Import Models from a Provider
chunks.heading: 3. Review
chunks.text:
The selections are submitted to the gateway as a model manifest in preview
mode, so the whole import is validated before anything is written: each model
is listed as it would be created, with its fields and any warnings, and any
problem (an alias already taken, an `api_base` refused by the outbound URL
policy) is reported for every model at once. Confirm to create the routes.
Each imported model points at the provider's base URL and upstream id and
carries the API key you supplied, if any.

chunks.title: Import Models from a Provider
chunks.heading: Overview
chunks.text:
Registering models one route at a time is fine for a handful, but tedious when
a provider serves dozens. **Import from provider** takes any OpenAI-compatible
base URL (and an optional API key), asks the provider which models it serves,
and registers the ones you pick as normal model routes, with batch defaults you
set once and per-model overrides where you need them.

The catalog is fetched **server-side**, so the API key you supply never reaches
the browser. The flow only creates routes for models you do not already have,
so you can re-run it at any time to pick up what is new.

chunks.title: Import Models from a Provider
chunks.heading: Related
chunks.text:
- [Model Registry](/docs/guides/model-registry): every route field, aliases,
  quantization, and manifest import and export.
- [OpenAI-compatible API](/docs/guides/openai-compatible-api): the request
  surface your imported models serve.
- [Multi-modal Models](/docs/guides/multi-modal-models): embeddings, audio,
  and image routes.

chunks.title: Import Models from a Provider
chunks.heading: Walkthrough
chunks.text:
Open the dashboard **Models** page and choose **From provider**. The wizard
runs in three steps.

chunks.title: Import Models from a Provider
chunks.heading: What it does and does not change
chunks.text:
- **New routes only.** Existing models are excluded from selection, so the
  wizard never edits a route you already have.
- **No restart.** Imported routes are live as soon as they are created.
- **Re-runnable.** Run it again later and only new models are offered.

chunks.title: Import Models from a Provider
chunks.heading: When to use it
chunks.text:
- Onboarding a provider (vLLM, an OpenAI-compatible gateway, a hosted endpoint)
  that exposes many models at once.
- Periodically checking a provider for **new** models without re-reviewing the
  ones you already serve.

For one or two routes, create them directly on the **Models** page (or with
the [Management API](/docs/reference/management-api)). To edit many existing
routes, or to copy a registry to another instance, use an
[`obleth-models` manifest](/docs/guides/model-registry#export-and-import-the-registry).

chunks.title: Knowledge Base (RAG)
chunks.heading: Backups
chunks.text:
[Configuration backups](/docs/operations/backup-restore) do not include
collections, documents, chunks, or model-to-collection attachments. The retrieval
settings are included, because they live in the boon settings. Re-create
collections and re-upload documents on a restored instance.

chunks.title: Knowledge Base (RAG)
chunks.heading: Chunking
chunks.text:
Each collection carries its own chunking configuration:

| Field | Default | Notes |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `chunk_tokens` | `400` | Target chunk length in tokens; must be greater than `0` |
| `chunk_overlap_tokens` | `50` | Tokens shared with the previous chunk; must be `0` or more and less than `chunk_tokens` |

Change them from the collection's **Edit** form or with
`PUT /api/v1/knowledge/collections/{id}`. Existing chunks keep the old settings
until you reindex the collection.

chunks.title: Knowledge Base (RAG)
chunks.heading: Concepts
chunks.text:
| Term | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| **Collection** | A named set of documents with one embedding model and one chunking configuration. A model can read several collections. |
| **Document** | One uploaded file (`.txt`, `.md`, or `.csv`, UTF-8 text). Each document is indexed independently. |
| **Chunk** | A slice of a document, about `chunk_tokens` long, overlapping its neighbour by `chunk_overlap_tokens`. Chunks are what retrieval scores and injects. |
| **Embedding model** | A registered model with `model_type: embedding`. It embeds chunks at index time and the user's question at request time. |

chunks.title: Knowledge Base (RAG)
chunks.heading: Fail-open behaviour

chunks.title: Knowledge Base (RAG)
chunks.heading: How retrieval works
chunks.text:
For each chat request to a model that has the boon, at least one attached
collection, and the feature enabled:

1. **Capture the query.** The last `query_turns` user messages are joined (newest
   first, capped at 2,000 characters). This happens before any
   [compression](/docs/guides/model-boons#the-compression-boon) pass, so the query
   is always the user's own words.
2. **Embed the query** once per distinct embedding model among the attached
   collections, bounded by `embed_timeout_ms`. Query vectors are cached in Redis
   (`obleth:knowledge:q:<hash>`, keyed by embedder and query, for
   `query_cache_ttl_s`).
3. **Score and merge.** Chunks from every attached collection are scored by cosine
   similarity, those below `min_score` are dropped, and the best `top_k` are kept.
4. **Pack against the budget.** Hits are added in score order while they fit
   `max_context_tokens`, further limited so the prompt, the injected block, and a
   512-token reserve for the answer still fit the model's context window.
5. **Inject.** The passages are rendered as a `<knowledge>` block with a short
   instruction to use them only when relevant. If the model supports system
   messages, the block is appended to the existing system message (or becomes one);
   otherwise it is prepended to the latest user message.

Injection happens after compression and after the tenant's input
[guardrails](/docs/guides/guardrails) scan, so retrieved text is never compressed
and never trips the tenant's own P

chunks.title: Knowledge Base (RAG)
chunks.heading: Indexing lifecycle
chunks.text:
A background indexer claims `pending` documents one at a time, chunks them,
embeds the chunks in batches of `index_batch_size`, and commits the new chunks
and the `ready` status in one transaction.

- **Restart-safe.** A document left in `indexing` by a crash or redeploy is
  reclaimed by another worker once it has been claimed for longer than
  `index_stale_after_secs`. Only one worker's result can be committed.
- **Per-document generations.** Reindexing one document never touches another's
  chunks; the old chunks keep serving until the new generation commits.
- **Re-uploads.** Uploading a document with identical content again updates the
  existing document. If it is currently indexing, a fresh pass is queued for when
  the current one finishes.
- **Embedder changes.** Changing a collection's embedding model marks it
  **needs re-index** (`needs_reindex: true`) instead of silently mixing vectors
  from two embedders. Reindex the collection to rebuild it with the new model.
- **Reindexing.** `POST /api/v1/knowledge/collections/{id}/reindex` re-queues
  every document (a document that is mid-index gets its fresh pass afterwards);
  `POST /api/v1/knowledge/documents/{id}/reindex` re-queues one. The dashboard
  offers both, including after a failed document is fixed.

The gateway refreshes its in-memory index every 15 seconds. Unchanged collections
are reused as they are; only collections attached to at least one model are
loaded. If Postgres is unavailable during a refresh, t

chunks.title: Knowledge Base (RAG)
chunks.heading: Management API
chunks.text:
| Method | Path | Purpose |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `POST`, `GET` | `/api/v1/knowledge/collections` | Create (`name`, `description`, `embedding_model`) or list collections |
| `GET`, `PUT`, `DELETE` | `/api/v1/knowledge/collections/{id}` | Read, update (name, description, embedding model, chunking), or delete a collection |
| `GET`, `POST` | `/api/v1/knowledge/collections/{id}/documents` | List documents, or upload one (`title`, `filename`, `content_base64`) |
| `POST` | `/api/v1/knowledge/collections/{id}/reindex` | Reindex every document in the collection |
| `POST` | `/api/v1/knowledge/collections/{id}/search` | Retrieval preview |
| `DELETE` | `/api/v1/knowledge/documents/{id}` | Delete a document |
| `POST` | `/api/v1/knowledge/documents/{id}/reindex` | Reindex one document |
| `GET`, `PUT` | `/api/v1/models/{id}/knowledge` | Read or set the collections attached to a model (`collection_ids`) |
| `GET`, `PUT` | `/api/v1/settings/knowledge` | Read or update retrieval settings |

Writes are recorded in the [audit log](/docs/operations/audit-log). Full request
and response shapes are in the [Management API reference](/docs/reference/management-api).

chunks.title: Knowledge Base (RAG)
chunks.heading: Observability
chunks.text:
- **Metric.** `obleth_knowledge_retrievals_total{outcome}` counts retrieval
  attempts by outcome: `hit` (passages injected), `miss` (nothing scored or fit),
  `no_query`, `error` (every embedding attempt failed for a non-empty collection),
  and `no_window` (the model has no context window). See
  [Prometheus Metrics](/docs/reference/prometheus-metrics).
- **Header.** A response whose request had passages injected lists `knowledge` in
  `x-obleth-boons`.
- **Spans.** With tracing enabled for the key, a `boon:knowledge` span records the
  outcome and the injected chunk ids and scores; chunk text is included only
  with **Debug snapshot** on. See [Observability](/docs/operations/observability).

chunks.title: Knowledge Base (RAG)
chunks.heading: Overview
chunks.text:
The knowledge base lets a chat model answer from documents you curate: policies,
catalogs, handbooks, runbooks. You upload files into **collections**, obleth
splits them into chunks and embeds them through a registered embedding model, and
a model granted the `knowledge` [boon](/docs/guides/model-boons) has the most
relevant passages retrieved and placed ahead of the conversation on every
request. Clients need no changes; they send ordinary chat requests.

Retrieval runs entirely inside the gateway from an in-process vector index, so
the request path never queries Postgres. It is off by default and fails open.

chunks.title: Knowledge Base (RAG)
chunks.heading: Retrieval preview
chunks.text:
Each collection has a retrieval preview on the **Knowledge** page. Type a
question and it shows the chunks that match, their scores, and which of them
would actually be injected under the current `min_score` and
`max_context_tokens`. The same preview is available from the Management API:

```bash
curl -X POST http://localhost:9180/api/v1/knowledge/collections/$COLLECTION_ID/search \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{ "query": "How many credits can a student transfer?", "top_k": 5 }'
```

Each hit carries `chunk_id`, `document_id`, `score`, `token_count`, `text`, and
`would_inject`.

chunks.title: Knowledge Base (RAG)
chunks.heading: Retrieval settings
chunks.text:
**Settings → Knowledge** holds the fleet-wide retrieval settings. A retrieval
profile sets the first four at once:

| Profile | Top K | Minimum score | Max context tokens | Query turns |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| **Standard** (default) | 5 | 0.35 | 1500 | 2 |
| **Precise** | 3 | 0.5 | 800 | 1 |
| **Broad** | 10 | 0.25 | 4000 | 4 |

Editing any value under **Advanced** switches the profile to **Custom**.

| Setting | Field | Default | Meaning |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Enable knowledge retrieval | `enabled` | `false` | Master switch |
| Top K | `top_k` | `5` | Chunks considered per request before thresholding |
| Minimum score | `min_score` | `0.35` | Cosine-similarity floor (`0`–`1`); a chunk below it is dropped even when it is the best match |
| Max context tokens | `max_context_tokens` | `1500` | Ceiling on injected tokens, before the context-window clamp |
| Query turns | `query_turns` | `2` | How many trailing user messages form the retrieval query |
| Embed timeout (ms) | `embed_timeout_ms` | `1500` | Bound on the request-path query embedding call |
| Query cache TTL (secs) | `query_cache_ttl_s` | `600` | Lifetime of cached query embeddings in Redis |
| Max upload size | `max_upload_bytes` | `10485760` (10 MiB) | Per-file upload cap, checked before parsing |
| Max chunks per collection | `max_chunks_per_collection` | `100000` | Indexing refuses to grow a collection past this |
| Index batch size | `index_batch_size` | `32` | Chunks per embedding call during in

chunks.title: Knowledge Base (RAG)
chunks.heading: Workflow
chunks.text:
1. **Register an embedding model** on the **Models** page (or the Management API)
   if you do not have one.
2. **Create a collection.** Open **Knowledge** in the dashboard, choose **New
   collection**, and give it a name, an optional description, and the embedding
   model. Names are unique.
3. **Upload documents.** Drop one or more files onto the collection's upload area.
   Each file is limited by the **Max upload size** setting (default 10 MiB) and
   must be valid UTF-8 text; the content type is taken from the extension
   (`.csv`, `.md`/`.markdown`, anything else as plain text).
4. **Wait for indexing.** Each document moves through `pending` → `indexing` →
   `ready` (or `failed`, with the error shown). Indexing runs in the background.
5. **Grant the boon and attach collections.** Open the model that should answer
   from the collection, tick **knowledge** under **Boons**, save, then attach
   collections from the model's edit page. A new model must be saved before
   collections can be attached. The boon retrieves nothing until at least one
   collection is attached.
6. **Enable retrieval** under **Settings → Knowledge** (**Enable knowledge
   retrieval**).
7. **Check what would be retrieved** with the collection's retrieval preview
   (see [Retrieval preview](#retrieval-preview)).

chunks.title: MCP Gateway
chunks.heading: Calling through the gateway
chunks.text:
Clients point their MCP client at obleth using their **obleth API key**:

```
POST https://{obleth-host}/mcp/github
Authorization: Bearer sk_...
Content-Type: application/json

{ "jsonrpc": "2.0", "method": "tools/list", "id": 1 }
```

The key can also be sent as `x-api-key: sk_...`, and a trusted
[identity token](/docs/guides/identity-tokens) works here exactly as it does for
LLM traffic.

obleth:

1. authenticates the credential (same keys as LLM traffic) and applies the full
   tenant gate: a disabled key, a tenant that is not active, or a tenant outside
   its activation window, expiry, or weekly schedule is refused with `403`,
2. resolves the registered server from its hot cache,
3. strips the client's credential, injects the server's `auth_header`,
4. reverse-proxies the request and streams the response back (JSON or SSE).

Sub-paths are supported: `/mcp/{server}/{rest}` forwards `{rest}` (and the query
string) to the upstream. A `{rest}` containing path traversal is rejected with
`400`. Request bodies are capped at 16 MiB. Upstream response headers, including
`mcp-session-id`, are passed back to the client.

chunks.title: MCP Gateway
chunks.heading: Errors
chunks.text:
| Status | Body message | Meaning |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `400` | `invalid request path` | the sub-path contains path traversal |
| `401` | `missing bearer token`, `invalid api key`, `invalid token` | no credential, an unknown key, or an identity token that fails verification |
| `403` | `api key disabled`, `tenant is not active`, or a schedule reason | the key or tenant is not allowed to call right now |
| `403` | `mcp server is disabled` | the server is registered but disabled |
| `404` | `mcp server '<name>' is not registered` | no MCP server under that name |
| `413` | `request body too large` | the body exceeds 16 MiB |
| `502` | `mcp upstream request failed` | the upstream MCP server could not be reached |
| `503` | `authentication backend unavailable`, `identity provisioning unavailable` | the credential lookup failed against Redis or Postgres |

An upstream that answers with its own error status (including 5xx) is passed back
to the client unchanged.

chunks.title: MCP Gateway
chunks.heading: Observability
chunks.text:
Per-call counts are exported as Prometheus metrics (server names are
low-cardinality):

- `obleth_mcp_requests_total{server, status="2xx|4xx|5xx"}`

Registry changes (create/update/delete) appear in the audit log. With OTLP
tracing enabled, each call produces an `mcp_request` span tagged with the server
name.

Operator alerts (delivered through **Settings → Alerts**):

- `mcp_upstream_request_failed` — the upstream could not be reached.
- `mcp_upstream_5xx_response` — the upstream answered with a 5xx status.
- `redis_mcp_lookup_failed` — the server registry lookup failed against Redis.
- `mcp_tool_discovery_failed` — the gateway's background tool-cache warm-up could
  not list a granted server's tools.

See [Alerting](/docs/operations/alerting) for delivery and cooldown.

chunks.title: MCP Gateway
chunks.heading: Overview
chunks.text:
obleth can front **MCP (Model Context Protocol) servers** with the same identity
layer it applies to LLM traffic. Clients authenticate once with an obleth API key
and reach any registered MCP server through a single endpoint —
`/mcp/{server}` — while obleth injects the upstream credential and records access.

This keeps obleth lean: as a reverse proxy it is transport-transparent — it does
**not** parse JSON-RPC, so any MCP-over-HTTP server (streamable-HTTP or SSE) works
unchanged.

obleth uses registered MCP servers in two ways:

1. **As an authenticated reverse proxy** — clients reach a server directly at
   `/mcp/{server}` and run tool calls themselves (this guide, below).
2. **As tools the gateway runs for a model** — grant a model one or more MCP
   servers and obleth injects their tools into the model's chat requests and
   executes the tool calls itself, looping until the model produces a final
   answer. This is the **gateway tool loop** ([below](#the-gateway-tool-loop)).

chunks.title: MCP Gateway
chunks.heading: Registering a server
chunks.text:
From the dashboard (**MCP Servers → Register**) or the Management API:

```bash
curl -X POST "${OBLETH_ADMIN_BASE_URL}/api/v1/mcp-servers" \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $OBLETH_ADMIN_TOKEN" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{
        "name": "github",
        "upstream_url": "https://mcp.githubcopilot.com/mcp",
        "auth_header": "Bearer ghp_…"
      }'
```

- `name` — the path segment clients use: `/mcp/github`.
- `upstream_url` — the MCP server's base URL.
- `auth_header` — optional full `Authorization` header value obleth injects toward
  the upstream (stored encrypted-at-rest in production). Clients never see it.

Other endpoints: `GET /api/v1/mcp-servers`, `GET/PUT/DELETE
/api/v1/mcp-servers/{id}`. All writes are audited and synced to every gateway
pod via Redis.

The `auth_header` is write-only. Responses report `auth_header_set: true` or
`false` in its place, and an update that omits the field keeps the stored value:

```json
{
  "id": "…",
  "name": "github",
  "upstream_url": "https://mcp.githubcopilot.com/mcp",
  "auth_header_set": true,
  "enabled": true,
  "created_at": "…",
  "updated_at": "…"
}
```

Deleting a server also strips it from the `tool_servers` grant of every model
that had it, so no model is left pointing at a server that no longer exists. The
affected model names are recorded on the audit entry.

chunks.title: MCP Gateway
chunks.heading: The gateway tool loop
chunks.text:
Beyond proxying, obleth can **run** an MCP server's tools on a model's behalf. A
client sends a plain OpenAI chat request and gets back a grounded final answer —
it never sees tool definitions or tool calls. obleth discovers the granted
servers' tools, injects them into the request, executes the model's tool calls
against the MCP upstream, appends the results, and re-asks the model, looping
(bounded) until the model answers.

```text
client ──▶ obleth                         (plain chat request, no tools)
             │  model is granted MCP servers + native function calling
             │  inject discovered tools, add the nudge
             ├──▶ model                    "I should search…" → tool_calls
             │  execute tool calls against the MCP server(s)
             ├──▶ MCP server               tools/call → result
             │  append results, re-ask
             ├──▶ model                    (loops up to max_turns)
             │◀── final answer
client ◀─────┘                            grounded answer (no tool_calls)
```

To turn it on:

1. **Register the MCP server** (above).
2. **Grant it to a model.** In the dashboard, open the model and tick the server
   under the **Tools** section; or via the API set `tool_servers` on the model.
   The model must have native `supports_function_calling` — the loop is skipped
   (with a logged warning) for models without it.
3. **Enable the loop globally** under **Settings → Boons → MCP tool loop →
   Enable gateway tool loo

chunks.title: MCP Gateway
chunks.heading: Verifying a server
chunks.text:
The gateway is transport-transparent, so a bad upstream URL or a rejected
credential only shows up when something actually calls the server. Two paths
verify a registration end-to-end, both driving the real MCP handshake
(`initialize` → `notifications/initialized` → `tools/list`) through the gateway
at `/mcp/{name}`:

- **Dashboard** — the MCP Servers page has a **Test** button per server. It
  reports reachability, the server's advertised name and protocol version, the
  tools it exposes, and the round-trip latency. Registering a new server runs
  the same probe immediately, so registration doubles as verification.
- **The Playground assistant (Charo)** — its `test_mcp` tool sweeps every registered server (or
  a named subset) and returns one pass/fail row per server with its tool list.
  See [Charo](/docs/guides/charo).

A name that is not registered comes back as a failure; a server that is
registered but disabled is skipped rather than probed. Probes authenticate as
the reserved internal identity, which is flagged synthetic, so verification
traffic stays out of usage and cost statistics.

chunks.title: Model Boons
chunks.heading: A/B compression from the API
chunks.text:
Two request headers let a client compare compression on a single request,
without touching any settings:

- `x-obleth-boons: off` — bypass all boons (the uncompressed baseline).
- `x-obleth-boons: lossy` — force the **lossy pass on for this request** even
  where the tenant hasn't opted in. The boon must still be granted to the model
  — the header widens a granted boon, it never enables an ungranted one.

Whenever the compression boon ran, the response carries an
`x-obleth-compression` header summarizing what it did:

```
x-obleth-compression: before=18423;after=11278;saved=7145
```

Diff the same request with and without the headers to measure savings
back-to-back — no dashboard or trace round-trip needed.
[`obench compression`](/docs/guides/benchmark-harness#compression-savings-obench-compression)
automates exactly this A/B across payload corpora.

chunks.title: Model Boons
chunks.heading: Behaviour and limits
chunks.text:
- **Sizes.** The tool schema offers the configured sizes; a requested size
  outside the list is clamped to the first entry.
- **Image count.** Each call produces at most the configured number of images
  (hard ceiling `4`), and the cap spans the whole request.
- **Attachment size.** Images attached to one reply are capped at 3 MiB in total;
  an image over the budget is dropped with a visible note rather than
  discarding the batch.
- **Fail-open.** An unregistered or disabled image model, an upstream failure,
  a timeout, or an empty response is reported back to the model as a failed
  receipt, and the model answers in prose. The request itself never fails
  because of the boon.
- **Structured output wins.** A request that also carries a `response_format`
  schema keeps its validated JSON: the generated images are not attached, and
  the response carries `x-obleth-boons-warning: image_suppressed_by_response_format`.
- **Billing.** Each generated image is billed per image against the tenant at
  the image model's `cost_per_image`, as an `image_generation_boon` usage row
  under the image model's name with `admission = boon`, and counts toward term
  budgets. An image that was generated is billed even when it is suppressed.

chunks.title: Model Boons
chunks.heading: Billing and attribution
chunks.text:
Every describe call is metered against the calling tenant and written to the
usage ledger as its own record:

- `model` is the **describer** model name (so its cost lands on the describer's
  line).
- `admission` is `boon` and `request_type` is `vision_boon`, so boon traffic is
  easy to isolate in the request log and cost breakdown.
- Cost is computed from the describer's `input_cost_per_token` /
  `output_cost_per_token` using the token usage the describer reports.

The original request is billed normally on top, against the target model.

chunks.title: Model Boons
chunks.heading: Enabling and granting it
chunks.text:
From the control plane, open **Settings → Boons → MCP tool loop** and turn on
**Enable gateway tool loop**, optionally adjusting **Max tool turns** (1–8,
default `4`), **Tool execution timeout** (default `30000` ms), and the **Tool
nudge**. Or via the Management API, which also sets the per-request deadline:

```bash
curl -X PUT http://localhost:9180/api/v1/settings/boons \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{
    "tool_loop_enabled": true,
    "tool_loop_max_turns": 4,
    "tool_loop_tool_timeout_ms": 30000,
    "tool_loop_deadline_secs": 300
  }'
```

`tool_loop_deadline_secs` is clamped to `1`–`3600`; omitting it or sending `0`
leaves the stored value unchanged.

Then grant the MCP servers to each model. In the dashboard, open the model and
tick the servers under its **Tools** section; or set `tool_servers` via the API:

```bash
curl -X PUT http://localhost:9180/api/v1/models/$MODEL_ID \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{ "tool_servers": ["searxng"] }'
```

Send `tool_loop_nudge` as `""` to reset it to the built-in default. See the
[Management API](/docs/reference/management-api#model-boons) for the full settings
shape.

Deleting an MCP server **strips its grant from every model that had it**, so a
stale name can't sit in a `tool_servers` list and fail tool discovery on every
request. To confirm a server actually answers before granting it, use the
dashboard's **Test** butto

chunks.title: Model Boons
chunks.heading: Enabling it
chunks.text:
From **Settings → Boons → Structured output**, turn on **Enable structured
output boon**, choose a **Fixer model**, and set the repair attempts and timeout. Or via the
Management API:

```bash
curl -X PUT http://localhost:9180/api/v1/settings/boons \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{
    "structured_output_enabled": true,
    "structured_output_fixer_model": "qwen3-235b",
    "structured_output_max_repair_attempts": 1,
    "structured_output_timeout_ms": 30000
  }'
```

`structured_output_max_repair_attempts` is clamped to a maximum of `3`. Send
`structured_output_fixer_model` as `""` to repair with the request's own model
instead of a dedicated fixer. Then grant `structured_output` to each model that
should be enforced.

chunks.title: Model Boons
chunks.heading: Enabling it
chunks.text:
From **Settings → Boons → Image generation**, turn on **Enable image generation
boon**, pick the **Image model**, and set the allowed sizes, images per call, and
timeout. Or via the Management API:

```bash
curl -X PUT http://localhost:9180/api/v1/settings/boons \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{
    "image_generation_enabled": true,
    "image_generation_model": "flux-schnell",
    "image_generation_allowed_sizes": ["512x512", "1024x1024"],
    "image_generation_max_images_per_request": 2,
    "image_generation_timeout_ms": 120000
  }'
```

| Field | Default | Notes |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `image_generation_enabled` | `false` | Master switch |
| `image_generation_model` | none | `model_name` of a registered `image` model; `""` clears it, which deactivates the boon |
| `image_generation_allowed_sizes` | `["512x512", "1024x1024"]` | An empty list resets to the default |
| `image_generation_max_images_per_request` | `2` | Clamped to `1`–`4`; `0` leaves the value unchanged |
| `image_generation_timeout_ms` | `120000` | Per generation call |
| `image_generation_tool_description` | built-in text | What the model reads when deciding to call the tool; `""` resets it |

Then grant `image_generation` to each function-calling chat model that should be
able to draw. For registering the image model itself, see
[Multi-modal Models](/docs/guides/multi-modal-models).

chunks.title: Model Boons
chunks.heading: Enabling it (global)
chunks.text:
Compression settings live in the `app_settings` store (key `boons`) and are
hot-reloadable. From the control plane, open the **Settings → Compression** tab —
it also shows live **neural sidecar status** (configured / reachable, plus the
model name and revision it reports) — or use the Management API:

```bash
curl -X PUT http://localhost:9180/api/v1/settings/boons \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{
    "compression_enabled": true,
    "compression_min_tokens": 128,
    "compression_max_segments": 64,
    "compression_max_lossy_segments": 4,
    "compression_code_compaction": false,
    "compression_dedup": false,
    "compression_compact_logs": false,
    "compression_allow_lossy": false,
    "compression_original_ttl_secs": 3600,
    "compression_neural_keep_ratio": 0.5
  }'
```

- `compression_min_tokens` (default `128`) — skip segments smaller than this; the
  overhead isn't worth it.
- `compression_max_segments` (default `64`) — cap on lossless segments compacted
  per request.
- `compression_max_lossy_segments` (default `4`) — cap on dedup + lossy segments
  per request (a guard against over-rewriting a single request).
- `compression_code_compaction` (default `false`) — the global default for code
  compaction; a tenant policy overrides it.
- `compression_dedup` / `compression_compact_logs` / `compression_allow_lossy`
  (all default `false`) — global defaults for the three per-piece toggles
  (cross-turn dedup, near-l

chunks.title: Model Boons
chunks.heading: Enabling the boon
chunks.text:
Vision boon settings live in the `app_settings` store (key `boons`) and are
hot-reloadable — the proxy picks up changes within its refresh interval, no
restart required.

From the control plane, open **Settings → Boons → Vision**:

- **Enable vision boon** — the master switch.
- **Describer model** — a dropdown of your vision-capable models.
- **Describe prompt** — the instruction sent to the describer.
- **Max images per request** — cap on how many images are described per request
  (default `6`).
- **Describe timeout (ms)** — per-image timeout (default `30000`).

Or via the Management API:

```bash
curl -X PUT http://localhost:9180/api/v1/settings/boons \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{
    "vision_enabled": true,
    "vision_fallback_model": "glm-4-5v",
    "vision_describe_prompt": "Describe this image in thorough, faithful detail: all visible text (verbatim), UI elements, code, diagrams, charts, and layout.",
    "vision_max_images": 6,
    "vision_timeout_ms": 30000
  }'
```

Send `vision_fallback_model` as `""` to clear the describer (which deactivates
the boon, since no describer is set). See the
[Management API](/docs/reference/management-api) for the full settings shape.

> **The boon is disabled by default.** If you configure a describer but leave
> **Enable vision boon** off, images pass straight through to the target model —
> which, if it is text-only, will typically reject them. Make sure the master
> switch

chunks.title: Model Boons
chunks.heading: Fail-open, billing, and observability
chunks.text:
- **Fail-open.** Redis unavailable or a parse error skips that segment; the boon
  never blocks or fails a request.
- **Billing.** Compression makes **no helper-model calls**, so it adds no
  per-segment usage charges — the savings simply lower the upstream token bill.
- **Savings & spans.** Tokens saved are counted in the
  `obleth_compression_tokens_saved_total` metric, and the tracer records a single
  `boon:compression` span with `json_compacted`, `dedup_refs`, `lossy_segments`,
  and before/after token totals.

chunks.title: Model Boons
chunks.heading: Fail-open by design
chunks.text:
The vision boon never blocks or fails a request. If the describer is
unreachable, returns an error, times out, or returns an empty description, the
affected image is **left unchanged** and the request is forwarded as-is. A flaky
describer must not take down traffic the target model might still handle.

Each image is described independently, so one failed image does not discard the
descriptions already produced for the others in the same request.

chunks.title: Model Boons
chunks.heading: Granting and tuning per tenant
chunks.text:
Grant the boon to a model by adding `compression` to its `boons` list (dashboard:
**Models** → a row → **Boons** → **compression**, or `PUT /models/{id}` with
`{ "boons": ["compression"] }`).

Each tenant then controls **which pieces** apply via a per-tenant policy. In the
dashboard, open a tenant and use the **Compression** tab — five independent
toggles: **Enabled** (master), **Code compaction**, **Cross-turn dedup**,
**Log compaction**, and **Allow lossy**. Or via the Management API:

```bash
curl -X PATCH http://localhost:9180/api/v1/tenants/$ID/compression \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{ "policy": { "enabled": true, "code_compaction": true, "dedup": true, "compact_logs": true, "allow_lossy": true } }'
```

Send `{ "policy": null }` to clear a tenant's policy and fall back to the global
defaults. **A tenant with no policy inherits the global per-piece defaults**
(`compression_dedup` / `compression_compact_logs` / `compression_allow_lossy` /
`compression_code_compaction` from **Settings → Compression**). All ship `false`,
so out of the box a policy-less tenant gets lossless structural compaction only —
nothing lossy happens until an operator flips a global default or the tenant opts
in with its own policy.

chunks.title: Model Boons
chunks.heading: Granting the boon to a model
chunks.text:
The global switch turns the vision boon *on*; each model then **opts in**
individually. A model only receives a boon when its `boons` list contains that
boon's name — nothing is granted by default, so you choose exactly which
text-only models should fall back to the describer.

From the dashboard, open a model's config and tick the boon under the **Boons**
group (**Models** → a row → **Boons** → **vision**). Via the Management API, set
the `boons` array on create or update:

```bash
curl -X PUT http://localhost:9180/api/v1/models/$MODEL_ID \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{ "boons": ["vision"] }'
```

`boons` is a fixed-vocabulary list (`vision`, `structured_output`, `compression`,
`knowledge`, `image_generation`, `speculation`) stored per model. Values are
trimmed and lowercased, and unknown values are dropped on write. Leave it empty
(the default) to keep a model boon-free — images sent to a text-only model with
no boon are forwarded unchanged.

chunks.title: Model Boons
chunks.heading: How boons work
chunks.text:
A few rules apply to every boon:

- **Opt-in, twice.** A boon never fires unless it is **enabled globally**
  (**Settings → Boons**, or **Settings → Compression** and **Settings →
  Knowledge** for those two; stored in `app_settings` and hot-reloaded within
  15 seconds) *and* the target model has the boon in its per-model `boons` list.
  Nothing is granted by default. The model form shows a warning when a granted
  boon is switched off globally. Most boons also need their helper configured
  before the global switch has any effect: vision needs a describer, image
  generation needs an image model, and knowledge needs collections attached to
  the model.
- **Native capability wins.** The vision and structured-output boons step aside
  when the model already has the capability — vision skips models flagged
  `supports_vision`, structured output skips `supports_response_schema`. The
  tool loop and image generation work the other way round: they *require*
  `supports_function_calling`, because the model has to call the tools.
- **Fail-open, always.** Any error — no helper model configured, an upstream
  failure, a timeout, an unparseable reply — leaves the request or response
  unchanged. A flaky helper must never block traffic the target model might still
  handle on its own. Speculation's form of this is *abstaining*: on any doubt,
  the target model answers normally.
- **Applied in order, composed per request.** For a single chat request obleth
  applies vision, captures the

chunks.title: Model Boons
chunks.heading: How it works
chunks.text:
1. **Discover & inject.** obleth fetches each granted server's tool list (cached)
   and merges the definitions into the request's `tools` array. For plain chat
   clients it also injects a system **nudge** so the model actually reaches for a
   tool when a question needs external information.
2. **Execute & loop.** When the model returns `tool_calls`, obleth executes each
   one against its MCP server, appends the result as a `tool` message, and
   re-dispatches the conversation. It repeats until the model answers with no
   tool calls, or until `max_turns` is reached — at which point it strips the
   tools and asks the model to conclude from what it gathered, so a plain chat
   client never receives unexpected `tool_calls`.
3. **Bounded & efficient.** One MCP session is opened per server for the whole
   request (a rate-limited server sees a single initialization, not one per
   call), and a session that fails is not retried within the same request. Each
   tool result is truncated to 16,000 characters to bound context growth. At
   most 16 tool calls are executed from a single model turn — excess calls get
   an error result instead — and the whole loop stops dispatching once its
   per-request deadline (`tool_loop_deadline_secs`, default `300`, maximum
   `3600`) elapses. A server whose tool list cannot be fetched is skipped for
   45 seconds rather than retried on every request.

chunks.title: Model Boons
chunks.heading: How it works
chunks.text:
1. **Request.** obleth removes the `response_format` field and injects a system
   section instructing the model to reply with a single JSON document — the
   provided JSON Schema for `json_schema`, or a generic "valid JSON object"
   instruction for `json_object`. Schemas larger than 64 KB are rendered into the
   prompt but **not** validated (a guard against pathological documents).
2. **Response.** obleth extracts the JSON document from the reply (tolerating
   markdown fences and stray prose) and validates it against the schema. If it
   passes, the canonical JSON replaces the message content.
3. **Repair.** If validation fails, obleth re-prompts a **fixer model** (the
   configured one, or the request's own model when none is set) with the invalid
   output and the validation errors, up to `max_repair_attempts` times. Each
   repair call is billed to the tenant as a `structured_output_boon` record.
4. **Fail-open.** If every attempt still fails, the original completion passes
   through unchanged and the response carries
   `x-obleth-boons-warning: structured_output_validation_failed`.

chunks.title: Model Boons
chunks.heading: Neural prose scoring (optional compressor sidecar)
chunks.text:
The lossy prose pass ranks sentences by importance and keeps the top ones. By
default it uses a built-in deterministic heuristic. If you'd rather use a
**trained extractive scorer**, deploy the **compressor** sidecar — a small
self-hosted service that scores sentence importance with a trained ModernBERT-based
