chunks.title: OpenAI-compatible API
chunks.heading: TypeScript / Node.js

chunks.title: Playground
chunks.heading: Chat
chunks.text:
Choose one model to chat with, or add up to four and send each prompt to all of
them. Answers appear side by side, and each model keeps its own conversation
context. **Continue with this model** narrows the conversation to one of them.

The model picker offers:

| Entry | What it is |
| --- | --- |
| **Assistant** | The built-in assistant, with guided tools and benchmarks. See [Charo](/docs/guides/charo) |
| **Automatic routing** | The `auto` model: the gateway chooses. See [Auto Model Routing](/docs/guides/auto-model-routing) |
| Registered `chat` and `image` models | Called directly by name |

The **Parameters** panel holds the system prompt, temperature (0–2), and max
output tokens (1–131072), shared by every model in the session. Leaving a field
blank uses the model's default. A prompt can carry one attached image (up to
6 MB) via the paperclip or drag and drop.

When a chat model with the [image generation boon](/docs/guides/model-boons)
returns an image, the image is shown in the answer but not replayed to the model
as data on later turns. The model receives a short text receipt of the
`generate_image` call instead; a vision-capable model is also sent the most
recent generated image as an image part, so follow-ups such as "make it darker"
still work.

chunks.title: Playground
chunks.heading: How Playground traffic is handled
chunks.text:
Chat, Image, and Verdicts requests go through the normal data plane as the
reserved internal control-plane tenant. Admission, budgets, boons, and
telemetry apply exactly as they would for a real client, so a boon configured on
a model fires in the Playground. The internal tenant is
[synthetic](/docs/guides/control-plane#synthetic-tenants): its traffic is billed
under request type `benchmark` and excluded from usage statistics by default.
The key it uses stays on the dashboard server and never reaches the browser.

The dashboard reaches the data plane at `OBLETH_PROXY_BASE_URL` (default
`http://localhost:8080`).

chunks.title: Playground
chunks.heading: Image
chunks.text:
The Image workspace drives `POST /v1/images/generations` on an `image` model
directly, so every generation parameter is settable:

- Prompt, model, size (`256x256`, `512x512`, `768x768`, or `1024x1024`), and
  images per generation (1–4)
- In **Parameters**: negative prompt, steps (1–150), and seed. These are not
  part of the OpenAI images API; they are passed through to the backend, which
  may ignore them
- Each result shows its latency and cost (the model's `cost_per_image`), can be
  downloaded, and can be retried with the same parameters

The size list is independent of the image generation boon's allowed sizes,
because the workspace calls the image model directly rather than through a chat
model.

chunks.title: Playground
chunks.heading: Overview
chunks.text:
The Playground is a dashboard workspace for exercising models through the
gateway. Open it from **Operations → Playground**. It requires the `admin`
role, and it is available while **Enable Playground in the dashboard** is on
under **Settings → Assistant**.

The Playground has four modes, chosen in the session toolbar: **Chat**,
**Router**, **Image**, and **Verdicts**. Each mode keeps its request parameters
behind the **Parameters** button.

chunks.title: Playground
chunks.heading: Router
chunks.text:
Router mode shows how the auto router would score a prompt, without sending it
to a model. Paste the request to route; the gateway returns the decision from
`POST /api/v1/router/simulate`.

- The result lists the classified difficulty and routing tags with their
  source, the temperature and random draw, classifier latency, and each scored
  candidate
- Candidates removed by a hard filter appear under **Not considered** with the
  reason, such as `disabled`, `auto_excluded` (the model is not eligible for
  auto), `unhealthy`, `context_window`, `vision`, or `tenant_allowlist`
- **Live classifier** (on by default) classifies the prompt with the configured
  classifier model, as serving does. Unchecked, a keyword heuristic is used and
  its tags can differ from what a real request would get
- The **Weights** sliders (capacity, cost, and tag weight, temperature, default
  soft cap, and difficulty tiering) start from the saved settings. Editing them
  runs a second simulation and compares the result against the live weights,
  stating whether the chosen model changes. Sliders only simulate; **Apply to
  gateway** is the only control that saves them to **Settings → Routing**

The **Parameters** panel sets the simulated request's tenant id, effort, max
output tokens, and whether it needs function calling, forced tool choice, or a
response schema.

chunks.title: Playground
chunks.heading: Sessions
chunks.text:
- Sessions are stored in the browser, scoped to your account. The session list
  holds up to 50 sessions; each can be renamed, deleted, or exported as JSON
  with the export button (`playground-session.json`)
- A session remembers its mode, its models, and each mode's form inputs, so a
  prompt survives a reload and a switch between modes
- Router and Verdicts results and generated images are kept in memory only and
  are not saved with the session

chunks.title: Playground
chunks.heading: Verdicts
chunks.text:
Verdicts mode is a builder for the [Verdicts API](/docs/guides/verdicts). Enter
the state text, choose a chat model, and add up to 32 questions. Each question
has an id, instructions, and a type:

| Type | Criteria |
| --- | --- |
| `boolean` | Optional descriptions of what yes and no mean |
| `choice` | Up to 26 named options, each with an optional description |
| `score` | Up to 10 level descriptions |

**Run** sends the request and shows each verdict's value, probabilities, and
confidence, with token usage and latency.

chunks.title: Priority Boost
chunks.heading: Audit trail
chunks.text:
Every weight change is recorded in `audit_log`:

```bash
curl http://localhost:9180/api/v1/audit \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" | jq '.[] | select(.action == "update_weight")'
```

Each entry includes the actor (admin token identifier), the tenant ID, the new weight, and a timestamp. The previous value is not recorded — read it from the preceding entry.

chunks.title: Priority Boost
chunks.heading: Boosting via the API
chunks.text:
```bash
# Double the weight from 100 to 200
curl -X PATCH http://localhost:9180/api/v1/tenants/$TID/weight \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"weight": 200}'
```

The response is the updated tenant object. The change:
1. Is written to Postgres (`tenants.weight`) and logged to `audit_log`.
2. Is synced to Redis (the `ResolvedKey` JSON is updated).
3. Triggers a pub/sub invalidation on `obleth:invalidate` to evict the key from every pod's moka cache.

Effective latency: the change is live within milliseconds of the API call returning.

chunks.title: Priority Boost
chunks.heading: Boosting via the dashboard
chunks.text:
Navigate to **Tenants** → select a tenant → open the **Controls** tab → drag the **Fairshare weight** slider (or type a value) → **Apply**. The estimated share updates live as you change the weight.

The dashboard calls `PATCH /api/v1/tenants/{id}/weight` under the hood.

chunks.title: Priority Boost
chunks.heading: Group weights (hierarchical mode)
chunks.text:
Under `OBLETH_FAIRSHARE_ALGORITHM=hierarchical` (the default), you can also adjust group weights:

```bash
# Boost the entire prod group
curl -X PATCH http://localhost:9180/api/v1/fairshare/groups/prod/weight \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"weight": 1000}'
```

This changes how much of each model's pool the `prod` group receives, affecting all tenants in that group simultaneously. The change re-pushes only the keys of tenants in that group to Redis, and is audited as `update_fairshare_group_weight`.

Hierarchical mode first splits each pool's slots among groups by group weight, then ranks tenants inside the winning group on the same `served / weight` score. Group shares cap **contended** demand only: capacity a quiet group leaves idle is lent to whoever is queued, and the group reclaims its share as the borrowed requests finish.

chunks.title: Priority Boost
chunks.heading: Incident response
chunks.text:
Your production chatbot is being saturated by a batch analytics job that someone started at peak time:

```bash
# Find the batch tenant
curl http://localhost:9180/api/v1/tenants -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" | jq '.[] | select(.name == "batch-analytics") | .id'

# Find the chatbot tenant
CHATBOT_ID=...
BATCH_ID=...

# Boost chatbot to 10x the batch job
curl -X PATCH http://localhost:9180/api/v1/tenants/$CHATBOT_ID/weight \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"weight": 1000}'

# Throttle the batch job
curl -X PATCH http://localhost:9180/api/v1/tenants/$BATCH_ID/weight \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"weight": 10}'
```

The scheduler picks this up on the next admission decision. No restart, no config file, no deployment.

chunks.title: Priority Boost
chunks.heading: Overview
chunks.text: Priority boosts are one of obleth's headline features: you can change a tenant's weight at runtime and it takes effect on the **next admission decision**, without restarting obleth or reloading any config.

chunks.title: Priority Boost
chunks.heading: Restoring normal weights
chunks.text:
```bash
curl -X PATCH http://localhost:9180/api/v1/tenants/$CHATBOT_ID/weight \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"weight": 200}'

curl -X PATCH http://localhost:9180/api/v1/tenants/$BATCH_ID/weight \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"weight": 50}'
```

chunks.title: Priority Boost
chunks.heading: What weight controls
chunks.text:
Every model has its own scheduling pool. Within each pool the scheduler admits the waiting tenant with the lowest **share score**, `share_score = served_tokens / weight`, so a higher weight burns fair share more slowly and translates directly into a larger share under contention. A tenant with `weight=500` gets roughly 10× the throughput of one with `weight=50` on a saturated model. Weight does not affect:
- Token budget (TPM) — that's `tokens_per_minute`
- Per-tenant concurrency cap — that's `max_in_flight`, enforced per model

Tenant weight is separate from key weight. Each API key carries its own `weight`
(default 100) that splits the tenant's share among the tenant's own keys; raising
a tenant's weight raises the share of all its keys together, while raising one
key's weight shifts share toward that key inside the tenant. To boost a single
key, send its full field set to `PUT /api/v1/keys/{id}` with a new `weight` (see
[API Keys](/docs/guides/api-keys#per-key-fairshare-weight-and-concurrency)), or
edit it inline on the **Fairshare** page's tenant workbench. The full model is on
[Fairshare Engine](/docs/concepts/fairshare-engine).

chunks.title: Production Checklist
chunks.heading: Capacity planning
chunks.text:
- [ ] Size each model's pool: set `max_in_flight` on every route to what its backend can serve concurrently. Routes without one use `OBLETH_DEFAULT_MODEL_MAX_IN_FLIGHT` (32). Use **static** capacity with a manual cap for cloud APIs.
- [ ] Keep `OBLETH_GLOBAL_MAX_IN_FLIGHT` (default 1024) above the sum of the pools you expect to be busy at once. It is a total ceiling, not a fairness input; if it binds before the pools do, the gateway logs a warning at start-up. See [Fairshare Engine](/docs/concepts/fairshare-engine).
- [ ] For self-hosted chat/embedding models, run [capacity auto-tune](/docs/guides/capacity-autotune) in a quiet window before go-live (avoid probing busy production models — the probe sends real upstream load).
- [ ] Decide the obleth replica count deliberately. Each pod enforces its own pools and ceiling, so the concurrency reaching an upstream is replicas × that model's pool size. `values-production.yaml` runs 3 replicas at `globalMaxInFlight: 256` per pod; size per-model pools with the replica count in mind.
- [ ] Leave `hpa.enabled=false` when the replica count is load-bearing — an autoscaled replica count moves the aggregate concurrency with no config change. To autoscale anyway, size the pools for `maxReplicas` and accept that the upstream is under-subscribed below full scale-out. See [Scaling](/docs/operations/scaling).
- [ ] Review `OBLETH_ADMISSION_TIMEOUT_SECS` (default 60). A request queued longer than this returns 503 with `Retry-After: 5`; make sure

chunks.title: Production Checklist
chunks.heading: Datastores
chunks.text:
- [ ] **Postgres**: Use a managed service (CloudNativePG, RDS, Cloud SQL) or HA setup. Do not use the bundled Docker Compose Postgres in production.
- [ ] **Redis**: Password required (`REDIS_PASSWORD` in Compose, `redis.password` in Helm, or embedded in `OBLETH_REDIS_URL` as `redis://:PASSWORD@host:6379`). For HA, use a managed or operator-run Redis that presents a **single primary endpoint** with failover; clustered Redis is not supported because the gateway runs multi-key Lua scripts. obleth treats Redis as a hot cache — keys, models, and MCP servers are re-pushed from Postgres every `OBLETH_REDIS_REWARM_SECS` (300 s) and after each reconnect — so a failover loses no configuration.
- [ ] **ClickHouse**: Use a replicated cluster or a managed ClickHouse service. The gateway boots without ClickHouse and spills usage rows to its local write-ahead file until the ledger returns.
- [ ] All connection URLs set via environment variables or Kubernetes Secrets, not hardcoded.
- [ ] **On Kubernetes:** point the chart at pre-created Secrets (`obleth.existingSecret` / `controlPlane.existingSecret`) so credentials never enter values files or `--set`/CLI history. The obleth Secret must carry `OBLETH_REDIS_URL`, plus `POSTGRES_PASSWORD` / `REDIS_PASSWORD` for any bundled datastore. See [Helm Values — Pre-created Secrets](/docs/reference/helm-values#pre-created-secrets-existingsecret).

chunks.title: Production Checklist
chunks.heading: Initial configuration
chunks.text:
- [ ] Create your tenant hierarchy and fairshare groups before sending production traffic.
- [ ] Register all models (`POST /api/v1/models`, the dashboard, or a manifest import — see [Model Registry](/docs/guides/model-registry)) — a fresh install has none. Use `api_base` ending in `/v1` and the bare `upstream_model` name.
- [ ] Mint tenant API keys — there is no shared proxy key; each client needs its own `sk_...` secret. Set key `weight` where one tenant's users need different shares.
- [ ] Set conservative `tokens_per_minute` quotas initially; increase based on observed usage.
- [ ] If Claude Code or Anthropic SDK clients will connect, set **Default model for Anthropic clients** (Settings → Routing).
- [ ] Verify the audit log is recording changes: `GET /api/v1/audit`.

chunks.title: Production Checklist
chunks.heading: Kubernetes workload hardening
chunks.text:
These are toggles in the Helm chart, defaulted sensibly and tuned for the
[Production](/docs/guides/self-hosting#scenario-4-production) profile.

- [ ] **Restricted Pod Security Standard.** The stateless workloads (obleth, control-plane, benchmark-backend) run with `runAsNonRoot`, `seccompProfile: RuntimeDefault`, `allowPrivilegeEscalation: false`, and all capabilities dropped. On by default — verify they aren't overridden.
- [ ] **Spread across nodes.** `affinity.antiAffinity: soft` (or `hard` on multi-node clusters) so a single node failure can't take the whole data plane down.
- [ ] **PodDisruptionBudget.** `podDisruptionBudget.enabled: true` keeps a minimum number of obleth pods available during node drains and rolling upgrades. It renders only when the minimum replica count is greater than 1, so a single-pod deployment never blocks a drain.
- [ ] **NetworkPolicy.** `networkPolicy.enabled: true` restricts the bundled datastore ports to the pods that need them and the Management API port to the dashboard and provisioner pods. Requires a CNI that enforces NetworkPolicy.

chunks.title: Production Checklist
chunks.heading: Monitoring
chunks.text:
- [ ] Prometheus scraping `:9091/metrics`.
- [ ] Alert on `obleth_queue_depth` > threshold (admission saturation).
- [ ] Alert on `obleth_telemetry_dropped` > 0 (spill pressure).
- [ ] Alert on `obleth_requests_total{status="5xx"}` spike (upstream failures).
- [ ] Configure gateway alerts (Slack or email) under Settings → Alerts. See [Alerting](/docs/operations/alerting).
- [ ] Enable `serviceMonitor.enabled=true` if using Prometheus Operator.
- [ ] (Optional) Set `OBLETH_OTEL_ENDPOINT` for distributed tracing.

chunks.title: Production Checklist
chunks.heading: Overview
chunks.text: This checklist covers the minimum steps to harden an obleth deployment for production traffic.

chunks.title: Production Checklist
chunks.heading: Pre-launch testing
chunks.text:
- [ ] Run the benchmark harness against staging to verify fairshare behavior.
- [ ] Run [`obench score`](/docs/guides/benchmark-harness#the-deployment-scorecard-obench-score) against staging for a graded readiness scorecard, and keep the run as the baseline later runs are diffed against.
- [ ] Run the chaos harness against staging to verify fail-open and WAL replay.
- [ ] Verify ClickHouse rows appear after test requests.
- [ ] Smoke test the dashboard against the production Management API.
- [ ] Confirm [backups](/docs/operations/backup-restore) of Postgres and ClickHouse, and test a restore.

chunks.title: Production Checklist
chunks.heading: Reliability and shutdown
chunks.text:
- [ ] Decide on `OBLETH_FAIL_OPEN`: `true` (admit requests when the budget check cannot reach Redis) or `false` (strict budget enforcement). Key lookup never fails open: a Redis error there returns 503.
- [ ] Give the telemetry write-ahead file (`OBLETH_WAL_PATH`) a writable location with enough disk for a ClickHouse outage. The Helm chart mounts a volume at `/var/lib/obleth` for it; on other platforms use a persistent path rather than `/tmp`. Usage rows are spilled there on every ClickHouse failure, regardless of `OBLETH_FAIL_OPEN`.
- [ ] Keep the orchestrator's stop timeout above the drain window. On SIGTERM obleth drains in-flight requests for up to `OBLETH_SHUTDOWN_GRACE_SECS` (300) and then flushes telemetry; the chart sets `terminationGracePeriodSeconds: 345` with a 5 s `preStop` sleep and Compose sets `stop_grace_period: 345s`. If you raise the grace, raise those by the same amount. See [Shutdown & Timeouts](/docs/operations/graceful-shutdown-and-timeouts).
- [ ] After any direct Redis maintenance (flush, restore, failover to an empty replica), run `POST /api/v1/resync` (Settings → Data → **Reconcile cache**) rather than waiting for the next rewarm.

chunks.title: Production Checklist
chunks.heading: Secrets
chunks.text:
- [ ] `OBLETH_ADMIN_TOKEN`: strong random token (≥32 chars). No default — the gateway will not start without it. Use a Kubernetes Secret or Vault. Never commit to source control.
- [ ] `OBLETH_ENCRYPTION_KEY`: set to a base64 32-byte key (`openssl rand -base64 32`) so model `api_key` and MCP `auth_header` are AES-256-GCM encrypted at rest. Without it they are stored in plaintext. The Management API never returns them either way; responses carry `api_key_set` / `auth_header_set`.
- [ ] `OBLETH_API_KEY_PEPPER`: (optional, recommended) set a stable secret to strengthen API-key hashes against a DB leak.
- [ ] `DASHBOARD_SESSION_SECRET`: required, ≥32 characters. The dashboard fails closed if missing or too short.
- [ ] `DASHBOARD_ADMIN_EMAIL` (valid email) / `DASHBOARD_PASSWORD` (≥8 chars): required to seed the break-glass admin. Email sign-up is closed; this admin is seeded directly on first boot.
- [ ] `DATABASE_URL`: required for the control plane — the auth tables (users, sessions) live here. Point it at the same database the gateway uses.
- [ ] `TRUSTED_ORIGINS`: set when the dashboard is reached by a LAN IP or an alternate hostname rather than the exact `BETTER_AUTH_URL` — comma-separated origins. Without it those logins are rejected as invalid-origin. `*` trusts every origin and belongs on trusted private networks only.
- [ ] ClickHouse and Postgres passwords: required (no default in Compose/Helm).
- [ ] If running the Compose `observability` profile: set `GRAFANA_ADMIN_PA

chunks.title: Production Checklist
chunks.heading: TLS and network
chunks.text:
- [ ] TLS terminated at HAProxy or your Ingress controller — the data plane is HTTP-only.
- [ ] obleth data plane (`:8080`) reachable only from HAProxy/Ingress, not from the internet.
- [ ] Admin port (`:9180`) **not publicly accessible** — restrict to internal network or VPN. The admin token is the only auth and is compared in constant time.
- [ ] Metrics port (`:9091`) accessible only to your Prometheus scraper.
- [ ] **On Docker Compose:** the stack publishes the Management API (9180), metrics (9091), Postgres (5432), Redis (6379), ClickHouse (8123/9000), Prometheus (9090), and Jaeger (16686/4317/4318) on `127.0.0.1` only. The data plane (8088), dashboard (3002), and the `edge` HAProxy (80) are published on all interfaces — put a TLS-terminating proxy or firewall in front of those. See [Endpoints & Ports](/docs/reference/endpoints-and-ports).
- [ ] SSRF policy: default (local-first) mode allows private/LAN `api_base` targets; link-local and cloud metadata are always blocked. For strict mode (`OBLETH_BLOCK_PRIVATE_NETWORKS=1`), set `OBLETH_ALLOWED_PRIVATE_CIDRS` to trusted internal ranges (e.g. `10.0.0.0/8`) so cluster Services can be registered.
- [ ] Control plane served over HTTPS; verify the built-in security headers (CSP, HSTS, `X-Frame-Options`) and login rate limiting are active.

chunks.title: Quotas & Rate Limits
chunks.heading: How the limits interact
chunks.text:
The limits are enforced independently, at different layers. A request can be held
or rejected by any of them:

| Check | Where | Outcome if exceeded |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Model pool, global ceiling, per-tenant and per-key `max_in_flight` | Fairshare scheduler | Queued; `503 timed out waiting for model capacity` (with `Retry-After: 5`) after `OBLETH_ADMISSION_TIMEOUT_SECS` (default 60) |
| Per-key term budget | Redis Lua | `403 api key term budget exhausted` |
| Token budget (`tokens_per_minute`) | Redis Lua | `429 token budget exceeded` |
| Tenant term budget (`budget_tokens` / `budget_cost_usd`) | Redis Lua | `403 tenant term budget exhausted` |

Concurrency limits queue the request (it may be admitted later, up to the
admission timeout); the TPM and term budgets are hard rejections. Budgets are
checked after admission, so a rejected request releases its fairshare permit
and is not proxied.

If Redis cannot run a budget check, the outcome follows `OBLETH_FAIL_OPEN`. Fail
open (the default) admits the request without a reservation and raises a
`redis_budget_reserve_failed_open` or `redis_key_budget_reserve_failed_open`
alert. Fail closed rejects it with `503 budget check failed` or
`503 key budget check failed` and raises the matching `*_failed_closed` alert.

chunks.title: Quotas & Rate Limits
chunks.heading: Monitoring quota utilization
chunks.text:
Query ClickHouse for TPM utilization per tenant:

```sql
SELECT
  tenant_id,
  sum(input_tokens + output_tokens) AS tokens_used,
  count() AS requests,
  countIf(admission = 'rejected') AS rejected
FROM usage
WHERE ts_ms > (toUnixTimestamp(now() - INTERVAL 1 HOUR) * 1000)
GROUP BY tenant_id
ORDER BY tokens_used DESC
```

Or use the Management API:

```bash
curl "http://localhost:9180/api/v1/usage?since_ms=$(date -d '1 hour ago' +%s000)" \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" | jq .
```

chunks.title: Quotas & Rate Limits
chunks.heading: Overview
chunks.text:
obleth has two independent throttling mechanisms per tenant: a **token budget** (TPM) and an optional **concurrency cap** (`max_in_flight`). They operate at different layers and can be used together.

Both are set per tenant from the dashboard on the **Tenants → Controls** tab, under **Safety limits** — or via the Management API shown below:

chunks.title: Quotas & Rate Limits
chunks.heading: Per-tenant concurrency cap (max_in_flight)
chunks.text:
`max_in_flight` is an optional hard cap on how many requests a single tenant can have in flight simultaneously. It is enforced **per model**: a tenant with `max_in_flight=10` may hold up to 10 requests on each model's pool at once.

With `max_in_flight=null` (default), a tenant is only constrained by the model's pool size, the total `OBLETH_GLOBAL_MAX_IN_FLIGHT` ceiling, and the fairshare scheduler. Setting it adds an additional per-tenant ceiling. Individual keys can carry their own `max_in_flight` as well; see [API Keys](/docs/guides/api-keys#per-key-fairshare-weight-and-concurrency).

chunks.title: Quotas & Rate Limits
chunks.heading: Reserve, then reconcile
chunks.text:
Term budgets are enforced atomically in Redis so concurrent requests cannot
collectively overshoot a cap:

1. **Reserve at admission.** Before dispatch, the request's estimated tokens and
   cost are reserved against the cap in `obleth:term_reserved:{scope}`, next to
   the committed usage in `obleth:term_usage:{scope}`. A request whose reservation
   would exceed the cap is rejected.
2. **Reconcile at completion.** Settlement releases the reservation and commits
   the actual usage exactly once.
3. **Stale reservations expire.** A reservation that never settles (for example,
   after a crash) expires after 10 minutes.

What is charged:

- **Failed requests bill nothing.** An upstream failure without a usage block
  records zero tokens and zero cost, and a `502` or `504` after exhausted retries
  refunds the reservation in full.
- **Helper calls count.** Gateway helper calls made on a request's behalf —
  vision descriptions, structured-output repairs, tool-loop turns, speculative
  drafts and verification, image generation, and guardrails classification —
  are committed to the same tenant and key term budgets. Knowledge-base query
  embeddings are not.

The gateway raises a `term_budget_warn:<tenant_id>` alert when a tenant reaches
80% of a cap and `term_budget_exhausted:<tenant_id>` at 100%; the per-key
equivalents are `key_term_budget_warn:<key_id>` and
`key_term_budget_exhausted:<key_id>`.

An individual API key can carry its own term budget with the same three fields,
e

chunks.title: Quotas & Rate Limits
chunks.heading: Setting max_in_flight
chunks.text:
```bash
curl -X PUT http://localhost:9180/api/v1/tenants/$TID/quota \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{
    "tokens_per_minute": 2000000,
    "max_in_flight": 10
  }'
```

Remove the cap:

```bash
curl -X PUT http://localhost:9180/api/v1/tenants/$TID/quota \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"tokens_per_minute": 2000000, "max_in_flight": null}'
```

chunks.title: Quotas & Rate Limits
chunks.heading: Setting TPM at creation
chunks.text:
```bash
curl -X POST http://localhost:9180/api/v1/tenants \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{
    "name": "chatbot",
    "weight": 500,
    "tokens_per_minute": 2000000
  }'
```

chunks.title: Quotas & Rate Limits
chunks.heading: Term budgets (cumulative caps)
chunks.text:
`tokens_per_minute` is a *rate* limit; a **term budget** is a *cumulative* cap on
how much a tenant may consume over a longer period. It is independent of the
per-minute bucket and is the right tool for a monthly spend ceiling or a fixed
trial allowance.

A term budget has three parts:

| Field | Purpose |
| --- | --- |
| `budget_tokens` | Optional cap on total tokens for the period. |
| `budget_cost_usd` | Optional cap on total USD cost (using per-model pricing) for the period. |
| `budget_period` | `lifetime`, `monthly`, or `term`. `monthly` rolls over each calendar month in the tenant's configured timezone; `term` resets when the budget's start date changes; `lifetime` never resets. |

Either cap (or both) may be set. When usage for the current period meets either
cap, the data plane returns `403 tenant term budget exhausted` until the period
rolls over or you raise the cap.

chunks.title: Quotas & Rate Limits
chunks.heading: Token budget (tokens_per_minute)
chunks.text:
`tokens_per_minute` is a token-bucket rate limit. It controls how many tokens a tenant can consume in a sustained period.

**Token bucket mechanics:**
- Capacity (burst ceiling) = `tokens_per_minute`
- Refill rate = `tokens_per_minute / 60000` tokens per millisecond
- A tenant that's been idle can consume up to `tokens_per_minute` tokens in a single burst
- After the burst, the bucket refills at the sustained rate

When the bucket is empty, the next request that would exceed it gets `429 token budget exceeded`. The fairshare permit is released and the request is not proxied.

chunks.title: Quotas & Rate Limits
chunks.heading: TPM sizing guidance
chunks.text:
| Use case | Suggested TPM |
| --- | --- |
| Internal dev/test tenant | 50,000–200,000 |
| Single chat user | 100,000–500,000 |
| Production chatbot service | 1,000,000–5,000,000 |
| Batch processing job | 500,000–2,000,000 |

A 70B model at typical throughput consumes ~1,000–3,000 tokens/second per concurrent request.

chunks.title: Quotas & Rate Limits
chunks.heading: Updating TPM
chunks.text:
```bash
curl -X PUT http://localhost:9180/api/v1/tenants/$TID/quota \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{
    "tokens_per_minute": 5000000,
    "max_in_flight": null
  }'
```

chunks.title: Quotas & Rate Limits
chunks.heading: When to use max_in_flight
chunks.text:
- **Protect backends from tenant bursts**: a batch job might have a very high TPM budget but shouldn't hold more than 10 concurrent slots.
- **Enforce priority tiers**: a low-priority tenant capped at 2 concurrent requests vs a high-priority tenant at 20.
- **Debug a misbehaving client**: temporarily cap a tenant at 1 while investigating.

chunks.title: Reliability & Failover
chunks.heading: Connection reuse
chunks.text:
Upstream connections are pooled. An idle pooled connection is closed after
`OBLETH_UPSTREAM_POOL_IDLE_SECS` (default `15`; `0` never reuses an idle
connection), which stays under the idle reaping of common inference servers, and
live connections send TCP keepalives every `OBLETH_UPSTREAM_TCP_KEEPALIVE_SECS`
(default `30`). A connection-level send failure (typically a stale pooled
socket) never reached the upstream, so once the configured retries are spent it
gets one extra attempt on a fresh connection after 50 ms before the request
fails over. This extra attempt is on top of `max_retries`.

chunks.title: Reliability & Failover
chunks.heading: Debugging upstream failures
chunks.text:
Some `502`/`504` failures are intermittent and hard to attribute after the fact —
the upstream looks up, but a request to it gave up. To turn those cases into
concrete evidence, enable **Debug upstream failures** for a model (its
`debug_diagnostics` flag, in the **Reliability → Delivery** panel). When it is on
and a request to that model exhausts its attempts with a `502`/`504`, obleth runs
a quick **read-only** check of the upstream — does its hostname still resolve in
DNS, and is the port reachable over TCP — and records the result as a span in the
request trace.

That converts an "it's up, but I got a 502" mystery into a specific finding
(e.g. a DNS blip, or a port that stopped accepting connections). It is:

- **Opt-in and off by default** — models without it enabled behave exactly as
  before, with no extra checks.
- **Diagnose-only** — the probe **never changes routing** or retry behavior. It
  runs *after* the request has already failed, purely to annotate the trace.

See [Observability](/docs/operations/observability) for reading the trace span,
and [Model Health](/docs/guides/model-health) for proactive (pre-failure) health
probing.

chunks.title: Reliability & Failover
chunks.heading: Managing endpoints
chunks.text:
From the dashboard, expand a model on the **Models** page and use the
**Reliability & endpoints** panel to set the timeout/retry policy, choose the
selection mode, and add, enable/disable, or remove endpoints.

From the Management API:

```bash
# List endpoints for a model
curl "${OBLETH_ADMIN_BASE_URL}/api/v1/models/$MODEL_ID/endpoints" \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $OBLETH_ADMIN_TOKEN"

# Add a second cluster (priority 200 = standby behind the primary at 100)
curl -X POST "${OBLETH_ADMIN_BASE_URL}/api/v1/models/$MODEL_ID/endpoints" \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $OBLETH_ADMIN_TOKEN" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{
    "name": "cluster-b",
    "api_base": "http://cluster-b.internal/v1",
    "api_key": "sk_cluster_b",
    "priority": 200,
    "weight": 100,
    "enabled": true
  }'

# Update (omit api_key to keep the stored secret; send "" to clear it)
curl -X PUT "${OBLETH_ADMIN_BASE_URL}/api/v1/models/$MODEL_ID/endpoints/$ENDPOINT_ID" \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $OBLETH_ADMIN_TOKEN" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"name": "cluster-b", "api_base": "http://cluster-b.internal/v1", "priority": 150, "weight": 100, "enabled": false}'

# Remove
curl -X DELETE "${OBLETH_ADMIN_BASE_URL}/api/v1/models/$MODEL_ID/endpoints/$ENDPOINT_ID" \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $OBLETH_ADMIN_TOKEN"
```

Endpoint `api_base` URLs are SSRF-validated like any admin-registered upstream
(see `OBLETH_ALLOWED_PRIVATE_CIDRS`). Endpoint secrets are encrypted at rest
when

chunks.title: Reliability & Failover
chunks.heading: Multiple endpoints per model
chunks.text:
A model can front several upstream clusters that all serve the same
`upstream_model` — for example a primary and a standby cluster, or two regions
behind one client-facing name. Each endpoint carries its own `api_base`,
optional `api_key`, `priority`, `weight`, and `enabled` flag, plus its own
health state.

When a model has one or more **enabled and healthy** endpoints, the data plane
routes across them. When it has none, it falls back to the model's own `api_base`
/`api_key` (the legacy single-upstream path), so adding endpoints is always
optional.

chunks.title: Reliability & Failover
chunks.heading: Observability
chunks.text:
Every upstream attempt increments `obleth_upstream_attempts_total{outcome=...}`:

| `outcome` | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| `success` | Attempt returned a usable (non-retryable) response |
| `retry` | Retryable failure with attempts remaining on the same endpoint |
| `conn_retry` | Connection-level send failure given its one extra fresh-connection attempt |
| `timeout` | Attempt hit the per-request timeout |
| `failover` | Endpoint exhausted; moved to the next endpoint |
| `exhausted` | All endpoints and attempts failed; request returned `502`/`504` |

```promql
# Failover rate (how often the primary endpoint isn't serving)
rate(obleth_upstream_attempts_total{outcome="failover"}[5m])

# Retry amplification
rate(obleth_upstream_attempts_total{outcome="retry"}[5m])
  / rate(obleth_upstream_attempts_total{outcome="success"}[5m])
```

chunks.title: Reliability & Failover
chunks.heading: Overview
chunks.text:
obleth can keep a model serving when a single upstream call is slow, fails
transiently, or a whole cluster goes down. Three controls work together, all
configured per model:

- a **per-request timeout** that bounds how long any one attempt may run;
- **automatic retries** with exponential backoff for transient failures; and
- **multiple endpoints** — the same model fronted by several upstream clusters,
  selected by `failover` (priority order), `load_balance` (weighted), or
  `session_hash` (conversation-sticky).

All three are opt-in and additive: a model with none configured behaves exactly
as before — one attempt against its `api_base`, bounded by the global timeout.

chunks.title: Reliability & Failover
chunks.heading: Per-endpoint health
chunks.text:
The model health worker probes each enabled endpoint independently with the same
minimal real-inference probe used for the model itself — the request matching the
model's `model_type`, not a generic `/models` fetch — and records a per-endpoint
`health_status`. Only endpoints that are both `enabled` and **not** explicitly
unhealthy are eligible for routing — an endpoint whose probe confirms it is down
(or that an operator disables) is removed from rotation until it recovers, while
`unknown`/`degraded` states soft-pass. A `degraded` probe clears a stale
`unhealthy` but never downgrades a confirmed `healthy`, so a reachable endpoint
returns to rotation on its own. The model is only reported fully down when
**all** of its endpoints are unhealthy. For models with no static `api_base`
(Slurm-provisioned), the model-level verdict is graded against the managed
spec's `min_replicas`. See [Model Health](/docs/guides/model-health).

chunks.title: Reliability & Failover
chunks.heading: Per-request timeout
chunks.text:
Every upstream attempt is wrapped in a timeout. By default it inherits the
global `OBLETH_UPSTREAM_TIMEOUT_SECS` (300s, until response headers arrive). Set a
per-model `request_timeout_secs` to override it for slow or latency-sensitive
routes; leave it `null` to use the global default.

```bash
curl -X PUT "${OBLETH_ADMIN_BASE_URL}/api/v1/models/$MODEL_ID/reliability" \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $OBLETH_ADMIN_TOKEN" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{
    "request_timeout_secs": 60,
    "max_retries": 2,
    "retry_backoff_ms": 200,
    "endpoint_selection_mode": "failover"
  }'
```

When an attempt exceeds the timeout, it counts as a retryable failure: obleth
retries (if attempts remain) or fails over to the next endpoint. If every
attempt times out, the client receives `504 Gateway Timeout`.

chunks.title: Reliability & Failover
chunks.heading: Point of no return
chunks.text:
Retries and failover only happen **before the first response byte is streamed to
the client**. Once obleth has started forwarding the upstream response, the
request is committed to that endpoint — a mid-stream failure surfaces to the
client rather than silently restarting. This preserves correct streaming (SSE)
semantics and avoids duplicate side effects.

When an upstream breaks off a stream before its terminal chunk, the gateway
aborts the response to the client instead of ending it cleanly, so a truncated
body cannot be mistaken for a complete one. The request is recorded with status
`502`, the `upstream_stream_error` alert is raised, and it is billed for what
reached the client: the usage the upstream reported, or else the prompt estimate
plus the streamed text, and nothing if nothing streamed.

Retries replay the JSON request body. **Multipart routes** (audio
transcription/translation) are not replayable, so they always get a single
attempt against the first endpoint — no retry, no failover.

A single fairshare permit and a single token-budget reservation cover the whole
attempt sequence, so retries and failover never double-charge a tenant. When
every attempt fails with a `502` or `504`, the request records zero tokens and
zero cost and its budget reservation is refunded in full.

chunks.title: Reliability & Failover
chunks.heading: Read timeout
chunks.text:
Separately, the upstream HTTP client has a read timeout,
`OBLETH_UPSTREAM_READ_TIMEOUT_SECS`, which bounds how long the gateway waits for
the next bytes from an upstream — including the wait for response headers. It
defaults to `OBLETH_UPSTREAM_TIMEOUT_SECS` (and never less than 120 seconds);
`0` disables it. A backend that sends headers and then stalls is cut off instead
of holding its fairshare slot indefinitely. Because the read timeout also
bounds a non-streaming generation, a per-model `request_timeout_secs` longer than
the read timeout is never reached; the gateway logs a warning naming such models.

chunks.title: Reliability & Failover
chunks.heading: Relationship to cross-model fallback
chunks.text:
This feature fails a model over between **endpoints of the same model** — same
`upstream_model`, same capabilities, same cost. It deliberately does **not**
swap to a *different* model, which would change pricing, capabilities, and
capacity accounting. Cross-model fallback chains are not supported; to spread
load across different models, use [auto-routing](/docs/guides/auto-model-routing).

chunks.title: Reliability & Failover
chunks.heading: Retries and backoff
chunks.text:
`max_retries` (default `0`) is the number of **additional** attempts against the
same endpoint after the first one fails with a retryable error. `retry_backoff_ms`
(default `200`) is the base delay; it grows exponentially per attempt
(`base`, `base×2`, `base×4`, …) and is capped at `base×64`.

```
attempt 0 → fail (retryable) → wait 200ms
attempt 1 → fail (retryable) → wait 400ms
attempt 2 → success
```

chunks.title: Reliability & Failover
chunks.heading: Selection modes
chunks.text:
`endpoint_selection_mode` controls ordering of the eligible endpoints:

| Mode | Behavior |
| --- | --- |
| `failover` (default) | Endpoints are tried in ascending `priority` (lowest number first). Traffic sticks to the highest-priority healthy endpoint; lower ones are standbys used only when those ahead fail. |
| `load_balance` | Endpoints are ordered by a weighted random shuffle (A-Res) so the first choice is picked in proportion to `weight`. The remaining endpoints stay available as failover targets for the same request. |
| `session_hash` | A whole conversation is pinned to the same endpoint by a consistent hash of its session id, so a session keeps hitting the upstream replica that already has its KV cache warm. The other endpoints stay available as failover targets, and if the pinned endpoint is removed the session re-pins deterministically. |

`session_hash` needs a [conversation id](/docs/guides/conversations-and-sessions)
to pin on. obleth derives one from each request (or honors a client-supplied
`x-session-id`), so no client change is required — but a request that genuinely
has no session key falls back to the `load_balance` weighted order for that
request (and logs a warning), so the mode degrades safely rather than pinning
everything to one endpoint.

In both modes a single request walks the ordered list: it tries an endpoint
(with its retry budget), and on exhaustion fails over to the next, until one
succeeds or the list is exhausted (`502 Bad Gateway`, or `504`

chunks.title: Reliability & Failover
chunks.heading: What counts as retryable
chunks.text:
Only transient transport or overload conditions are retried or failed over.
Client errors are returned immediately so a bad request isn't amplified into
several upstream calls.

| Outcome | Classification |
| --- | --- |
| Connection / DNS / transport error | Retryable |
| Timeout (per-request) | Retryable |
| HTTP `408`, `429` | Retryable |
| HTTP `500`, `502`, `503`, `504` | Retryable |
| HTTP `400`, `401`, `403`, `404`, `422` (any other 4xx) | Fatal — returned as-is |
| HTTP `2xx` | Success |

chunks.title: Response Cache
chunks.heading: Caveats
chunks.text:
- Exact-match only. Requests that differ by a single byte miss; there is no
  semantic or similarity matching.
- The cache trusts that identical inputs yield equivalent outputs. Disable it for
  models whose responses must be unique per call (e.g. high-temperature sampling
  where you want variety), or keep the TTL short.

chunks.title: Response Cache
chunks.heading: Enabling it
chunks.text:
Per model, from the dashboard (**Models → Cache** toggle) or the Management API:

```bash
curl -X PUT "${OBLETH_ADMIN_BASE_URL}/api/v1/models/$MODEL_ID/cache" \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $OBLETH_ADMIN_TOKEN" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"cache_enabled": true, "cache_ttl_secs": 300}'
```

- `cache_enabled` — turn the cache on/off for this model.
- `cache_ttl_secs` — entry lifetime in seconds. `0` disables caching for the
  model: no lookup is made and nothing is written, even with `cache_enabled`
  on.

Changes propagate to every gateway pod immediately via the Redis invalidation
channel.

chunks.title: Response Cache
chunks.heading: How it works
chunks.text:
```
auth → resolve model → cache check ─ hit ─→ return cached response (no permit, no budget)
                                  └ miss ─→ fairshare admit → reserve budget → upstream → store on success
```

- **Cache key** = `sha256(tenant_id ‖ model ‖ request_body)`, with a zero byte
  between the parts. Two requests collide (a hit) only when they come from the
  same tenant and the client-facing model and the full request body are
  byte-identical. Entries are never shared across tenants.
- **Storage**: the full upstream response (body + content-type + token counts)
  is buffered on a miss and written to Redis (`obleth:cache:<key>`) with the
  model's TTL. Streaming (SSE) responses are buffered and replayed verbatim on a
  hit, so streaming clients keep working.
- **Hits are marked.** A cached response carries `x-obleth-cache: hit`. Its usage
  row records `cache_status: hit` with the cached token counts and their cost at
  the model's rates, but nothing is admitted, reserved, or committed against the
  tenant's budgets.
- **Safety**: responses larger than 512 KiB are streamed through uncached (the
  cache can't be used to balloon Redis memory). Only `200 OK` responses are
  stored, so an error or partial response can't poison later reads.
- **Tool-loop answers are never cached.** A request handled by the
  [gateway tool loop](/docs/guides/mcp-gateway#the-gateway-tool-loop) depends on
  live tool results (e.g. a web search), so a cached answer would be wrong by
  definition

chunks.title: Response Cache
chunks.heading: Overview
chunks.text:
obleth can serve identical requests from an exact-match response cache instead of
hitting the upstream. A cache hit skips **admission, the token budget, and the
upstream entirely** — it returns immediately and costs nothing against fairshare
or quota. This is the cleanest possible offload: real requests removed from the
backend, not just smoothed.

The cache is **opt-in per model** and **off by default**.

chunks.title: Response Cache
chunks.heading: Verifying real offload
chunks.text:
The benchmark fixture backend exposes `GET /stats` with a true request counter. Run a load
test twice (cache off, then on) and compare `requests` against the number of
requests you issued — the delta is exactly the requests the cache absorbed.

chunks.title: Response Cache
chunks.heading: Visibility
chunks.text:
Each request records a `cache_status` of `hit`, `miss`, or `off` in the
ClickHouse usage ledger.

**Dashboard:** the Models page shows a cache panel with 24h hit rate, hits,
misses, and tokens saved.

**Management API:**

```bash
curl "${OBLETH_ADMIN_BASE_URL}/api/v1/usage/cache?since_ms=..." \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $OBLETH_ADMIN_TOKEN"
# { "hits": 1234, "misses": 5678, "tokens_saved": 987654 }
```

**Prometheus:**

- `obleth_cache_lookups_total{result="hit|miss"}`
- `obleth_cache_tokens_saved_total`

chunks.title: Self-Hosting
chunks.heading: 1. Pre-create the Secrets
chunks.text:
So real credentials never touch values files, git, or `--set`/CLI history,
production references **pre-created** Secrets via `existingSecret` instead of
letting the chart render its own. Use your secrets manager / SOPS / External
Secrets Operator in place of raw `kubectl` below:

```bash
kubectl create secret generic obleth-secrets -n obleth \
  --from-literal=OBLETH_ADMIN_TOKEN="$(openssl rand -hex 32)" \
  --from-literal=OBLETH_DATABASE_URL="postgres://obleth:PASS@pg-rw.db.svc:5432/obleth" \
  --from-literal=OBLETH_REDIS_URL="redis://:PASS@redis-master.db.svc:6379" \
  --from-literal=OBLETH_CLICKHOUSE_PASSWORD="CLICKHOUSE_PASS" \
  --from-literal=OBLETH_ENCRYPTION_KEY="$(openssl rand -base64 32)" \
  --from-literal=OBLETH_API_KEY_PEPPER="$(openssl rand -hex 32)" \
  --from-literal=OBLETH_SLACK_WEBHOOK_URL="" \
  --from-literal=OBLETH_JWT_ISSUERS=""

SESSION_SECRET="$(openssl rand -hex 32)"
kubectl create secret generic obleth-control-plane -n obleth \
  --from-literal=DASHBOARD_ADMIN_EMAIL="admin@example.com" \
  --from-literal=DASHBOARD_PASSWORD="$(openssl rand -hex 16)" \
  --from-literal=DASHBOARD_SESSION_SECRET="$SESSION_SECRET" \
  --from-literal=BETTER_AUTH_SECRET="$SESSION_SECRET" \
  --from-literal=DATABASE_URL="postgres://obleth:PASS@pg-rw.db.svc:5432/obleth" \
  --from-literal=BETTER_AUTH_URL="https://dashboard.example.com" \
  --from-literal=TRUSTED_ORIGINS="" \
  --from-literal=OIDC_PROVIDERS=""   # JSON array to enable SSO; empty = break-glass admin only
```

chunks.title: Self-Hosting
chunks.heading: 1. Start the stack
chunks.text:
```bash
cd deploy/docker
cp datastores.env.example datastores.env   # then edit the passwords
docker compose --env-file datastores.env -f datastores.compose.yml up -d
```

`datastores.env` controls credentials and the bind address:

```bash
# Loopback only by default — change to a private interface IP to allow an
# off-box obleth, and protect it with a firewall / private network.
BIND_ADDR=127.0.0.1

POSTGRES_USER=obleth
POSTGRES_PASSWORD=change-me-postgres
POSTGRES_DB=obleth

# Required: Redis always runs with AUTH. Use URL-safe characters.
REDIS_PASSWORD=change-me-redis

CLICKHOUSE_USER=obleth
CLICKHOUSE_PASSWORD=change-me-clickhouse
CLICKHOUSE_DB=obleth
```

| Service | Port | Notes |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Postgres | 5432 | config source of truth |
| Redis | 6379 | AUTH required; AOF persistence (`appendfsync everysec`) |
| ClickHouse | 8123 (HTTP), 9000 (native) | obleth uses the HTTP port |

Data persists in the `pgdata`, `redisdata`, and `chdata` named volumes across
`docker compose down`/`up`. (`docker compose down -v` deletes them.)

ClickHouse's built-in `default` user is restricted to localhost, so the stack
provisions a network-accessible `obleth` user via `CLICKHOUSE_USER` /
`CLICKHOUSE_PASSWORD`. Use those credentials from obleth, not `default`.

chunks.title: Self-Hosting
chunks.heading: 2. Hardening the values turn on
chunks.text:
```yaml
obleth:
  replicas: 3
  globalMaxInFlight: 256                # total ceiling across model pools, per pod
  existingSecret: obleth-secrets        # no inline secrets
  upstreamBaseUrl: "https://my-vllm-or-aibrix-endpoint/v1"

postgres:   { enabled: false, external: { url: "postgres://obleth:PASS@pg-rw.db.svc:5432/obleth" } }
redis:      { enabled: false, external: { url: "redis://:PASS@redis-master.db.svc:6379" } }
clickhouse: { enabled: false, user: obleth, db: obleth, password: "", external: { url: "http://clickhouse.db.svc:8123" } }
benchmarkBackend: { enabled: false }

hpa:
  enabled: false                        # the replica count is load-bearing — see below
  minReplicas: 3
  maxReplicas: 20

affinity:
  antiAffinity: soft                    # "hard" to require distinct nodes on multi-node clusters

podDisruptionBudget:
  enabled: true
  minAvailable: 2

controlPlane:
  enabled: true
  replicas: 2
  existingSecret: obleth-control-plane

serviceMonitor:
  enabled: true                         # requires the Prometheus Operator CRDs

ingress:
  enabled: true
  className: nginx
  host: obleth.example.com
  servicePort: 8080
  tls:
    - secretName: obleth-tls
      hosts: [obleth.example.com]
```

The external URLs in the values only satisfy chart rendering; with
`existingSecret` set, the live URLs come from the Secret. Keep them consistent.

Fairshare admission state is **per process**. Each obleth replica runs its own
scheduler with one pool per model (the model

chunks.title: Self-Hosting
chunks.heading: 2. Point obleth at them
chunks.text:
**Bare-metal binary** (`OBLETH_*` env vars). Replace `DB_HOST` with the Docker
host's reachable address:

```bash
export OBLETH_DATABASE_URL="postgres://obleth:change-me-postgres@DB_HOST:5432/obleth"
export OBLETH_REDIS_URL="redis://:change-me-redis@DB_HOST:6379"
export OBLETH_CLICKHOUSE_URL="http://DB_HOST:8123"
export OBLETH_CLICKHOUSE_USER=obleth
export OBLETH_CLICKHOUSE_PASSWORD=change-me-clickhouse
export OBLETH_CLICKHOUSE_DB=obleth
export OBLETH_ADMIN_TOKEN="$(openssl rand -hex 32)"
./target/release/obleth
```

**Helm** (`values-external.yaml`):

```yaml
postgres:
  enabled: false
  external: { url: "postgres://obleth:change-me-postgres@DB_HOST:5432/obleth" }
redis:
  enabled: false
  external: { url: "redis://:change-me-redis@DB_HOST:6379" }
clickhouse:
  enabled: false
  user: obleth
  password: "change-me-clickhouse"
  db: obleth
  external: { url: "http://DB_HOST:8123" }
```

obleth applies its embedded schema on boot — there is no separate migration
step. It connects, creates tables idempotently, and starts serving.

The datastore ports bind to `127.0.0.1` by default so they are not exposed to
your network. Only widen `BIND_ADDR` to a private interface and put the ports
behind a firewall / private network. **Never expose Postgres, Redis, or
ClickHouse to the public internet.**

---

chunks.title: Self-Hosting
chunks.heading: 3. Install
chunks.text:
```bash
helm install obleth ./deploy/k8s/obleth -n obleth --create-namespace \
  -f deploy/k8s/obleth/examples/values-production.yaml
```

No `--set` for secrets — they all come from the pre-created Secrets.

Point the datastores at purpose-built tooling for backups, HA, and PITR:
[CloudNativePG](https://cloudnative-pg.io/) or managed Postgres, the
[Altinity ClickHouse operator](https://github.com/Altinity/clickhouse-operator)
or managed ClickHouse, and a managed or operator-run Redis that presents a
single primary endpoint. obleth treats Redis as a hot cache and re-warms from
Postgres, but HA avoids cold-start latency spikes.

---

chunks.title: Self-Hosting
chunks.heading: After install
chunks.text:
Helm and the binary bring services up but do **not** register models or create
tenant keys. Continue with:

- [First Tenant & Key](/docs/getting-started/first-tenant-and-key) — mint a `sk_...` key
- [Installation — post-install steps](/docs/getting-started/installation#post-install-steps-kubernetes)
- [Backup & Restore](/docs/operations/backup-restore) — protect Postgres and ClickHouse
- [Production Checklist](/docs/guides/production-checklist) — secrets, TLS, scaling
- [Helm Values](/docs/reference/helm-values) — full chart reference

chunks.title: Self-Hosting
chunks.heading: Choosing a scenario
chunks.text:
| Scenario | Who manages the data | Survives restart? | Use for |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| [Persistent (PVC)](#scenario-1-bundled-datastores-with-pvcs) | the chart, on PVCs | **Yes** | Self-hosted single cluster, no external DBs yet |
| [Ephemeral](#scenario-2-bundled-datastores-without-persistence-test-only) | the chart, in `emptyDir` | **No — data is lost** | Demos, CI, kicking the tires |
| [External](#scenario-3-external-datastores) | **you** (managed / Docker / operator) | Managed by you | Self-host with your own managed datastores |
| [Production](#scenario-4-production) | **you** (operator / managed) | Managed by you | Redundant production: external datastores + full hardening |

The profiles differ along two independent axes — **datastore durability** (where
state lives) and **workload posture** (how the stateless obleth pods are
hardened and made redundant). External and Production share the same datastore
story; Production layers on pre-created Secrets, pod spread, disruption budgets,
and restricted security contexts.

Ready-made values files for each live in
[`deploy/k8s/obleth/examples/`](https://github.com/thediymaker/obleth-gateway/tree/main/deploy/k8s/obleth/examples).
The commands below install from the local chart path; to install the published
chart instead, replace `./deploy/k8s/obleth` with
`oci://ghcr.io/thediymaker/charts/obleth --version 1.3.0` and download the
example values file for that release.

---

chunks.title: Self-Hosting
chunks.heading: Hosting external datastores in Docker
chunks.text:
If you want external datastores without a managed service or a database operator,
the repo ships a dedicated Compose stack tuned to be a durable backing tier
(named volumes, healthchecks, `restart: unless-stopped`, host-published ports):
[`deploy/docker/datastores.compose.yml`](https://github.com/thediymaker/obleth-gateway/blob/main/deploy/docker/datastores.compose.yml).

This is separate from the all-in-one `docker-compose.yml` — it runs **only** the
three datastores so that an obleth elsewhere (a Helm install with
`*.enabled: false`, or a bare-metal binary) can connect to them.

chunks.title: Self-Hosting
chunks.heading: Overview
chunks.text:
obleth is built to be self-hosted. This guide covers the decisions that matter
once you move past a throwaway demo: **where your data lives** and **who manages
the datastores**.

obleth needs three backing stores (see [Datastores](/docs/concepts/datastores)):

| Store | Role | Lose it and… |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Postgres** | Config source of truth (tenants, keys, models, audit, dashboard accounts) | you lose all configuration |
| **ClickHouse** | Usage / cost ledger | you lose usage history |
| **Redis** | Hot cache, token buckets, term-budget counters, response cache | nothing permanent — obleth re-pushes keys, models, and MCP servers from Postgres every `OBLETH_REDIS_REWARM_SECS` (300 s) and after every reconnect |

Redis always requires a password: the request path reads API keys from it, so an
unauthenticated instance would let anyone who reaches it mint keys. obleth
connects to a single Redis primary (a standalone instance, or a managed failover
endpoint that presents one primary). Clustered Redis is not supported, because the
gateway runs multi-key Lua scripts.

How you host those three stores is the single biggest self-hosting decision. The
Helm chart in `deploy/k8s/obleth/` supports four scenarios.

Beyond the data plane and control plane, the chart also ships two optional
components, both off by default: the [Slurm provisioner](/docs/guides/slurm-provisioning)
(`provisioner.enabled`) and the compression sidecar (`compressor.enabled`) used
by the compression boon.

chunks.title: Self-Hosting
chunks.heading: Scenario 1: bundled datastores with PVCs
chunks.text:
The chart runs its own Postgres, Redis, and ClickHouse and stores their data on
PersistentVolumeClaims. Data survives pod restarts, reschedules, and node
drains. This is the recommended starting point when you don't yet have managed
datastores.

Each datastore has a `persistence` block (enabled by default):

```yaml
postgres:
  enabled: true
  persistence:
    enabled: true
    size: 10Gi
    storageClass: ""          # "" = cluster default StorageClass; set a name to pin one
    accessMode: ReadWriteOnce
redis:
  persistence: { enabled: true, size: 1Gi }
clickhouse:
  persistence: { enabled: true, size: 20Gi }
```

The datastore Deployments use the `Recreate` rollout strategy so a new pod never
tries to attach the same `ReadWriteOnce` PVC while the old pod still holds it.
The chart's bundled Redis runs with a 512Mi memory limit, `maxmemory 400mb`, and the
`volatile-lru` policy: only entries with a TTL (response cache, compression
originals, per-minute buckets, and the term-budget counters) are evicted, and
when Redis is full it refuses writes to keys without a TTL rather than evicting
API keys or model routes. An evicted term counter restarts that budget period's
usage; see [Redis Layout](/docs/reference/redis-layout#eviction).

**Requirements:** a `StorageClass` must exist in the cluster. Check with:

```bash
kubectl get storageclass
```

Most managed clusters (EKS/GKE/AKS), k3s, and kind ship a default. If none is
marked `(default)`, set `persistence.storageClass` explicit

chunks.title: Self-Hosting
chunks.heading: Scenario 2: bundled datastores without persistence (test only)
chunks.text:
Set `persistence.enabled: false` and the datastores use `emptyDir` volumes.

**All data is lost when a datastore pod restarts.** That includes every tenant,
API key, registered model, audit entry (Postgres) and all usage history
(ClickHouse). A `helm upgrade` that rolls the pods, a node drain, or an OOM kill
all wipe the data. Use this only for throwaway demos, CI, or a cluster with no
`StorageClass`.

```yaml
postgres:   { persistence: { enabled: false } }
redis:      { persistence: { enabled: false } }
clickhouse: { persistence: { enabled: false } }
```

```bash
helm install obleth ./deploy/k8s/obleth -n obleth --create-namespace \
  -f deploy/k8s/obleth/examples/values-ephemeral.yaml \
  --set obleth.adminToken="$(openssl rand -hex 32)" \
  --set postgres.password=devpassword \
  --set redis.password=devpassword \
  --set clickhouse.password=devpassword \
  --set controlPlane.dashboardPassword=devpassword \
  --set controlPlane.dashboardSessionSecret=dev-session-secret-at-least-32-chars
```

This profile keeps the GPU-free benchmark fixture backend enabled, so inference
calls succeed without a real upstream.

---

chunks.title: Self-Hosting
chunks.heading: Scenario 3: external datastores
chunks.text:
obleth runs only its stateless workloads (data plane + control plane) and
connects to Postgres, Redis, and ClickHouse you operate yourself. This is the
recommended production topology — stateful systems get purpose-built backups,
HA, and point-in-time recovery instead of plain Deployments.

```yaml
postgres:
  enabled: false
  external:
    url: "postgres://obleth:STRONGPASSWORD@my-pg-host:5432/obleth"
redis:
  enabled: false
  external:
    url: "redis://:STRONGPASSWORD@my-redis-host:6379"
clickhouse:
  enabled: false
  # obleth authenticates to ClickHouse with these even when external:
  user: obleth
  password: ""                # REQUIRED — set via --set or a Secret
  db: obleth
  external:
    url: "http://my-clickhouse-host:8123"
benchmarkBackend:
  enabled: false
obleth:
  upstreamBaseUrl: "https://my-vllm-or-aibrix-endpoint/v1"
```

When a store is `enabled: false`, its `external.url` is **required** — the chart
fails to render with a clear message if it is missing, so obleth never boots
half-configured. The external URLs are rendered into the obleth Secret, so they
may carry credentials.

```bash
helm install obleth ./deploy/k8s/obleth -n obleth --create-namespace \
  -f deploy/k8s/obleth/examples/values-external.yaml \
  --set obleth.adminToken="$(openssl rand -hex 32)" \
  --set obleth.encryptionKey="$(openssl rand -base64 32)" \
  --set clickhouse.password="CLICKHOUSE_PASSWORD" \
  --set controlPlane.dashboardPassword="$(openssl rand -hex 16)" \
  --set controlPla

chunks.title: Self-Hosting
chunks.heading: Scenario 4: production
chunks.text:
Production is the [External](#scenario-3-external-datastores) datastore topology
plus full hardening of the stateless data plane. Nothing stateful runs in the
chart; the difference is how the obleth pods are secured and kept redundant. The
ready-made
[`values-production.yaml`](https://github.com/thediymaker/obleth-gateway/blob/main/deploy/k8s/obleth/examples/values-production.yaml)
wires all of this together.

chunks.title: Self-Hosting
chunks.heading: Upgrading
chunks.text:
To apply chart or values changes to a release that already exists, use `helm
upgrade --install` — **not** `helm install`, which fails against a live release
with `cannot re-use a name that is still in use`.

```bash
helm upgrade --install obleth ./deploy/k8s/obleth -n obleth \
  -f my-values.yaml \
  --wait
```

Point the upgrade at the **same chart source you installed from**. The command
above uses the local chart path; to track a published release instead, use the
OCI chart pinned to a version:

```bash
helm upgrade --install obleth oci://ghcr.io/thediymaker/charts/obleth \
  --version 1.3.0 -n obleth \
  -f my-values.yaml \
  --wait
```

Image tags left empty (`image.tag: ""`, `compressor.image.tag: ""`) resolve to
`v{appVersion}` from the chart, so each chart release pins its own images.
Override the tag only to test a specific build (e.g. `dev` for edge images).

The two sources are **not** interchangeable. Editing the chart's own
`deploy/k8s/obleth/values.yaml` only affects the local chart path — the OCI
artifact carries the values published with that version. Keep per-deployment
settings in your own `-f` values file so they apply regardless of source.

When a value that flows into the chart-rendered obleth Secret changes
(`obleth.adminToken`, a datastore URL or password, `obleth.encryptionKey`,
`obleth.apiKeyPepper`), the obleth, bundled Redis, and bundled ClickHouse pods
carry a `checksum/secret` annotation and roll automatically.

Secrets the chart does not render a

chunks.title: Serving GGUF Models
chunks.heading: Answer the health path
chunks.text:
The provisioner promotes a replica only once `GET <health_path>` returns a 2xx.
The header's `health_path` wins when set; otherwise the default is `/health`, or
`/` for the `ollama` engine. `llama-server` serves `/health`, so the shipped
recipe leaves it unset.

chunks.title: Serving GGUF Models
chunks.heading: Declare the serving format
chunks.text:
Deploying a recipe does not set the route's `quantization`. Set it to `gguf` on
the model form after deployment, so `GET /v1/models` and `GET /model/info`
report the format and the model name does not have to carry it. See
[Model Registry](/docs/guides/model-registry).

chunks.title: Serving GGUF Models
chunks.heading: Editing the spec after deployment
chunks.text:
The model's **Provisioning** tab shows the submitted script in an editable
**Launch script** box, alongside the placement and service fields. Saving relaunches
replicas with the new settings. A recipe-deployed model keeps its script as the
spec's `script_body`, so the Apptainer image, preamble, and launch-command fields
that the hand-filled path uses do not apply and are hidden.

chunks.title: Serving GGUF Models
chunks.heading: Keeping weights off a slow shared filesystem
chunks.text:
Large GGUF models read poorly over NFS. The shipped recipe points `LLAMA_CACHE`
at node-local scratch, so `llama-server -hf` pulls the weights onto fast local
storage:

```bash
# EDIT FOR YOUR CLUSTER: node-local scratch path for weight caching.
export LLAMA_CACHE=/path/to/job_tmp/glm52
```

If you would rather stage the files yourself, the script is plain bash — put the
download before the launch line and point `llama-server` at what you staged:

```bash
HF_REPO=unsloth/GLM-5.2-GGUF
HF_DIR=UD-IQ2_M
STAGE=/mnt/job_tmp/glm52/$HF_DIR; mkdir -p "$STAGE"
FILES="GLM-5.2-UD-IQ2_M-00001-of-00006.gguf GLM-5.2-UD-IQ2_M-00002-of-00006.gguf"
for f in $FILES; do
  curl -fsSL -C - -o "$STAGE/$f" \
    "https://huggingface.co/$HF_REPO/resolve/main/$HF_DIR/$f" &
done; wait
```

`curl -C -` resumes a partial download, so a preempted job that restarts on the
same node with its local storage intact does not re-fetch what it already has.

The job runs on whatever node Slurm allocates, so anything written to node-local
scratch is fetched again after a reschedule. Weights on shared storage are read
once per job either way — the trade is transfer time against read throughput
during serving.

chunks.title: Serving GGUF Models
chunks.heading: Listen on `$OBLETH_SERVING_PORT`
chunks.text:
The provisioner gives each replica a **disjoint port window** — `serving_port + i
× OBLETH_PORT_SPAN` (span defaults to 8) — and prepends a bash block to the
submitted script that binds the first free port in that window and exports it as
`OBLETH_SERVING_PORT`. It then probes every port in the window to find where the
server actually came up. Bind that variable, not a hardcoded port, and two
replicas can share a node without colliding:

```bash
llama-server -hf unsloth/GLM-5.2-GGUF:UD-IQ2_M \
  --host 0.0.0.0 --port "$OBLETH_SERVING_PORT" --alias glm-5.2 \
  -ngl 99 --ctx-size 1048576 --parallel 4 --threads "$(nproc)"
```

`--host 0.0.0.0` matters too: the provisioner's health probe and the gateway's
proxied traffic both reach the server from **outside** the compute node.

chunks.title: Serving GGUF Models
chunks.heading: Overview
chunks.text:
llama.cpp is handed weights — a Hugging Face repo to pull, or files already on
disk — rather than a model name. obleth does **not** fetch weights for you: what
the job needs must already exist on the cluster, or be downloaded by the job
script itself before `llama-server` starts.

A llama.cpp model is deployed like any other Slurm-provisioned model, from a
**deployment recipe**: a small YAML header carrying the routing metadata, plus the
raw `sbatch` script obleth submits verbatim. See
[Slurm Provisioning — Step 3](/docs/guides/slurm-provisioning#step-3-create-a-slurm-provisioned-model)
for how recipes are listed, overridden, and deployed. The repo ships one to start
from at `control-plane/recipes/glm-5.2-multiuser.recipe`.

chunks.title: Serving GGUF Models
chunks.heading: Placement comes from the header and the overrides
chunks.text:
`#SBATCH` directives in the body are lifted into the submit fields, because
`slurmrestd` ignores them in the script. Header fields override the directives,
and the deploy dialog's **Deploy overrides** (partition, QoS, replicas, time
limit, plus any variables the recipe declares) override both — for that
deployment only. The shipped llama.cpp recipe deliberately leaves partition, QoS,
and time limit out of the script so it stays cluster-agnostic and you supply them
at deploy time.

chunks.title: Serving GGUF Models
chunks.heading: Serve the name clients will ask for
chunks.text:
Deploying a recipe registers the model route with `upstream_model` set to the
header's `api_model_name`, so that exact string is what obleth forwards upstream.
Keep `llama-server --alias` equal to the header's `api_model_name` (`glm-5.2` in
the shipped recipe) or the upstream will not recognise the model it is asked for.

The serving format does not have to be spelled into the client-facing name:
since v1.2.0 a route carries a `quantization` field (`gguf` for these models,
from a fixed vocabulary) and optional `aliases`, so the name clients call can
stay clean — set both on the model from the dashboard or
`PUT /api/v1/models/{id}` after deployment, and register any old
format-suffixed spelling as an alias so pinned clients keep working.

chunks.title: Serving GGUF Models
chunks.heading: What the launch script has to get right
chunks.text:
Three things in the script are load-bearing for obleth. Everything else is
ordinary `llama-server` tuning.

chunks.title: Slurm Provisioning
chunks.heading: A job reaches `RUNNING` but the replica never becomes `healthy`
chunks.text:
There are **two independent health checks**, and a replica is only promoted when the *provisioner's* probe passes:

1. **Provisioner probe (promotes the replica).** Each tick the provisioner does `GET http://<address>:<port><health_path>` **from wherever the provisioner runs** (its container or host — *not* from the compute node), for every port in the replica's window, concurrently. `<address>` is the node's resolved address — the [override](#node-address-overrides) if one is set, otherwise the cached or freshly resolved IP. The replica is promoted on the lowest port that answers `2xx`; the outcome is logged either way:

   ```
   health probe: healthy          replica_id=... job_id=12345 port=8000
   health probe: not yet healthy  replica_id=... job_id=12345 port_base=8000 port_span=8
   ```

   `not yet healthy` almost always means the provisioner **cannot reach the node**, not that the model is down. A `curl` that works *on the node itself* proves nothing — the probe originates from the provisioner. Verify reachability from inside the provisioner container:

   ```bash
   getent hosts gpu-node-01                                                   # name resolves?
   curl -s -o /dev/null -w '%{http_code}\n' http://gpu-node-01:8000/api/tags  # port reachable?
   ```

   If the log instead says `job is RUNNING but slurmrestd returned no nodes`, that is a different problem — `slurmrestd` is not returning the allocated nodelist. Check that your API version matches `/openapi/v3`

chunks.title: Slurm Provisioning
chunks.heading: Apptainer image requirements
chunks.text:
When the spec has no `script_body` (the hand-filled path), the provisioner
assembles a Slurm batch script that runs:

```bash
#!/bin/bash
set -euo pipefail
<preamble>
apptainer exec --nv <image> <launch_command>
```

With `image` blank, `launch_command` runs directly on the node instead. A
non-empty `script_body` — what a recipe produces — is submitted verbatim and
replaces this assembly entirely.

- `<image>` — the path to an Apptainer `.sif` image on shared cluster storage. This path is used verbatim on each compute node, so all nodes must be able to read it.
- `<preamble>` — the spec's `preamble` lines, verbatim, before the exec line (module loads, `PATH` changes).
- `<launch_command>` — the inference server startup command to run inside the container, e.g. `python -m vllm.entrypoints.openai.api_server --model /data/models/llama3 --port "$OBLETH_SERVING_PORT"`.
- `--nv` — passes NVIDIA GPU devices through to the container.

Either way, the provisioner prepends a short bash block that binds the first free
port in **this replica's** port window and exports it as `OBLETH_SERVING_PORT`. The
window is `serving_port + i × OBLETH_PORT_SPAN` (span defaults to 8) for the
smallest `i` no live replica already holds, so two replicas can share a node
without colliding. Have your launch command listen on `$OBLETH_SERVING_PORT`
rather than a hardcoded port — the provisioner probes the whole window to find
where the server actually came up.

chunks.heading: Cargo (development)
chunks.text:

cd obleth
OBLETH_ADMIN_TOKEN=dev-admin-token \
