chunks.title: Slurm Provisioning
chunks.heading: Disabling Slurm globally vs per model
chunks.text:
| Scope | Effect |
| --- | --- |
| Dashboard Settings → Slurm enabled = off | Provisioner idles; existing replicas are **not** drained. |
| Per-model `enabled = false` | Replicas drained to zero; jobs cancelled; endpoints detached. The spec is kept and the model can be re-enabled later. |
| Delete managed spec (`DELETE /api/v1/models/{id}/managed`) | Same drain behavior as disabling, but the spec is removed. |

chunks.title: Slurm Provisioning
chunks.heading: Docker Compose
chunks.text:
The provisioner is gated behind the `slurm` profile. Opt in via **config** by adding `slurm` to `COMPOSE_PROFILES` in `deploy/docker/.env` (copy it from `.env.example` if you haven't):

```bash
# deploy/docker/.env
COMPOSE_PROFILES=benchmark,edge,observability,slurm
```

Then one command — run from `deploy/docker/`, with no `-f` flags — builds and starts everything, the provisioner included:

```bash
cd deploy/docker

docker compose up -d --build      # build + start the whole stack (provisioner too)
docker compose down               # tear it all down
```

Running from `deploy/docker/` lets Compose auto-load `.env`, so the profile activates without a `--profile` flag. The container only needs `OBLETH_ADMIN_TOKEN` (inherited from the core stack's `.env`) and `OBLETH_ADMIN_BASE_URL` (set by the Compose file); Slurm connection details are configured in the dashboard, not in `.env`.

If you run Compose from another directory with explicit `-f` paths and the provisioner does not start, add `--profile slurm` to the command.

chunks.title: Slurm Provisioning
chunks.heading: Endpoints and the OpenAI `/v1` root
chunks.text:
When a replica passes its health probe, the provisioner registers it as a model **endpoint** with `api_base = http://<resolved-address>:<discovered-port>/v1` — the node's [override or resolved IP](#node-address-overrides), and the port in its window that answered. The `/v1` root matches the convention used by every statically-registered model and the [model health check](/docs/guides/model-health), which appends `/models` to a model's `api_base` expecting `…/v1/models`. OpenAI-compatible inference servers (vLLM, SGLang, LiteLLM, Ollama) all serve their OpenAI surface under `/v1`.

This is distinct from the provisioner's **own** liveness probe, which uses the spec's `health_path` (e.g. Ollama's native `/api/tags`, or vLLM's `/health`) against the bare node — it does not assume `/v1`.

chunks.title: Slurm Provisioning
chunks.heading: Environment variables
chunks.text:
| Variable | Default | Meaning |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `OBLETH_ADMIN_BASE_URL` | `http://localhost:9180` | Management API base URL |
| `OBLETH_ADMIN_TOKEN` | required | Management API token (shared with the gateway) |
| `OBLETH_PROVISIONER_INTERVAL_SECS` | `15` | Reconcile tick cadence |
| `OBLETH_PROVISIONER_HEALTH_TIMEOUT_SECS` | `5` | Per-port health-probe timeout |
| `OBLETH_PROVISIONER_WARMUP_TIMEOUT_SECS` | `600` | Budget for the post-promotion warmup request; `0` disables warmup |
| `OBLETH_PROVISIONER_LOST_RETENTION_SECS` | `900` | How long a `lost` replica row is kept |
| `OBLETH_PROVISIONER_RESTART_AFTER_FAILURES` | `20` | Net failing probe ticks before a zombie replica is restarted; `0` disables |
| `OBLETH_PORT_SPAN` | `8` | Width of each replica's port window |
| `OBLETH_PROVISIONER_JOB_PREFIX` | `obleth-` | Slurm job-name prefix |

See also [Environment Variables](/docs/reference/environment-variables#obleth-provisioner).

chunks.title: Slurm Provisioning
chunks.heading: Every tick reports an error
chunks.text:
The Settings → Slurm tab shows the failure text. Common causes:

- `slurm job lookup failed; holding tick` — slurmrestd is unreachable, rejected the JWT, or returned an unexpected status. Use **Test connection**.
- `slurmrestd 404 without a job-not-found error (wrong URL or API version?)` — the URL or API version does not match the cluster.
- `all N tracked slurm jobs reported not found; holding tick` — the provisioner is talking to a different cluster than the one that ran the jobs, or the API version changed. Correct the settings; the next successful tick reconciles normally.

While ticks hold, replica states on model pages are frozen at their last reconciled values.

chunks.title: Slurm Provisioning
chunks.heading: Giving containers a route to cluster nodes
chunks.text:
Before reaching for container plumbing, try the
[node address overrides](#node-address-overrides) in Settings → Slurm: they pin
each node to an IP inside obleth itself, so both the probe and proxied traffic
stop depending on name resolution, and they need no restart.

When the container cannot resolve node names at all, give **both** the
provisioner and the gateway host entries. On Kubernetes use
`nodeResolution.hostAliases`. With Compose, add `extra_hosts` to the
`obleth-provisioner` and `obleth` services in a Compose override file you keep
out of version control, so node addresses never land in git:

```yaml
services:
  obleth-provisioner:
    extra_hosts:
      - "gpu-node-01:10.0.0.10"        # routable IP of the node
  obleth:                               # the model health check + data plane need it too
    extra_hosts:
      - "gpu-node-01:10.0.0.10"
```

`extra_hosts` is applied at container-create time, so recreate the containers to pick it up (`--force-recreate` if Compose thinks they are current).

`extra_hosts` only fixes name→IP resolution; the container must still be able to **route** to that IP (same LAN/VPN). On Docker Desktop, arbitrary LAN cluster hosts are often unreachable — in that case run the provisioner on a login/head node via systemd instead.

chunks.title: Slurm Provisioning
chunks.heading: Holding on uncertainty
chunks.text:
The provisioner takes no destructive action on information it cannot trust. The
tick **holds** (makes no changes and retries next interval) when:

- the Management API returns an error — an error is never read as "no models" or "no replicas";
- a `slurmrestd` job lookup fails. A `404` counts as "job gone" only when its body carries Slurm's job-not-found error (`Invalid job id specified`); a bare `404` from a wrong URL, an unsupported API version, or a proxy holds the tick;
- **every** tracked job behind a live replica (at least two) comes back not found in the same tick. A whole fleet vanishing at once almost always means the wrong cluster, URL, or API version, so the provisioner logs an error and holds instead of marking the fleet lost and resubmitting it.

Management API and `slurmrestd` calls time out after 30 s (5 s to connect);
health probes and warmup requests use their own timeouts. The provisioner does
not follow redirects.

Each tick's outcome — `ok`, `idle` (with the reason), or `error` (with the failure
text) — is reported back to the gateway on the next poll, so the dashboard can
tell a live reconcile loop from a frozen one. When ticks keep failing for 10
minutes while Slurm is enabled, the `slurm_reconcile_held` alert fires, followed
by `slurm_reconcile_recovered` when a tick succeeds again. See
[Step 2](#step-2-configure-slurm-system-settings).

chunks.title: Slurm Provisioning
chunks.heading: How it works
chunks.text:
Every reconcile tick (`OBLETH_PROVISIONER_INTERVAL_SECS`, default 15s):

1. **Read Slurm settings** from the Management API. If Slurm is not configured, not enabled, or has no slurmrestd URL, the tick is skipped (`idle`).
2. **List enabled managed models and every replica row** via the Management API.
3. **Look up each tracked job by id** in `slurmrestd`. The provisioner never lists the whole controller.
4. For each managed model: probe replicas with a running job, submit new jobs when below target, promote healthy replicas into the endpoint pool, mark lost replicas (preempted/finished), and cancel excess jobs.
5. **Drain models that left the managed set** — cancel jobs, detach endpoints, GC rows.

Jobs are submitted with the name prefix `OBLETH_PROVISIONER_JOB_PREFIX` (default
`obleth-`). A job whose replica row cannot be recorded is cancelled immediately,
so no untracked jobs are left on the cluster.

chunks.title: Slurm Provisioning
chunks.heading: How model health is shown for Slurm models
chunks.text:
A Slurm-provisioned model has **no static `api_base`** — its live URL lives in the endpoint pool, which changes as replicas come and go. So the model-level health badge is derived from the **endpoint pool**, not from a single static base:

- **healthy** — at least `min_replicas` live endpoints are **serving**
- **degraded** — some endpoints are serving, but fewer than `min_replicas`
- **unhealthy** — no live endpoint is serving, or none is registered
- **unknown** — every live endpoint came back unverified (a model type that is not auto-probed), so the pool is non-alerting rather than confirmed down

"Serving" counts an endpoint that answered, whether or not the upstream catalog
advertised the model id — the provisioner already confirmed the model was up
before promoting the replica, so reachability is the right signal here. This is
why a Slurm model whose framework renames the id (`qwen2.5-0.5b` vs
`qwen2.5:0.5b`) is not marked down for it.

A replica can be promoted to `healthy` (the provisioner reached it) while the model badge still shows `unhealthy` if the **gateway** cannot reach the endpoint — the two checks run from different places. See [Troubleshooting](#troubleshooting).

chunks.title: Slurm Provisioning
chunks.heading: Kubernetes (Helm)
chunks.text:
Set `provisioner.enabled: true` in your values. `provisioner.intervalSecs`,
`provisioner.restartAfterFailures`, `provisioner.logLevel`, and
`provisioner.resources` map to the environment variables below. slurmrestd
connection details and the master enable switch are configured at runtime in the
dashboard, not in values.

The provisioner is a reconciler and runs as a **singleton**: the chart pins
`replicas: 1` with the `Recreate` rollout strategy so two of them can never submit
jobs for the same model at once. Do not scale it.

chunks.title: Slurm Provisioning
chunks.heading: Limitations
chunks.text:
- **No replica self-registration.** A replica does not announce itself; the provisioner discovers it by probing the replica's port window. `serving_port` is the base of that window, not a fixed port.
- **Single-node health probe.** The health probe targets the first node of a job. Multi-node nodelist bracket-ranges (e.g. `gpu[01-04]`) are not expanded.
- **No autoscaling.** `target_replicas` is a fixed count. The provisioner only maintains it and replaces preempted jobs — it does not scale based on load.
- **Global disable does not drain.** Turning off the master switch idles the provisioner without cancelling existing Slurm jobs. Per-model disable does drain.

chunks.title: Slurm Provisioning
chunks.heading: Monitoring replicas
chunks.text:
On the model detail panel, the **Provisioning** tab appears only for Slurm-provisioned models. It shows:

- **Edit provisioning spec** — change partition, GRES, image, launch command, replica count, etc.
- **Replica panel** — live table of each replica: Slurm job ID, node, state (`pending`, `starting`, `healthy`, `draining`, `lost`), and the latest message (for example `promoted`, or Slurm's pending reason), plus a warning banner when those states can no longer be trusted because reconciliation is held.

Replicas transition through states automatically:
- `pending` — job submitted, waiting on the Slurm queue for an allocation
- `starting` — job submitted, not yet health-probed
- `healthy` — health probe passed; the replica is in the endpoint pool
- `lost` — job preempted or gone; the endpoint is detached and a new job will be submitted on the next tick
- `draining` — the replica is being removed on purpose (scale-down, disable, cancel); the row says why

chunks.title: Slurm Provisioning
chunks.heading: Node address overrides
chunks.text:
Slurm allocations name compute nodes by short hostname (`gpu-node-01`). Where the
pods running obleth resolve those names unreliably — a corporate resolver behind
a long DNS search list, for instance — that flakiness lands on *every* health
probe and on *every* proxied request, because the data plane resolves the
endpoint host per call. One missed lookup then surfaces as an instant
`502 upstream request failed`.

The **Node address overrides** list takes DNS off that path. Each entry is a
hostname and an IP literal; the address must parse as an IP, because a hostname
there would just push the flaky lookup back onto the proxy. The provisioner
registers each replica's endpoint **by IP** and probes by IP, so neither the
health check nor proxied traffic depends on per-request DNS. Edits take effect on
the next provisioner tick without a restart.

Two behaviours follow from this, and neither needs any configuration:

- **Existing endpoints migrate in place.** An endpoint registered by node name is
  rewritten to the resolved address on the next tick, keeping its name,
  priority, weight, and enabled flag, so running replicas stop depending on DNS
  without being re-provisioned.
- **Hostnames without an override resolve robustly.** With the list empty, a
  node name is resolved at promotion with a short retry, a per-node success
  cache, and a last-known-address fallback, so one transient miss does not
  decide where an endpoint points. Model warm-up requests target the resolved

chunks.title: Slurm Provisioning
chunks.heading: Overview
chunks.text:
The Slurm provisioner is an **optional plugin service** — `obleth-provisioner` — that keeps managed models alive on a preemptible [Slurm](https://slurm.schedmd.com/) cluster. It submits batch jobs via `slurmrestd`, probes replicas for health, and promotes each healthy replica into obleth's model endpoint pool so the gateway routes traffic to it automatically.

The provisioner is not part of the obleth core stack. You opt in via **config** — add `slurm` to `COMPOSE_PROFILES` in your `.env` — after which it builds and starts with the same single command as the rest of the stack (or run the binary yourself).

chunks.title: Slurm Provisioning
chunks.heading: Prerequisites
chunks.text:
Before enabling the provisioner, verify that your cluster has:

- **`slurmrestd` running** and reachable from the provisioner. The provisioner authenticates with `X-SLURM-USER-NAME` + `X-SLURM-USER-TOKEN` headers; no username/password login is used.
- **`apptainer` (or `singularity`) installed on all compute nodes** if you use container images. Jobs run as `apptainer exec --nv <image> <launch_command>`. The `--nv` flag passes NVIDIA GPU devices through; Apptainer must be able to find it on the job's `PATH` (`/opt/apptainer/bin` and `/opt/singularity/bin` are included in the job's default `PATH` automatically).
- **A Slurm JWT for authentication.** Generate one on your Slurm head node with `scontrol token`, or via your cluster's token service. The token's user must be the Slurm user you configure, or job cancellation fails with a permission error. Paste the raw JWT into the dashboard — it is encrypted at rest with the gateway's `OBLETH_ENCRYPTION_KEY`.
- **Shared storage accessible by all nodes.** The Apptainer `.sif` image file must be reachable by all nodes that could run the job (NFS, Lustre, GPFS, etc.). The path you give in the `image` field is used as-is on every compute node.

chunks.title: Slurm Provisioning
chunks.heading: Restarting a replica
chunks.text:
Each Slurm-backed endpoint has a **Restart** action on the model's
[Reliability](/docs/guides/reliability-and-failover) tab: it cancels that
replica's Slurm job, and the provisioner launches a fresh one to hold the target
count. Static (non-managed) endpoints are unaffected. Cancelling a replica
deregisters its endpoint **before** the job is killed, so it leaves the routing
pool immediately rather than serving a few more requests into a dying process.

chunks.title: Slurm Provisioning
chunks.heading: Self-healing zombie replicas
chunks.text:
A Slurm job can report `RUNNING` while the inference server inside it is dead or
wedged. The provisioner restarts such a replica on either of two independent
signals:

1. **Its own probe has been failing for a sustained window.** Each tick the
   provisioner probes every `healthy` replica whose job reports `RUNNING`. A miss
   increments a per-replica counter; a pass **decays** it by one rather than
   resetting it. Once the counter reaches
   `OBLETH_PROVISIONER_RESTART_AFTER_FAILURES` (default **20**, `0` disables), the
   replica is restarted. The decay is what keeps a *flapping* replica alive: a
   busy single-threaded server such as llama.cpp misses the occasional probe and
   passes the next, so its counter hovers near zero and never trips, while a
   genuinely dead server climbs steadily. At the default 15 s tick, 20 ticks is
   roughly five minutes of sustained failure. Setting this very low (a few ticks)
   cancels healthy-but-busy replicas and resubmits them in a loop.
2. **The gateway's endpoint check says the server can't infer.** The gateway
   runs a real one-token inference against each registered endpoint on a slow
   cadence. Two consecutive `unhealthy` verdicts on a recent check are enough —
   this catches the zombie the provisioner's own `GET` probe cannot see, a server
   that answers metadata instantly but hangs forever on actual inference.

Restarts are capped at **one per model per tick**, so a probe-side network
problem rolls replicas gradually instea

chunks.title: Slurm Provisioning
chunks.heading: Shutdown
chunks.text:
On SIGTERM or Ctrl-C the provisioner finishes the tick in progress and exits
before the next one; a tick is never interrupted, so a submitted job is always
recorded. The Helm chart gives the provisioner pod a 60 s termination grace
period for this.

chunks.title: Slurm Provisioning
chunks.heading: Step 2: Configure Slurm system settings
chunks.text:
Open the dashboard → **Settings → Slurm**.

| Field | Description |
| --- | --- |
| **Enable Slurm** | Master switch. The provisioner idles until this is on. |
| **slurmrestd URL** | Base URL of your slurmrestd, e.g. `http://slurm.example.internal:6820`. Required when enabled. Checked against the same outbound URL policy as model `api_base` values. |
| **API version** | slurmrestd API version segment, e.g. `v0.0.40`. Match this to the version your cluster exposes at `/openapi/v3`. Default `v0.0.40`. |
| **Slurm user** | The Slurm username whose JWT you are using. Required when enabled. |
| **JWT** | The raw Slurm JWT. Write-only: leave blank when saving to keep the stored value. Encrypted at rest with `OBLETH_ENCRYPTION_KEY`. |
| **Node address overrides** | Optional list of compute-node hostname → IP entries. Empty (the default) resolves node names through DNS. See below. |

After saving, click **Test connection** to verify:
- **JWT health** — whether a JWT is set, whether it is expired, and when it expires.
- **slurmrestd ping** — whether the `GET /slurm/{version}/ping` endpoint responds with 2xx and how fast.

The provisioner reads these settings from the Management API on every tick, so changes take effect within one interval without a restart.

The **Settings → Slurm** tab also shows whether the provisioner process is
currently running and, when the provisioner reports it, its **version** (and short
commit). Because the provisioner ships as its own image and is deployed

chunks.title: Slurm Provisioning
chunks.heading: Step 3: Create a Slurm-provisioned model
chunks.text:
When creating a model in the dashboard → **Models → New model**, choose **Slurm provisioned** as the hosting mode. This choice is made at creation time — you cannot change it after creation.

Slurm-provisioned models have **no static upstream endpoint**. The provisioner registers replicas dynamically as they become healthy, so you do not provide `api_base` or `api_key` during creation. Boons that call the model on a request's behalf route through a healthy endpoint, so they work on managed models too.

Picking that hosting option lists the available [deployment recipes](/docs/guides/deployment-recipes) — an sbatch
script an admin has already tested, with a small YAML header carrying the routing
metadata (engine, API model name, port, health path, replica targets) and the
default placement. Deploying one creates the model route and its managed spec in a
single step. Recipes are read from `OBLETH_RECIPES_DIR` (default: `recipes/` beside
the dashboard) and from recipes authored on the dashboard's Recipes page; the deploy dialog
pre-fills **Deploy overrides** (partition, QoS, replicas, time limit, plus any
variables the recipe declares) and shows the launch script in an editable box.
Overrides and script edits apply to that deployment only — the recipe file is
unchanged. `#SBATCH` directives in the body are lifted into the submit fields,
because `slurmrestd` ignores them.

Everything below describes what the provisioner does with the resulting spec, and
applies equally to a spec

chunks.title: Slurm Provisioning
chunks.heading: systemd
chunks.text:
A unit file ships at `deploy/systemd/obleth-provisioner.service`. Put env vars in `/etc/obleth/provisioner.env`, then:

```bash
sudo cp deploy/systemd/obleth-provisioner.service /etc/systemd/system/
sudo cp obleth/target/release/obleth-provisioner /usr/local/bin/
sudo systemctl daemon-reload
sudo systemctl enable --now obleth-provisioner
```

chunks.title: Slurm Provisioning
chunks.heading: Warmup on promotion
chunks.text:
A replica passes its health check as soon as the inference server answers
`/health`, but its **first** request can still be slow — the model has to do its
first forward pass (graph capture, cache warmup), which on a cold box can take
long enough to surface to a user as a `502`/`504`. To avoid that, the provisioner
fires **one throwaway request** at each replica right after it is promoted, so the
cold first-token cost is paid by the gateway instead of by the first real user.

Warmup is on by default. Tune or disable it with
`OBLETH_PROVISIONER_WARMUP_TIMEOUT_SECS` (default `600`s; `0` disables).

chunks.title: Slurm Provisioning
chunks.heading: When a launch fails
chunks.text:
When `slurmrestd` rejects a submit — a bad account, partition, or QoS — the reason
is stored on the managed spec (`last_provision_error`) and shown as a banner on the
model. Fix the cause and dismiss the banner; it returns on its own if the next
launch also fails. Dismissing it is recorded in the audit log. Cancel failures
are logged with the response body from `slurmrestd` (for example
`Access/permission denied` from `slurm_kill_job2`), not just the HTTP status, so
causes like a JWT user / job owner mismatch are visible.

The Placement and Service fields on the Provisioning tab are validated in the
browser before the save — time-limit format, port range, replica counts, node and
CPU numbers — so a malformed value is highlighted inline instead of surfacing as
an opaque `slurmrestd` 500.

chunks.title: Speculative Drafting
chunks.heading: Billing and observability
chunks.text:
- The client's request is billed as a normal request for the **target** model,
  with the shipped draft's token counts when the draft was released.
- Draft calls are recorded as `speculation_draft` helper rows under the drafter's
  name, and verification prefills as `speculation_verify` rows under the target
  model's name. Both count against term budgets. A draft abandoned mid-stream
  before release is not billed, because its usage is unknown and dropping the
  connection stops its generation.
- `x-obleth-boons` lists `speculation` when the cascade was armed for the request.
  Whether the draft shipped, deferred, or escalated is logged by the gateway
  with the reason.

See [Model Boons](/docs/guides/model-boons#how-boons-work) for how helper rows
appear in the request log.

chunks.title: Speculative Drafting
chunks.heading: Category gates
chunks.text:
With a classify model set and at least one gate defined, each request is first
classified into the gate tags. A gate with `speculate: false` sends that
category straight to the target model before any draft is requested, at no draft
cost. A gate with `speculate: true` overrides the ship floors (`agree_min`,
`lp_min`) for that category; the abort floors stay global. A request that matches
no gate follows `speculation_unlisted_categories_speculate`.

chunks.title: Speculative Drafting
chunks.heading: Configuring a target model
chunks.text:
Speculation is configured on the **target** model — the model clients call. On
the **Models** page, tick **speculation** under **Boons** to reveal the model's
cascade settings:

| Field | Dashboard label | Meaning |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `draft_model` | Drafter | The registered chat model that writes this model's drafts. Empty uses the fleet default from **Settings → Boons**. It should be several times faster than the target. |
| `verify_api_base` | Scoring endpoint URL (under **Advanced wiring**) | A direct, non-gateway URL of a deployment of this model whose backend supports `prompt_logprobs` and exposes a `/tokenize` endpoint at the server root. Empty uses the fleet URL template. |
| `verify_upstream_model` | Scoring endpoint serves | The model name the scoring backend serves, when it differs from this model's `upstream_model`. Empty means the same name. |

The verifier is synthesized from the target model itself, with its address
swapped to the scoring endpoint, so verification calls carry the target model's
upstream key and are billed under the target model's name at its rates. The
scoring endpoint must be a direct service URL: gateway-routed bases often do not
forward `/tokenize`.

```bash
curl -X PUT http://localhost:9180/api/v1/models/$MODEL_ID \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{
    "boons": ["speculation"],
    "draft_model": "qwen3-4b",
    "verify_api_base": "http://glm-scoring.serving.svc.cluster.local:8000/v1"

chunks.title: Speculative Drafting
chunks.heading: Fleet settings
chunks.text:
**Settings → Boons → Speculation** holds the fleet-wide switch, defaults, and
gates. Two profiles set every threshold, cadence value, and category gate at
once:

- **Calibrated** (recommended) drafts only in the categories where verification
  measured reliably precise (coding, math, summarization, writing), each with its
  own tuned floor, and sends categories that never verify well straight to the
  target before any draft cost. It requires a classify model.
- **Cautious** holds every request to one strict global gate (the server
  defaults) with no category routing, and works without a classify model.

Editing any value under **Advanced** switches the panel to **Custom**.

| Field | Default | Meaning |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `speculation_enabled` | `false` | Master switch |
| `speculation_draft_model` | none | Fleet-default drafter for targets without their own `draft_model` |
| `speculation_classify_model` | none | A small registered model that tags each request with one of the category-gate tags before drafting. None applies the default gate to everything. |
| `speculation_agree_min` | `0.5` | Ship floor: minimum agreement, `0`–`1` |
| `speculation_lp_min` | `-1.0` | Ship floor: minimum mean log-probability (≤ 0) |
| `speculation_abort_agree` | `0.45` | Streaming abort floor on agreement |
| `speculation_abort_lp` | `-1.6` | Streaming abort floor on mean log-probability |
| `speculation_first_chunk_tokens` | `80` | Draft tokens before the first verification |
| `speculati

chunks.title: Speculative Drafting
chunks.heading: How the cascade works
chunks.text:
```text
client ──▶ obleth                          (request for the target model)
             │  admitted, budget reserved
             ├──▶ drafter                  writes the answer
             ├──▶ scoring endpoint         prompt_logprobs over the draft tokens
             │  gate: agreement and mean logprob above the ship floors?
             │     yes → release the draft to the client
             │     no  → abandon, dispatch to the target model as normal
client ◀─────┘
```

1. **Admission first.** Speculation runs after fairshare admission and budget
   reservation and before the normal upstream dispatch. The request is admitted
   and billed as a request for the target model either way.
2. **Draft.** The drafter answers the conversation, with `max_tokens` capped at
   `max_draft_tokens` and the configured `draft_chat_template_kwargs` applied to
   draft calls only.
3. **Verify.** The scoring endpoint scores the draft in one prefill. Two numbers
   come back: the **agreement** (the fraction of draft tokens the target model
   would itself have picked first) and the **mean log-probability** of the draft
   tokens.
4. **Gate.** A draft at or above both ship floors (`agree_min`, `lp_min`) is
   released. Anything else falls through to the target model.

Nothing is sent to the client until a verified span exists, so every failure
before release — a draft error, a verify error, a failed gate, or the
pre-release timeout — ends in an **abstain**: the request continues down

chunks.title: Speculative Drafting
chunks.heading: Interaction with image generation
chunks.text:
A model granted both `speculation` and
[`image_generation`](/docs/guides/model-boons#the-image-generation-boon) keeps
both. The image tool does not rule speculation out; instead, the per-request
classification decides. When the image tool is armed and the request's intent
cannot be classified (no classifier, a failed classification, or no matching
tag), speculation abstains, because a drafted answer can never produce the
picture the user may have asked for.

chunks.title: Speculative Drafting
chunks.heading: Overview
chunks.text:
The **speculation** [boon](/docs/guides/model-boons) answers requests with a fast
drafter model whenever the target model itself verifies the draft. A client asks
for the target model as usual; obleth has a smaller, faster model write the
answer, then has a scoring deployment of the target model check every draft
token before anything reaches the client. A draft that passes is shipped. One
that does not is abandoned, and the target model answers normally.

Unlike routing, which guesses from the prompt which model can handle a request,
speculation always lets the drafter try and always has the target model audit
the actual draft. Verification is a single prefill over the draft tokens with
`prompt_logprobs`, which is far cheaper than the target model decoding the same
tokens, so trying the cheap model first and verifying with the expensive one is
affordable.

chunks.title: Speculative Drafting
chunks.heading: Scoring URL template
chunks.text:
`speculation_verify_url_template` locates scoring endpoints for a whole fleet. It
may contain `{upstream}` (the model's `upstream_model`) and `{model}` (its
`model_name`), for example:

```text
http://{upstream}.serving.svc.cluster.local:8000/v1
```

- Placeholders are allowed in the **host** and the **path or query**, never in
  the scheme or credentials; a template that puts them there is rejected on save.
- A value substituted into the host must be plain DNS labels and the filled host
  must not be an IP literal, so a model's fields can name a per-model service but
  never an address such as a cloud metadata endpoint. A value substituted into
  the path is percent-encoded as one component.
- A template that cannot be filled safely for a model means that model has no
  scoring endpoint and is served normally.
- The template passes the same outbound destination policy as `api_base` when it
  is saved, and again when a backup is restored.

Only set the template once the fleet's backends can serve `prompt_logprobs`
scoring; pointing it at backends that cannot handle it can take them down.

chunks.title: Speculative Drafting
chunks.heading: Streaming
chunks.text:
For a streaming client the gate has three zones, evaluated as the draft grows:

| Zone | Condition | What happens |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Pass | agreement ≥ `agree_min` and mean logprob ≥ `lp_min` | The verified span is released to the client |
| Abort | agreement < `abort_agree` or mean logprob < `abort_lp` | Drafting stops and the target model answers |
| Defer | anything in between | Keep drafting and decide later |

The first verification happens after `first_chunk_tokens` draft tokens, so a
passing draft starts streaming early and a failing one is abandoned cheaply;
later verifications run every `chunk_tokens`. If nothing has been released by
`decide_by_tokens` and the draft still sits below the gate, the cascade gives up
and the target model answers. Released spans are paced at `pace_ms` per delta so
they play back as a continuous stream rather than in bursts.

Once a span has been released the cascade owns the stream. If a later chunk fails
the gate, the target model **continues** the already-released text through its
chat template (`continue_final_message`) rather than restarting, so the client
never sees its answer rewritten.

chunks.title: Speculative Drafting
chunks.heading: Which requests are eligible
chunks.text:
A request is drafted only when all of these hold:

- The speculation boon is **enabled** globally and the target model has
  **opted into** `speculation`.
- The target has a **drafter** (its own `draft_model`, or the fleet default) that
  is registered, enabled, and not the target itself.
- The target has a **scoring endpoint** (its own `verify_api_base`, or the fleet
  URL template).
- The request is a chat completion whose messages contain only text (image or
  audio parts make it ineligible), asks for a single choice (`n` of 1), and does
  not set `response_format`, `logit_bias`, `modalities`, `audio`, `logprobs`,
  `top_logprobs`, `prompt_logprobs`, or `echo`.
- The key is not an internal probe key; health probes always measure the target
  model itself.
- No other boon owns the response. Structured output, output guardrails, and a
  real MCP tool loop must see the target model's own answer, so speculation
  stands aside for them.

chunks.title: Training a Model
chunks.heading: Adapting it to your own task
chunks.text:
The routing tags are incidental. To distill a judge for any
[verdicts](/docs/guides/verdicts) workload, the task definition changes and
nothing else does. A task supplies four things:

1. **The questions.** Replace the routing tags and difficulty score with your
   own booleans, choices, and scores — inclusion criteria for a literature
   screen, severity levels for incident triage, a grading rubric.
2. **The rendering** — the exact strings production will send, which is what
   the student is trained on.
3. **The corpus.** Point the labeler at text from your domain. Public data
   keeps the recipe reproducible; your own archives make the student sharper
   on what you actually see.
4. **The probe set** used in stage 0 and the discrimination check — a handful
   of inputs whose correct answer is not in doubt.

The teacher audit, the soft-label ensemble, the KL-over-labels objective, the
in-set mass term, and the calibration checks all carry over untouched.

If you substitute your own operational data for public corpora, that is a
governance question as much as a technical one. Confirm the data
classification permits it, scrub identifiers, and obtain consent where the
text came from people. Distillation copies whatever is in the corpus into a
model you will keep.

chunks.title: Training a Model
chunks.heading: Cost and fleet impact
chunks.text:
Each input costs one prefill of its text plus one decoded token per question,
because the gateway fans the questions out over a shared prompt prefix against
one pinned replica. On the routing task that is roughly 350–900 prompt tokens
and 9 completion tokens per input per teacher.

Run it under a **dedicated tenant at fairshare weight 1**, the minimum.
Labeling is bulk background work: at the lowest weight it uses capacity other
tenants leave idle and loses every contended admission decision to
higher-weight tenants, so a multi-hour campaign barely affects interactive
traffic. Requests already in flight are not preempted. See
[Fairshare Engine](/docs/concepts/fairshare-engine) and
[Priority Boost](/docs/guides/priority-boost).

chunks.title: Training a Model
chunks.heading: Overview
chunks.text:
Most of the judgment work an application asks a language model to do is not
open-ended generation. It is classification: *is this ticket urgent, which
team owns it, does this abstract match my inclusion criteria, how rigorous is
this study, which model should serve this request.* Those jobs do not need a
100B-parameter model, but they are usually given one anyway, because nobody
has a labeled dataset and a small model prompted cold is unreliable.

This guide is the way out of that. The large models you already serve act as
**teachers** through [`POST /v1/verdicts`](/docs/guides/verdicts), generating
soft labels on public text; a sub-1B **student** learns to reproduce their
probability distributions in a single token. The result answers in around
100ms for a fraction of a cent, and it can be retrained whenever the task
changes.

```
public prompts ──> POST /v1/verdicts ──> soft labels ──> distillation ──> student
                   (teachers on your        (JSONL)      (KL over the     (sub-1B)
                    own hardware)                         label set)
```

Nothing leaves your cluster: the prompts come from public datasets or your own
corpus, the judging runs on your own models, and the student trains on your own
hardware.

chunks.title: Training a Model
chunks.heading: Reasoning models make poor teachers
chunks.text:
The most useful finding: **`gpt-oss-120b` answers "no" at p=0.89 to *is this
math?* on a grade-school math problem** — confidently and wrongly. Give it room
to think and it answers correctly.

This is not a gateway bug. A verdicts call reads the model's *first* token, and
for a reasoning-native model the judgment lives in a scratchpad the first token
necessarily skips. The gateway can make such a model *answerable* — the harmony
splice and the think prefill both do — but it cannot make a snap answer as good
as a reasoned one. Prefer instruction-tuned, non-reasoning models as teachers,
and verify rather than assume.

A candidate that returns errors is a fleet problem, not a judgment problem: fix
the crash-looping replicas, then re-audit.

chunks.title: Training a Model
chunks.heading: Sanity-check before training
chunks.text:
Per-source averages should show an obvious diagonal. From a real run of the
routing task:

| source | coding | creative | math | vision |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `gsm8k` | 0.22 | 0.09 | **1.00** | 0.12 |
| `magicoder` | **0.99** | 0.23 | 0.35 | 0.27 |
| `ultrachat` | 0.14 | **0.51** | 0.03 | 0.30 |
| `wildchat` | 0.16 | 0.46 | 0.04 | 0.26 |

A flat table means the teachers are not discriminating and stage 0 was skipped
or its result ignored. Teacher choice shows up in the yield too: including one
poor teacher pushed the disagreement-rejection rate to **83%** of inputs, while
two audited teachers dropped it to about **14%**.

chunks.title: Training a Model
chunks.heading: Stage 0: audit your teachers
chunks.text:
This is the stage people skip, and it decides whether the whole exercise
works. A large model is not automatically a good judge.

Run a handful of unambiguous inputs through `/v1/verdicts` and measure the gap
between p(yes) on categories that fit and categories that do not. Measured on
one production fleet, on the routing task:

| model | p(yes) when it fits | when it does not | margin | |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `glm-5-3` | 0.994 | 0.116 | **0.878** | good teacher |
| `gemma4-31b-it` | 0.700 | 0.000 | **0.700** | good teacher |
| `qwen3-235b-a22b-instruct-2507` | 0.750 | 0.171 | **0.579** | good teacher |
| `gpt-oss-120b` | 0.275 | 0.142 | 0.133 | under-fires |
| `olmo3-32b-instruct` | 0.174 | 0.098 | 0.076 | under-fires |
| `llama4-maverick-17b` | 0.009 | 0.047 | −0.038 | says no to everything |

Model size predicts nothing: the 31B model is the second-best judge, and two
far larger ones are unusable. Use three teachers from the top band if the
fleet allows — with two, the ensemble has no way to break a tie, and one
eccentric judgment moves the label by half its range.

chunks.title: Training a Model
chunks.heading: Stage 1: generate soft labels
chunks.text:
Stream prompts from a corpus and ask each teacher every question in one
`/v1/verdicts` round trip. The routing example uses four ungated,
redistributable datasets:

| source | licence | role in the mix |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `allenai/WildChat-1M` | ODC-BY | real user traffic — the in-distribution bulk |
| `HuggingFaceH4/ultrachat_200k` | MIT | instruction diversity |
| `ise-uiuc/Magicoder-OSS-Instruct-75K` | MIT | `coding` ballast |
| `openai/gsm8k` | MIT | `math` ballast |

Streaming means nothing is downloaded up front and no HuggingFace token is
needed. Runs are resumable.

**Keep the distributions, not the argmax.** A row recording `p(coding) = 0.62`
teaches the student to be uncertain exactly where the teachers were uncertain,
and that is what makes its confidence worth thresholding on later. Collapsing
to a hard label throws that away and produces a model that is confidently
wrong on the ambiguous middle — the worst possible failure mode for anything
downstream that acts on the answer.

**Filter per question, not per input.** Teachers routinely agree on eight
questions and split on the ninth; on a real sample the median worst-question
disagreement was 0.77. Rejecting the whole input for that discards eight good
labels to avoid one bad one.

chunks.title: Training a Model
chunks.heading: Stage 2: distill
chunks.text:
The student is never trained to write. The loss is the KL divergence between
its renormalized distribution **over the answer labels** and the teachers' —
precisely the quantity the gateway reads at inference, so training and serving
optimize the same number.

Three details carry most of the quality:

**Template fidelity.** The student must be trained on the exact bytes it will
be sent in production: the shared system message carrying the state, the
per-question user message, and the answer labels, exactly as described under
[How it works](/docs/guides/verdicts#how-it-works). Pin your training-side
renderer to that format with a test, so changing the prompt without
regenerating training data fails the build instead of quietly degrading the
deployed model. If you train on one string and serve another, your measured
accuracy does not describe the deployed model.

**Own the chat template.** Qwen3's stock template opens a `<think>` block,
which would put a scratchpad token — not an answer — in the first generated
position, forcing the gateway into its think-prefill retry on every fresh
process. A judge that emits one token has no use for a scratchpad, so the
fine-tuned model ships with plain ChatML instead.

**Reward in-set mass.** The gateway computes confidence as
`(1 − H/ln K) × in_set_mass`, so a student that leaks probability onto
unrelated tokens has its answers discounted even when they are right. This is
not a small effect: a stock Qwen3-0.6B puts about **4e-11** of its fi

chunks.title: Training a Model
chunks.heading: Stage 3: evaluate, then deploy
chunks.text:
Measure three things, in order of how much they matter:

1. **Discrimination** — p(yes) when a category fits versus when it does not.
   Requires no held-out labels, and a margin below 0.5 means the model is
   unusable no matter how good everything else looks.
2. **Agreement** with the teacher ensemble on held-out inputs.
3. **Calibration** — expected calibration error and Brier score. Anything
   thresholding on these probabilities is better served by an honestly
   uncertain model than a confidently wrong one.

Deployment needs no gateway change — the student is just a registered chat
model, and it answers `/v1/verdicts` calls like any other:

```bash
vllm serve runs/model-v1 --served-model-name my-judge --max-model-len 2048
```

For the routing case specifically, register the served model and point the
router's classifier at it (the classifier also needs `classifier_enabled`):

```bash
curl -X PUT "$ADMIN/api/v1/settings/auto-router" \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $ADMIN_TOKEN" -H 'content-type: application/json' \
  -d '{"classifier_enabled": true, "classifier_model": "my-judge"}'
```

Verify along the real deployment path by evaluating the *served* model, not
just the checkpoint. For routing you can also compare decisions against the
incumbent with
[simulate](/docs/guides/auto-model-routing#simulating-a-decision), which runs
the live classifier without dispatching anything:

```bash
curl -X POST "$ADMIN/api/v1/router/simulate" \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $ADMIN_TOKEN"

chunks.title: Training a Model
chunks.heading: The worked example
chunks.text:
The running example throughout is the
[intent classifier](/docs/guides/auto-model-routing#the-intent-classifier-optional)
the `auto` router consults to tag incoming requests, with measurements from a
real deployment. The classifier asks up to nine questions per request: one
yes/no per routing tag (eight tags), plus a three-level difficulty score.

The training pipeline is not part of obleth. The gateway's part is serving
`/v1/verdicts` to the teachers and, afterwards, serving the student like any
other chat model; the labeling, training, and evaluation run in whatever
tooling you use for fine-tuning. Keep that pipeline task-agnostic: a **task**
supplies the questions, the production prompt rendering, the corpora, and a
probe set, and everything else (teacher selection, the ensemble, the loss, the
evaluation) is shared. The [last section](#adapting-it-to-your-own-task) covers
defining your own task.

chunks.title: Training a Model
chunks.heading: When this is worth doing
chunks.text:
Distillation pays off when a judgment is **high-volume, narrow, and
repeated**. Screening a corpus of abstracts, triaging every inbound ticket,
scoring every model output against a rubric, classifying every request before
routing it. If you run the judgment a hundred times, prompt a big model; if
you run it a hundred thousand times, train a small one.

It is also the answer to a question researchers ask constantly: *how do I get
a classifier when I have no labeled data?* You do have labeled data — you just
have to generate it from models that already know the answer.

chunks.title: Training a Model
chunks.heading: Why not simply prompt a small model
chunks.text:
Because small models are unreliable judges out of the box, in two specific
ways that are easy to miss and easy to measure. Both were found on a
production fleet, not in theory.

**Yes-bias.** A 30B model used as a classifier answered "yes" to *every*
category — p(yes) between 0.84 and 0.98 across the board, including `vision`
for a text-only prompt. Every input looked like every class, so its output
carried no information at all.

**Position bias.** Asked instead to pick the single best option from a
lettered list, the same model put about 0.7 on whichever option happened to be
listed first. Rotating the option order changed its answer.

Distillation fixes both, because the training set contains thousands of
confident *no* examples that no amount of prompt engineering supplies.

chunks.title: Verdicts API
chunks.heading: Admission and billing
chunks.text:
- The request is authenticated and gated like any data-plane request (see
  [Authentication](/docs/reference/authentication)), including the tenant's
  model allowlist.
- The whole fan-out takes **one** permit in the model's fairshare pool, so a
  32-question request cannot multiply a tenant's concurrency. Admission is
  bounded by `OBLETH_ADMISSION_TIMEOUT_SECS`; a timeout returns 503 "timed out
  waiting for model capacity" with `Retry-After: 5`.
- Tenant and key budgets are reserved at admission from a no-cache estimate
  (the state and question for every question) and settled once with the summed
  real usage, under `request_type` `verdict`. There is one usage row per
  request, not per question; its `ttft_ms` is the fastest question's time.
- When any question fails, the usage of the calls that did run is still
  billed. A client that disconnects mid fan-out is recorded as unbilled.
- When the key has tracing enabled, each question is a `verdict:q:<id>` span
  carrying its answer, confidence, label mass, token counts, and whether the
  think prefill or harmony splice was used.
- Boons, the response cache, and guardrails do not apply to this endpoint.

chunks.title: Verdicts API
chunks.heading: Calling it from code
chunks.text:
`/v1/verdicts` is one HTTP POST; no SDK is required. From Python:

```python
import requests

GATEWAY = "http://localhost:8088"
KEY = "sk_..."

def verdicts(state, questions, model="auto"):
    r = requests.post(
        f"{GATEWAY}/v1/verdicts",
        headers={"Authorization": f"Bearer {KEY}"},
        json={"state": state, "model": model, "questions": questions},
        timeout=120,
    )
    r.raise_for_status()
    return r.json()["verdicts"]

v = verdicts(
    {"abstract": abstract_text},
    {
        "on_topic": {"type": "boolean",
                     "instructions": "Is this abstract about machine learning for genomics?"},
        "rigor":    {"type": "score",
                     "instructions": "Methodological rigor of the described study",
                     "criteria": ["No methodology", "Weak", "Adequate", "Strong", "Exemplary"]},
    },
)
if v["on_topic"]["probabilities"]["true"] > 0.85 and v["on_topic"]["confidence"] > 0.5:
    keep(abstract_text, rigor=v["rigor"]["expected_value"])
```

For batch workloads, loop states through the same `questions` map. Keeping the
question set stable and varying only the state keeps the per-question prompt
text warm in the backend's prefix cache across requests to the same model.

chunks.title: Verdicts API
chunks.heading: Confidence
chunks.text:
`confidence` is `(1 − H / ln K) × in_set_mass`, where `H` is the entropy of the
renormalized distribution over the `K` answer labels and `in_set_mass` is the
share of the model's raw first-token probability that landed on recognized
answer labels at all. It is separate from the probabilities:

- A 50/50 boolean has a confidence near 0, even though both probabilities are
  valid.
- A model that mostly wanted to emit something other than an answer label also
  scores low, even when the little label mass it had was lopsided.

Thresholds on `probabilities` answer "how likely is yes"; thresholds on
`confidence` answer "did the model engage with the label set." A pipeline that
acts automatically on verdicts should usually gate on both.

chunks.title: Verdicts API
chunks.heading: Errors
chunks.text:
Errors use the OpenAI-style envelope,
`{"error": {"message": "…", "type": "obleth_gateway_error"}}`.

| Status | Message (examples) |
| --- | --- |
| 400 | `invalid JSON body`; `invalid request: …`; `` `model` is required ``; `too many questions: 40 (maximum 32)`; `question 'x': a choice needs at least 2 options`; `verdicts requires a chat model; 'x' is registered as 'embedding'` |
| 401 | `missing bearer token`; `invalid api key`; `invalid token` |
| 403 | `model is disabled`; `model not permitted for tenant`; `tenant term budget exhausted`; `api key term budget exhausted` |
| 404 | `model 'x' is not registered` |
| 413 | `request body too large`; `rendered state is too large (…)` |
| 429 | `token budget exceeded` |
| 502 | `question 'x' on model 'y': …` when any question fails, for example `backend returned no logprobs (…)` or `model produced no recognizable answer label (is this a reasoning/thinking model?)`; `model has no usable upstream endpoint` |
| 503 | `timed out waiting for model capacity`; `no model is available to satisfy the auto request`; `scheduler unavailable`; `budget check failed` (Redis unavailable and fail-open off) |

chunks.title: Verdicts API
chunks.heading: How it works
chunks.text:
1. **One prompt per question.** The state is rendered once into a system
   message that is byte-identical across every question in the request. The
   question, its criteria, and an answer instruction go in the user message.
2. **Single-token answer labels.** Boolean questions answer `yes` or `no`;
   choice options and score levels are assigned letters `A` to `Z` in a
   deterministic order (choice options in sorted name order, which is part of
   the API). Letters are single tokens in mainstream vocabularies. Digits are
   not used, because `"10"` is two tokens on SentencePiece vocabularies and `1`
   is an ambiguous prefix of it.
3. **One greedy single-token call.** Each question becomes a chat-completions
   call with `max_tokens: 1`, `temperature: 0`, `logprobs: true`, and
   `top_logprobs: 20`. The first token's `top_logprobs` is the whole answer
   distribution.
4. **Renormalize over the label set.** Mass on token variants that normalize to
   a label (surrounding whitespace trimmed; for booleans also case and trailing
   punctuation) is summed per label and renormalized into `probabilities`. Mass
   outside the label set does not change the answer; it only lowers
   `confidence` through `in_set_mass`.

All questions of one request are sent concurrently to a single upstream
endpoint. Because they share a byte-identical prompt prefix, a backend with
prefix caching (vLLM `--enable-prefix-caching`, SGLang's RadixAttention)
prefills the state once, and each further questi

chunks.title: Verdicts API
chunks.heading: Limits
chunks.text:
| Limit | Value | On violation |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Questions per request | 1 to 32 | 400 |
| Choice options | 2 to 26 | 400 |
| Score levels | 2 to 10 | 400 |
| Question id | 64 bytes, non-empty | 400 |
| Choice option name | 200 bytes, non-empty | 400 |
| `state` type | string, object, or array | 400 |
| Rendered state | 2 MiB | 413 |

chunks.title: Verdicts API
chunks.heading: Making a high-volume verdict cheaper
chunks.text:
A verdict answered by a large model costs what that model costs. When the same
question set runs over a large corpus, it can be worth spending one batch of
those calls to distill a small model that answers the same questions directly:
the large models label a sample, a small student learns their probability
distributions, and the student then serves the same verdicts at a fraction of
the cost. See [Training a Model](/docs/guides/training-a-model).

chunks.title: Verdicts API
chunks.heading: Overview
chunks.text:
`POST /v1/verdicts` evaluates one **state** (a support ticket, a document, a
record, a conversation, your application's current state) against a set of
typed **questions** and returns a typed verdict for each: a boolean, a chosen
option, or a score level, each with a probability distribution over the
possible answers and a confidence. No prose comes back, so there is nothing to
parse and no output schema to coax the model into: the answer type is enforced
by construction.

Any registered `chat` model serves it. Each question is one single-token call to
the route's ordinary chat backend, and the first token's `top_logprobs` become
the distribution, so the backend must return logprobs on chat completions
(vLLM, SGLang, and llama.cpp servers do). No separate classifier model or
external service is involved. [How it works](#how-it-works) explains the
mechanics.

chunks.title: Verdicts API
chunks.heading: Question types
chunks.text:
| `type` | `criteria` | Answer labels | Verdict `value` | `probabilities` |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `boolean` | Optional `{"true": …, "false": …}` describing what yes and no mean | `yes` / `no` | `true` / `false` | `{"true": p, "false": p}` |
| `choice` | Required object: option name to a description (`null` for none) | Letters `A`, `B`, … assigned to options in sorted name order | The chosen option name | Option name to probability |
| `score` | Required array of level descriptions, lowest level first | Letters `A`, `B`, … for levels 1, 2, … | The 1-based level | An array in level order |

One request may mix question types freely. Every question is independent.

chunks.title: Verdicts API
chunks.heading: Reasoning models
chunks.text:
A reasoning model (GLM, Qwen thinking variants, DeepSeek-R1-style templates)
spends its first token inside a `<think>` scratchpad, so the plain call's
first-token distribution is scratchpad text, not an answer label. When a plain
call succeeds but less than 5% of its first-token mass lands on answer labels,
the gateway retries that question once, past the scratchpad:

- **Think prefill.** The assistant turn is pre-opened with a closed, empty
  `<think></think>` block and the backend is asked to continue it
  (`continue_final_message`, supported by vLLM and SGLang).
- **Harmony splice.** Models whose reasoning lives in harmony channels (the
  gpt-oss family) are recognized by the plain call's first token being a
  control token such as `<|channel|>`. The question is retried through the
  backend's `/v1/completions` endpoint with a harmony prompt whose assistant
  turn is already open in the final channel.

A retry that reaches the 5% floor is remembered for that model for the life of
the gateway process, so later requests go straight to the working form and pay
no double calls. Backends that reject the continuation fields never see them on
a model where the plain call works. When neither attempt reaches the floor, the
attempt with more label mass is used. Both attempts are billed.

chunks.heading: Request

chunks.title: Verdicts API
chunks.heading: Transient failures
chunks.text:
A 5xx, an unreachable upstream, or a degenerate 200 (invalid JSON, or missing or
empty logprobs, as crash-looping replicas behind a load balancer can produce)
gets one retry after 50 ms. If any question still fails, the whole request
returns 502 with a message naming the question and the model, for example
`question 'is_urgent' on model 'glm-5-3': …`.

chunks.title: Verdicts API
chunks.heading: Trying it in the dashboard
chunks.text:
The Playground has a **Verdicts** mode: enter a state (JSON is detected
automatically), pick a chat model or `auto`, build questions, and read each
verdict as probability bars with its confidence, alongside the request id for
looking up the per-question spans. See [Playground](/docs/guides/playground).

chunks.title: Verdicts API
chunks.heading: When to use it
chunks.text:
Use verdicts wherever you currently ask a chat model a question and parse its
prose, or force JSON mode for what is really a classification:

- **Triage and routing**: is this ticket urgent, which team owns it, how
  frustrated is the customer.
- **Gating**: should this request be escalated, blocked, or auto-approved, with
  a probability to threshold on instead of a bare yes/no.
- **Scoring and evaluation**: rate an answer against a rubric's ordered levels;
  `expected_value` gives a scalar from the full distribution rather than a
  single level.
- **Matching and deduplication**: "is record A the same entity as record B?" as
  a boolean over a state containing both records.
- **Batch labeling**: classify a corpus by looping states through the same
  question set; the shared prompt structure makes warm calls cheap.

Because you get distributions rather than just answers, you can act on
uncertainty: act automatically when `p(yes) > 0.9`, send `0.4`–`0.9` to a
person, and treat a low `confidence` as "the model did not commit to any
label."

chunks.title: Introduction
chunks.heading: Capabilities
chunks.text:
- **Per-model fairshare.** Every model has its own scheduling pool. Inside a pool, slots are split by fairshare group, tenant, and key weight, so one tenant cannot starve another and one key cannot starve its teammates. See [Fairshare Engine](/docs/concepts/fairshare-engine).
- **Client surfaces.** The OpenAI-compatible API (chat, completions, embeddings, audio, images, rerank, moderations) and the OpenAI Responses API ([OpenAI-compatible API](/docs/guides/openai-compatible-api)), the Anthropic Messages API for Claude Code and Anthropic SDKs ([Claude Code & Anthropic SDKs](/docs/guides/anthropic-messages-api)), and typed classification from logprobs ([Verdicts API](/docs/guides/verdicts)).
- **Model registry.** Aliases, a `quantization` field, routing tags, and a manifest that exports and imports the registry as a file. `GET /model/info` reports the gateway-side details no upstream has. See [Model Registry](/docs/guides/model-registry).
- **Auto routing.** `model: "auto"` picks a model from capacity, cost, tag, and vision signals. See [Auto Model Routing](/docs/guides/auto-model-routing).
- **Model boons.** Gateway-side capabilities granted per model: vision, structured output, compression, knowledge retrieval ([Knowledge Base](/docs/guides/knowledge-base)), image generation, and speculative drafting ([Speculative Drafting](/docs/guides/speculation)). See [Model Boons](/docs/guides/model-boons).
- **Budgets and accounting.** Per-minute token buckets and term budgets are reser

chunks.title: Introduction
chunks.heading: Overview
chunks.text:
**obleth** is a lightweight, high-performance, fairshare-first AI gateway for **self-hosted LLM environments**. It sits between your front door (HAProxy) and your inference backend (Aibrix, vLLM, or any OpenAI-compatible API) and owns multi-tenant identity, contention-based weighted fair queuing, token-accurate cost accounting, and reliability.

The project targets operators running shared GPU clusters on their own hardware — research labs, internal platform teams, and anyone migrating off managed APIs to self-hosted models. This documentation describes release **v1.3.0**.

chunks.title: Alerting
chunks.heading: Bootstrap from environment
chunks.text:
For existing deployments, the legacy environment variables still seed alerting on
first boot when no settings have been saved:

| Variable | Purpose |
| --- | --- |
| `OBLETH_SLACK_WEBHOOK_URL` | Initial Slack webhook (used only until settings are saved) |
| `OBLETH_SLACK_ALERT_MIN_INTERVAL_SECS` | Initial cooldown (default `300`) |

Once you save settings from the dashboard or API, the persisted configuration is
authoritative and these variables are ignored.

chunks.title: Alerting
chunks.heading: Cooldown
chunks.text:
Repeat alerts for the same issue are suppressed within a cooldown window (default
**300s**), set as **Alert cooldown (seconds)** on **Settings → Alerts**. This prevents a
flapping upstream from flooding a channel.

chunks.title: Alerting
chunks.heading: Email (SMTP)
chunks.text:
Deliver alerts over SMTP to one or more recipients. Configure on
**Settings → Alerts**:

| Field | Notes |
| --- | --- |
| SMTP host | e.g. `smtp.example.com` |
| SMTP port | `587` for STARTTLS (default), `25` for plaintext relays |
| Username / Password | Optional SMTP auth (omit for unauthenticated relays) |
| From address | Envelope/sender address |
| Recipients | One or more addresses (comma or newline separated) |
| STARTTLS | Enabled by default; disable only for trusted plaintext relays |

Leave the password blank to keep the stored value when editing other fields; tick
*Remove the stored password* to clear it.

With STARTTLS on, the gateway opens a STARTTLS relay to the configured host.
With it **off**, the connection is plain SMTP — the message body and, if you
configure them, the SMTP username and password travel unencrypted. Only turn it
off for a relay reachable over a trusted network path.

chunks.title: Alerting
chunks.heading: How it works
chunks.text:
A single in-process alert dispatcher is shared by both the data plane (proxy) and
the Management API. Because they run in the same process, saving settings swaps the
active configuration atomically and **takes effect instantly** — there is no
pub/sub propagation delay and no restart.

- **Persistence**: settings are stored in Postgres (`app_settings`, key `alerts`)
  so they survive restarts. On boot, obleth loads the saved settings; if none
  exist it falls back to the legacy `OBLETH_SLACK_WEBHOOK_URL` environment
  variable (see [Bootstrap](#bootstrap-from-environment)).
- **Non-blocking**: alert delivery never blocks the request hot path. Each alert
  is deduplicated by key within a cooldown window and dispatched on a background
  task.
- **Secrets**: the Slack webhook URL and SMTP password are write-only. The API and
  dashboard report only whether each is set; their values are never returned.

Everything below lives on the **Settings → Alerts** tab — paste a Slack webhook,
toggle email, and set the delivery cooldown, then save:

chunks.title: Alerting
chunks.heading: Management API
chunks.text:
Alerting is also configurable over the [Management API](/docs/reference/management-api#settings--alerting):

| Method | Path | Description |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `GET` | `/api/v1/settings/alerts` | Current alert settings (secrets masked) |
| `PUT` | `/api/v1/settings/alerts` | Update alert settings (applies live) |
| `POST` | `/api/v1/settings/alerts/test` | Send a test alert on all channels |

```bash
# Configure Slack + email in one call
curl -X PUT http://localhost:9180/api/v1/settings/alerts \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{
    "slack_webhook_url": "https://hooks.slack.com/services/T000/B000/XXXX",
    "min_interval_secs": 300,
    "email": {
      "smtp_host": "smtp.example.com",
      "smtp_port": 587,
      "username": "apikey",
      "smtp_password": "•••",
      "from_address": "alerts@example.com",
      "recipients": ["oncall@example.com", "sre@example.com"],
      "starttls": true
    }
  }'

# Send a test alert
curl -X POST http://localhost:9180/api/v1/settings/alerts/test \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN"
```

The `GET` response reports `slack_webhook_set` and `email.password_set` booleans
instead of the secret values. On `PUT`, omit `slack_webhook_url` / `smtp_password`
to keep the existing secret, or set `clear_slack_webhook` / `clear_smtp_password`
to `true` to remove it.

chunks.title: Alerting
chunks.heading: Overview
chunks.text:
obleth delivers operational alerts — model-health transitions, upstream failures,
budget/expiry warnings, and other gateway issues — to **Slack** and **email
(SMTP)**. Alerting is configured at runtime from the dashboard **Settings** page
(or the Management API) and applies immediately, without a restart.

chunks.title: Alerting
chunks.heading: Slack
chunks.text:
Deliver alerts to a Slack channel via an
[incoming webhook](https://api.slack.com/messaging/webhooks). Paste the webhook
URL into **Settings → Alerts** and save. To remove it later, tick *Remove the
configured Slack webhook* and save.

The gateway POSTs to this URL itself, so the webhook is held to the same
destination policy as any registered upstream: a URL that resolves to a blocked
address (link-local / cloud metadata) is rejected with `400` when you save it.
See [Security — SSRF](/docs/operations/security#upstream-url-validation-ssrf).

chunks.title: Alerting
chunks.heading: Test alert
chunks.text:
Use the **Send test alert** button on the Settings page to deliver a test message
through every currently-configured channel. The result is reported per channel so
you can confirm Slack and SMTP credentials before relying on them in production.

chunks.title: Alerting
chunks.heading: What raises an alert
chunks.text:
Alerts are issued by both the data plane and the Management API. The deduplication
key is shown in each message as *Issue*, so you can map a notification back to its
source:

| Issue key | Raised when |
| --- | --- |
| `model_health_down:<model-id>` / `model_health_recovery:<model-id>` | A model crosses its health-failure threshold, or recovers |
| `upstream_request_failed` | An upstream call fails after all retries and endpoints |
| `upstream_5xx_response` | An upstream returns a 5xx status that is passed back to the client |
| `upstream_stream_error` | An upstream stream breaks mid-response |
| `scheduler_unavailable` | The fairshare scheduler could not be reached |
| `term_budget_warn:<tenant-id>` / `term_budget_exhausted:<tenant-id>` | A tenant reaches 80% of, or exhausts, its cumulative term budget |
| `key_term_budget_warn:<key-id>` / `key_term_budget_exhausted:<key-id>` | The same, for a key's own term budget |
| `tenant_expiry:<tenant-id>` | A tenant's access window ends within 72 hours |
| `guardrails_input_<tenant-id>` / `guardrails_output_<tenant-id>` | A `log_only` [guardrails](/docs/guides/guardrails) policy flagged a request or a response |
| `guardrails_input_harm_<tenant-id>` / `guardrails_output_harm_<tenant-id>` | The harm scanner flagged content under a `log_only` policy |
| `redis_key_lookup_failed` | A Redis error during API-key lookup; the request is rejected with `503` |
| `redis_model_lookup_failed` / `redis_mcp_lookup_failed` | A Redis error while res

chunks.title: Audit Log
chunks.heading: Attribution
chunks.text:
Every event is attributed to an **actor**:

| Actor | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| an email address | The signed-in dashboard or self-service-portal user who made the change. |
| `system` | A change made automatically by the provisioner (e.g. recording or cancelling a replica). |
| `admin` | Fallback when no actor was supplied (e.g. a raw Management API call with no actor header). |

The actor is carried on each Management API write via the
`x-obleth-audit-actor` header. The control plane sets it to the signed-in user's
email on every write, including those made from live dashboard pages such as
Fairshare, so dashboard actions are attributed to a real person rather than a
generic `admin`; the provisioner sets it to `system`. A direct Management API call may set
the header itself to attribute the change, or omit it to record `admin`.

chunks.title: Audit Log
chunks.heading: Dashboard
chunks.text:
The dashboard **Audit** page (Configuration → Audit) loads the most recent 1,000
events and lets you:

- **Filter** by actor, action, or target entity.
- Read an **inline summary** for each event that expands to the full detail.
- See **tenant ids resolved to tenant names** instead of raw UUIDs.
- Page through history with a page-size control.
- Read **summary cards** showing event, actor, and target counts plus the latest
  event.

The view adapts to a mobile layout for reviewing the trail on a phone.

chunks.title: Audit Log
chunks.heading: Management API
chunks.text:
Read the same trail programmatically:

```bash
curl "${OBLETH_ADMIN_BASE_URL}/api/v1/audit?limit=100" \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $OBLETH_ADMIN_TOKEN"
```

`limit` defaults to 100 and is capped at 1,000; rows are returned newest first.
Each element is one audit row in the shape above. See
[Management API — Audit](/docs/reference/management-api#audit).

chunks.title: Audit Log
chunks.heading: Overview
chunks.text:
obleth records every configuration mutation in an append-only **audit log**: who
made the change, what they changed, when, and a structured detail payload. It
covers changes to **tenants, fairshare groups, API keys, models, endpoints,
managed models and replicas, MCP servers, recipes, knowledge collections, and
settings**, plus configuration backups, model manifests, and cache resyncs —
everything that changes state through the Management API. The full list is under
[Recorded actions](#recorded-actions).

chunks.title: Audit Log
chunks.heading: Related
chunks.text:
- [Security](/docs/operations/security) — access control and secret handling.
- [Dashboard SSO](/docs/guides/dashboard-sso) — how dashboard users (the actors
  recorded here) sign in.
- [Postgres Schema](/docs/reference/postgres-schema#audit_log) — the underlying
