chunks.title: Audit Log
chunks.heading: What a record contains
chunks.text:
Each audit row has:

| Field | Description |
| --- | --- |
| `ts` | When the change occurred. |
| `actor` | Who made it (see above). |
| `action` | The operation, e.g. `create_tenant`, `delete_key`, `update_model`. |
| `entity_type` | The kind of object touched, e.g. `tenant`, `api_key`, `model`. |
| `entity_id` | The id of the affected object. |
| `detail` | A structured JSON payload with the specifics of the change. |

The records are stored in the Postgres `audit_log` table (append-only, indexed by
time, actor, and entity). See [Postgres Schema](/docs/reference/postgres-schema).

Configuration backups are audited too: `export_backup` and `restore_backup` record
the entity counts involved (and, for a restore, the source instance's export
timestamp, gateway version, and any warnings) — never the backup payload, which
carries secrets and key hashes. See
[Backup & Restore](/docs/operations/backup-restore).

chunks.title: Backup & Restore
chunks.heading: After a ClickHouse outage without backup
chunks.text: If ClickHouse data is lost and no backup exists, usage history is gone. Current tenants, keys, and config are safe in Postgres. Rows still in a gateway's spill file are replayed into the new ClickHouse once it is reachable; anything already written to the lost instance is not recoverable.

chunks.title: Backup & Restore
chunks.heading: API key pepper
chunks.text: If the source instance used `OBLETH_API_KEY_PEPPER` when hashing keys, the target must use the same pepper or those keys will not authenticate after restore. obleth cannot detect a pepper mismatch from the stored hashes alone — the backup records only *whether* a pepper was set. When that flag disagrees with the target and the backup contains API keys, the restore still applies and the report carries a warning that the restored keys will not authenticate until the pepper matches or the keys are rotated. Two instances that both use a pepper, but different ones, cannot be detected at all.

chunks.title: Backup & Restore
chunks.heading: Audit
chunks.text:
Both endpoints record an entry in the audit log: `export_backup` and `restore_backup` with entity counts (never the backup payload, which contains ciphertext and key hashes).

---

chunks.title: Backup & Restore
chunks.heading: Backup
chunks.text:
For managed ClickHouse (ClickHouse Cloud, Altinity), use the provider's backup feature. For self-hosted:

```bash
clickhouse-backup create obleth-backup-$(date +%Y%m%d)
clickhouse-backup upload obleth-backup-$(date +%Y%m%d) --remote-storage=s3
```

Using [clickhouse-backup](https://github.com/AlexAkulov/clickhouse-backup).

chunks.title: Backup & Restore
chunks.heading: ClickHouse
chunks.text: ClickHouse holds the usage ledger. It is append-only and does not need to be consistent with real-time traffic: while it is unreachable, the gateway spills usage rows to its local write-ahead file and replays them when it returns.

chunks.title: Backup & Restore
chunks.heading: Config backup
chunks.text: The **Config backup** card on **Settings → Data** in the dashboard lets you export the gateway's routing and access configuration to a single JSON file and restore it onto any obleth instance. Usage history (audit log, request ledger, ClickHouse data) is never included.

chunks.title: Backup & Restore
chunks.heading: Continuous WAL archiving
chunks.text:
For production, configure WAL archiving with pgBackRest or Barman to get point-in-time recovery (PITR). With CloudNativePG:

```yaml
spec:
  backup:
    barmanObjectStore:
      destinationPath: "s3://my-bucket/obleth-pg/"
      s3Credentials:
        accessKeyId:
          name: pg-backup-creds
          key: ACCESS_KEY_ID
```

chunks.title: Backup & Restore
chunks.heading: Data retention
chunks.text: Retention is managed by the gateway, not by ClickHouse TTLs. A background worker prunes the raw `usage` table hourly to the configured window (`OBLETH_USAGE_RETENTION_DAYS`, default `180`, or **Settings → Data → Usage data retention**), dropping whole day-partitions. The permanent `usage_daily` rollup (one row per day, tenant, key, and model, kept current by a materialized view) is never pruned, so historical reports survive the raw-row window. Do not add your own TTL to `usage`: it would delete rows independently of the configured window.

chunks.title: Backup & Restore
chunks.heading: Datastore backup
chunks.text:
Infrastructure-level backup of all three datastores. Use this for complete disaster recovery, point-in-time restore, or when you need usage history alongside config.

| Datastore | Contains | Durability approach |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Postgres | All config, keys, tenants, knowledge base, audit log, and (by default) the dashboard's user and session tables | Full backup + WAL archiving |
| Redis | Configuration caches (rebuilt from Postgres), budget counters, response cache | AOF persistence when term budgets are enforced |
| ClickHouse | Usage ledger | Replication + optional external backup |

chunks.title: Backup & Restore
chunks.heading: Disaster recovery summary
chunks.text:
| Failure | Impact | Recovery |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Redis lost | Configuration caches empty; per-minute buckets, term-budget usage, and the response cache reset | Automatic within one rewarm interval (`OBLETH_REDIS_REWARM_SECS`), or immediately with `POST /api/v1/resync` |
| Postgres lost, config backup available | Config, keys, tenants restored; knowledge, recipes, managed specs, and the items listed under [What is included](#what-is-included) must be recreated | Restore the config backup via the dashboard or API |
| Postgres lost without any backup | All config, keys, tenants lost | No recovery |
| ClickHouse lost without backup | Usage history lost; billing data lost | Only rows still in gateway spill files are replayed |
| Pod lost | In-flight requests fail; that pod's un-replayed spill is lost with its local disk | Nothing to recover unless the spill path is on a persistent volume |

chunks.title: Backup & Restore
chunks.heading: Encryption and key compatibility
chunks.text:
The backup file embeds a `key_check` value: a known plaintext encrypted with the exporting instance's `OBLETH_ENCRYPTION_KEY`. On restore, obleth decrypts it first. If the keys don't match the restore is rejected with a `400` before any database write. The check also detects the case where the backup was made with encryption enabled but the target instance has no key configured.

| Scenario | Result |
| --- | --- |
| Same `OBLETH_ENCRYPTION_KEY` | Restore proceeds normally |
| Different key | Rejected: "created with a different OBLETH_ENCRYPTION_KEY" |
| Target has no key, backup is encrypted | Rejected: "OBLETH_ENCRYPTION_KEY not set on this instance" |
| Both instances have no key | Proceeds (secrets stored as plaintext) |
| Backup unencrypted, target has a key | Secrets are re-encrypted on write |

A backup exported with the cipher disabled carries no `key_check`. In that case the restore still refuses to proceed if the file contains `enc:v1:` ciphertext while the target has no key — secrets it could never decrypt.

chunks.title: Backup & Restore
chunks.heading: Exporting a backup
chunks.text:
In the dashboard go to **Settings → Data → Config backup** and click **Download backup**. The file is named `obleth-backup-<timestamp>.json`.

Via the Management API directly:

```bash
curl -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" \
  http://localhost:9180/api/v1/backup/export \
  -o obleth-backup-$(date +%Y%m%d-%H%M%S).json
```

chunks.title: Backup & Restore
chunks.heading: Merge semantics
chunks.text:
Restore is always a **merge**. Entities present in the backup are created or updated by their primary key; anything that exists only on the target instance is left untouched. Restore never deletes. The entire operation applies atomically — all or nothing.

After the write, obleth re-syncs the Redis hot caches (keys, models, MCP servers) and reloads alert settings live, so the data plane picks up the restored configuration without waiting for a refresh or a restart.

chunks.title: Backup & Restore
chunks.heading: Overview
chunks.text:
obleth has two complementary backup strategies:

| Strategy | Covers | Use when |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Config backup** (this page, first section) | All gateway configuration as a portable JSON file | Cloning an instance, promoting staging to production, lightweight disaster recovery |
| **Datastore backup** (second section) | Full Postgres/Redis/ClickHouse content including usage history | Complete disaster recovery, point-in-time restore, regulatory retention |

chunks.title: Backup & Restore
chunks.heading: pg_dump (simple)
chunks.text:
```bash
pg_dump -h localhost -U obleth -d obleth -F c -f obleth-$(date +%Y%m%d).dump
```

chunks.title: Backup & Restore
chunks.heading: Postgres
chunks.text: Postgres is the source of truth for all configuration. Back it up like any production Postgres database.

chunks.title: Backup & Restore
chunks.heading: Redis
chunks.text:
Redis holds two kinds of data:

- **Configuration caches** (keys, models, aliases, MCP servers). These are derived from Postgres and need no backup. The gateway re-pushes them every `OBLETH_REDIS_REWARM_SECS` (default `300`) and after every pub/sub reconnect, and `POST /api/v1/resync` rebuilds them on demand and prunes entries that no longer exist in Postgres.
- **Budget and cache state**: per-minute token buckets, term-budget usage counters and reservations, the response cache, and compression originals. These exist only in Redis. Losing them resets the current per-minute windows, resets term-budget consumption for the current period, and empties the response cache.

If you enforce term budgets, keep Redis persistence on so a restart does not reset them. The bundled Redis in both Compose and Helm runs with AOF persistence (`--appendonly yes`), and the standalone datastore stack (`datastores.compose.yml`) adds `--appendfsync everysec`. For your own Redis:

```
appendonly yes
appendfsync everysec
```

Redis requires a password in every supported deployment; keep `requirepass` when you change its command line.

chunks.title: Backup & Restore
chunks.heading: Restore
chunks.text:
```bash
pg_restore -h localhost -U obleth -d obleth obleth-20260101.dump
```

After restoring Postgres, rebuild the Redis caches from it so the data plane serves the restored keys, models, and MCP servers and stops serving ones that no longer exist:

```bash
curl -X POST http://localhost:9180/api/v1/resync \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN"
```

The same action is **Settings → Data → Reconcile cache** in the dashboard. Without it, the gateway's periodic rewarm (`OBLETH_REDIS_REWARM_SECS`, default `300`) reaches the same state within one interval.

chunks.title: Backup & Restore
chunks.heading: Restore
chunks.text: Restore the AOF or RDB file and start Redis. Then run `POST /api/v1/resync` (or wait one rewarm interval) so the configuration caches match Postgres.

chunks.title: Backup & Restore
chunks.heading: Restore
chunks.text:
```bash
clickhouse-backup download obleth-backup-20260101
clickhouse-backup restore obleth-backup-20260101
```

chunks.title: Backup & Restore
chunks.heading: Restoring a backup
chunks.text:
#### From the dashboard

1. Go to **Settings → Data → Config backup** and click **Restore from backup…**
2. Pick the `.json` file. The dashboard shows a preview: how many tenants, keys, models, etc. are in the file.
3. Tick the checkbox and type `RESTORE` to confirm.
4. A report shows how many entities were **added** vs **updated** per category.

#### From the API

```bash
curl -X POST http://localhost:9180/api/v1/backup/restore \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d @obleth-backup-20260101-120000.json
```

The response is a `RestoreReport`:

```json
{
  "fairshare_groups": { "inserted": 1, "updated": 0 },
  "tenants":          { "inserted": 5, "updated": 2 },
  "api_keys":         { "inserted": 12, "updated": 0 },
  "models":           { "inserted": 8, "updated": 1 },
  "model_endpoints":  { "inserted": 10, "updated": 1 },
  "mcp_servers":      { "inserted": 2, "updated": 0 },
  "app_settings":     { "inserted": 0, "updated": 6 },
  "warnings":         []
}
```

chunks.title: Backup & Restore
chunks.heading: Validation before any write
chunks.text:
Three checks run **before** the first row is written, and each rejects the whole restore:

1. **Format and version.** The file must be an obleth config backup at the version this gateway supports.
2. **Encryption key.** The `key_check` value must decrypt (see below).
3. **Destination policy.** Every outbound URL the restore would register is validated against the same SSRF policy the create and update forms enforce: `api_base` on models and endpoints, a model's `verify_api_base`, `upstream_url` on MCP servers, and the URLs inside restored settings (the Slack webhook, the energy Prometheus URL, the `slurmrestd` URL when Slurm is enabled, and the speculation `verify_url_template`). A backup pointing any of them at a blocked address — link-local or cloud metadata — fails with `400` naming the offending entry, because restored rows are dispatched to without any further check. See [Security — SSRF](/docs/operations/security#upstream-url-validation-ssrf).

chunks.title: Backup & Restore
chunks.heading: What is included
chunks.text:
| Section | Contents |
| --- | --- |
| `fairshare_groups` | Name and weight |
| `tenants` | Identity, fairshare group and weight, `tokens_per_minute`, `max_in_flight`, status, timezone, access window and weekly schedule, term budget, model allowlist |
| `api_keys` | Prefix and key hash (so existing keys keep working), `kind` and identity fields, key budget, `weight`, `max_in_flight`, disabled flag |
| `models` | The full route: name and `aliases`, upstream model and `api_base`, `api_key`, `model_type`, `quantization`, costs, context window, capacity (`max_in_flight`, capacity mode), capability flags, cache settings, `tags`, `boons`, `tool_servers`, `route_bias`, `auto_eligible`, speculation fields (`draft_model`, `verify_api_base`, `verify_upstream_model`), timeout and retry settings, endpoint selection, energy slots, and health-check settings |
| `model_endpoints` | Name, `api_base`, `api_key`, priority, weight, enabled flag |
| `mcp_servers` | Name, `upstream_url`, `auth_header`, enabled flag |
| `app_settings` | Every `app_settings` row: alerts, auto-router, boons (including knowledge retrieval), energy, Slurm, assistant, usage retention, and the dashboard's internal control-plane key |

Not included:

- Usage history: the audit log and everything in ClickHouse.
- Model health-check history and runtime health state.
- Knowledge collections, documents, and their collection attachments on models.
- Recipes, managed (Slurm) model specs, and replica records.
- Per-tenant guard

chunks.title: Shutdown & Timeouts
chunks.heading: Edge proxy timeouts
chunks.text:
The Compose HAProxy edge sets `timeout client 300s` and `timeout server 300s`.
An idle gap longer than that closes the connection at the edge, whatever the
gateway allows. If you raise the gateway's upstream timeouts, raise the edge and
ingress timeouts in step.

chunks.title: Shutdown & Timeouts
chunks.heading: Gateway shutdown sequence
chunks.text:
On the first SIGTERM (or Ctrl-C), the `obleth` process:

1. **Stops accepting connections** on all three listeners: data plane (`8080`),
   Management API (`9180`), and metrics (`9091`). It logs
   `shutdown signal received; waiting for in-flight connections`.
2. **Drains in-flight requests**, including open streams, for up to
   `OBLETH_SHUTDOWN_GRACE_SECS` (default `300`). When they finish it logs
   `in-flight requests drained`. If the grace elapses first it logs
   `shutdown grace elapsed; remaining connections end at process exit` and
   continues.
3. **Flushes telemetry** for up to 20 seconds: queued usage rows and spans are
   written to ClickHouse, or to the local spill file if ClickHouse is
   unreachable. If the flush does not finish in time it logs
   `telemetry did not finish flushing before shutdown; queued records may be lost`.
4. **Flushes OTLP traces** for up to 10 seconds, when `OBLETH_OTEL_ENDPOINT` is
   set.
5. **Exits**, logging `obleth gateway stopped`.

A second SIGTERM during the drain exits immediately without draining
(`second shutdown signal; exiting without draining`, exit code `130`).

The worst case is therefore `OBLETH_SHUTDOWN_GRACE_SECS` + 20 + 10 seconds. The
orchestrator's stop grace must be longer than that, or the process is killed
mid-flush and queued usage rows are lost.

chunks.title: Shutdown & Timeouts
chunks.heading: How the upstream timeouts interact
chunks.text:
- The **request timeout** covers the wait for response headers. For a streaming
  request that is time to first byte; for a non-streaming request it is the
  whole generation. A model's `request_timeout_secs` overrides
  `OBLETH_UPSTREAM_TIMEOUT_SECS` for that model.
- When a response-transforming boon is active, the upstream call is forced
  non-streaming, so the request timeout is raised to at least 120 seconds.
- The **read timeout** also bounds the header wait, so it cuts a slow
  non-streaming generation even when the request timeout is longer. A model whose
  `request_timeout_secs` exceeds the read timeout is cut at the read timeout,
  and the gateway logs `requests to  will be cut at s by the read
  timeout`. Raise `OBLETH_UPSTREAM_READ_TIMEOUT_SECS` or lower the model's value.
- A timeout refunds the request's budget reservation and bills nothing; a stream
  that breaks after tokens reached the client is billed for what streamed. See
  [Token-Measured Fairness](/docs/concepts/token-measured-fairness).

chunks.title: Shutdown & Timeouts
chunks.heading: Overview
chunks.text:
The gateway drains in-flight work before it exits, and every wait on the request
path is bounded. This page is the reference for both: the shutdown sequence, the
stop grace periods that cover it, and the timeouts that turn a stalled
dependency into a fast, well-defined error.

chunks.title: Shutdown & Timeouts
chunks.heading: Provisioner shutdown
chunks.text:
The Slurm provisioner never interrupts a reconcile tick: stopping mid-tick could
leave a submitted job unrecorded. A SIGTERM received during a tick takes effect
when the tick completes; one received while it waits for the next tick exits
immediately (`shutdown signal received; exiting after the completed tick`).

The Helm chart gives the provisioner pod `terminationGracePeriodSeconds: 60`.
The Compose `obleth-provisioner` service sets no `stop_grace_period`, so Docker's
default stop timeout applies.

chunks.title: Shutdown & Timeouts
chunks.heading: Related
chunks.text:
- [Saturation Behavior](/docs/concepts/saturation-behavior) — what queued
  requests experience before the admission timeout.
- [Reliability & Fail-Open](/docs/concepts/reliability-fail-open) — how Redis
  and ClickHouse failures are handled.
- [Reliability & Failover](/docs/guides/reliability-and-failover) — per-model
  retries, endpoints, and failover.
- [Troubleshooting](/docs/operations/troubleshooting)

chunks.title: Shutdown & Timeouts
chunks.heading: Stop grace periods
chunks.text:
| Deployment | Setting | Value | Why |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Docker Compose | `stop_grace_period` on the `obleth` service | `345s` | 300 s drain + 20 s telemetry + 10 s OTLP + margin |
| Helm | `terminationGracePeriodSeconds` on the gateway pod | `345` | Same budget |
| Helm | `lifecycle.preStop` on the gateway container | `sleep 5` | Keeps the pod serving while its endpoint is removed from Services and ingresses, so new connections are not refused during that window |

The Helm grace period is fixed in the chart template, not a value. If you raise
`obleth.shutdownGraceSecs` (Helm) or `OBLETH_SHUTDOWN_GRACE_SECS` (Compose
`.env`), the pod grace period or `stop_grace_period` must grow by the same
amount; with Helm that means editing the chart template.

Because the drain can take minutes when long streams are open, a
`docker compose stop`, `restart`, or `up --force-recreate` can take up to 345
seconds, and a Helm rolling update holds each old pod until its requests finish.

chunks.heading: Timeouts

| Upstream request, until response headers | 300 s | `OBLETH_UPSTREAM_TIMEOUT_SECS`, or per model `request_timeout_secs` | Retried per the model's `max_retries`; when attempts are exhausted, `504` `upstream request timed out` |

chunks.title: Shutdown & Timeouts
chunks.heading: Where each value is set
chunks.text:
| Variable | Helm value | Compose `.env` |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `OBLETH_ADMISSION_TIMEOUT_SECS` | `obleth.admissionTimeoutSecs` | Yes |
| `OBLETH_REDIS_RESPONSE_TIMEOUT_MS` | `obleth.redisResponseTimeoutMs` | Yes |
| `OBLETH_REDIS_CONNECT_TIMEOUT_MS` | `obleth.redisConnectTimeoutMs` | Yes |
| `OBLETH_UPSTREAM_TIMEOUT_SECS` | `obleth.upstreamTimeoutSecs` | Yes |
| `OBLETH_UPSTREAM_READ_TIMEOUT_SECS` | `obleth.upstreamReadTimeoutSecs` (empty = default) | Yes (empty = default) |
| `OBLETH_SHUTDOWN_GRACE_SECS` | `obleth.shutdownGraceSecs` | Yes |
| `OBLETH_PROVISIONER_HEALTH_TIMEOUT_SECS` | None | Not forwarded |
| `OBLETH_PROVISIONER_WARMUP_TIMEOUT_SECS` | None | Not forwarded |

All gateway variables are read once at start-up; restart the gateway after
changing them. Full descriptions are in
[Environment Variables](/docs/reference/environment-variables) and
[Helm Values](/docs/reference/helm-values).

chunks.title: Observability
chunks.heading: Enabling tracing
chunks.text:
Tracing is opt-in and controlled by the `tracing_enabled` flag, which can be
set at the **tenant** level (covers all of its keys) or per **API key**:

```bash
# Enable tracing for a tenant (all keys inherit it)
curl -X PUT http://localhost:9180/api/v1/tenants/$TENANT_ID/tracing \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"tracing_enabled": true}'

# Enable tracing for a single key
curl -X PUT http://localhost:9180/api/v1/keys/$KEY_ID/tracing \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"tracing_enabled": true}'
```

The dashboard also exposes these toggles on the **Tenants** and **API Keys**
pages.

chunks.title: Observability
chunks.heading: Health and provisioning state
chunks.text:
Two signals are surfaced in the dashboard rather than in Prometheus, because both
are per-model state rather than time series:

- **Model health.** Each model carries a health verdict from its own modality
  probe (chat, embedding, speech, transcription, and image models are each
  probed against the endpoint they actually serve). A model with recent
  successful traffic can be settled from the usage ledger instead of being
  probed, but only while a live endpoint is still serving. See
  [Model Health](/docs/guides/model-health).
- **Slurm provisioner tick status.** The provisioner reports each reconcile
  tick's outcome to the gateway. When it cannot reach Slurm, the model's
  Replicas panel shows the failure reason and how long replica states have been
  frozen, state badges gray out, and Settings → Slurm distinguishes "running"
  from "running but failing since X". If no successful reconcile has happened
  for 10 minutes while Slurm provisioning is enabled, a deduplicated alert fires,
  with a recovery notice when it clears. See
  [Slurm Provisioning](/docs/guides/slurm-provisioning).

chunks.title: Observability
chunks.heading: Identity-token signals
chunks.text:
Two counters cover the [identity-token](/docs/guides/identity-tokens) path when
`OBLETH_JWT_ISSUERS` is configured.

Alert on a **sustained** `obleth_jwks_refresh_total{result="error"}` rate for any
`issuer_index`. A failed refresh keeps the last good key snapshot rather than
emptying it, so verification keeps working and nothing breaks at the moment the
alert fires — until that issuer rotates a signing key, at which point every token
signed by the new key is rejected. Treat it as a warning with lead time, not an
outage. An isolated failure is transient; the rate is what matters. Each failure
also raises a gateway alert, deduplicated per issuer.

On `obleth_jwt_verify_total`, watch the shape rather than the volume. A spike
concentrated in a **single** `result` label points at one specific
misconfiguration rather than at general abuse: `unknown_issuer` or `bad_audience`
from a client pointed at the wrong issuer or issued the wrong audience,
`bad_subject` from an issuer whose `subject_claim` does not match the token,
`expired` from a client reusing a cached token past its lifetime (a small
clock-skew allowance already applies), `not_provisioned` from an issuer with
`jit_provision` disabled receiving a token for an identity that has no key yet.

Rejections are `total - ok`, **not** the sum of the non-`ok` labels:
`not_provisioned` and `provision_failed` are post-verification outcomes counted
in addition to `ok`, since those tokens verified successfully and failed later.
The full

chunks.title: Observability
chunks.heading: Notes
chunks.text:
- obleth uses the OTLP/HTTP (protobuf) exporter with a background batch processor,
  so trace export never blocks the request hot path.
- The service name is reported as `obleth`.
- Point `OBLETH_OTEL_ENDPOINT` at any OTLP-compatible backend (Jaeger, Tempo, an
  OpenTelemetry Collector, or a vendor endpoint).

chunks.title: Observability
chunks.heading: OTLP tracing
chunks.text:
Tracing is fully gated on `OBLETH_OTEL_ENDPOINT`. Unset, there is zero tracing
overhead and obleth logs to stdout as usual. Set it to an OTLP/**HTTP** collector
base URL and obleth exports spans to `{endpoint}/v1/traces`.

```bash
# Docker Compose (.env)
OBLETH_OTEL_ENDPOINT=http://jaeger:4318
```

```yaml
# Helm values
obleth:
  otelEndpoint: http://my-collector:4318
```

The Compose `observability` profile ships Jaeger all-in-one (OTLP enabled) with
its UI on http://localhost:16686.

chunks.title: Observability
chunks.heading: Overview
chunks.text:
obleth exposes Prometheus metrics always-on, and OpenTelemetry distributed tracing
when you point it at an OTLP collector.

chunks.title: Observability
chunks.heading: Per-request span tracing
chunks.text:
obleth has two independent span systems:

- **ClickHouse spans** (this section): opt-in per tenant or key, stored in the
  `spans` table, and shown in the dashboard's Request Detail panel. They cover
  the gateway's own pipeline phases, including routing, admission, and each boon.
- **OTLP spans** ([below](#otlp-tracing)): exported to your tracing backend for
  every request when `OBLETH_OTEL_ENDPOINT` is set. They cover the request
  handler, authentication, cache, budget, and upstream calls.

Some span names appear in both, but the sets differ; each is listed in its own
section.

chunks.title: Observability
chunks.heading: Prometheus metrics
chunks.text:
The data plane serves metrics on `OBLETH_METRICS_LISTEN` (default `0.0.0.0:9091`,

chunks.title: Observability
chunks.heading: Querying spans
chunks.text:
The `has_trace` field on each `GET /api/v1/usage/logs` row is `true` when at
least one span exists for that request. Fetch the full span set for one request:

```bash
GET /api/v1/usage/logs/{request_id}/spans
```

```json
[
  {
    "request_id": "a1b2c3d4-...",
    "span_name": "proxy_request",
    "parent_span": "",
    "start_ms": 1749427821000,
    "duration_ms": 1243,
    "status": "ok",
    "attributes": "{}"
  },
  {
    "request_id": "a1b2c3d4-...",
    "span_name": "auth_resolve",
    "parent_span": "proxy_request",
    "start_ms": 1749427821001,
    "duration_ms": 2,
    "status": "ok",
    "attributes": "{}"
  }
]
```

chunks.title: Observability
chunks.heading: Request detail panel
chunks.text:
On the **Request Logs** page in the dashboard, traced requests show a small
trace icon. Clicking a row that has a trace opens the **Request Detail** panel,
which renders the spans as a timeline waterfall — each phase is drawn
proportionally to its duration so you can immediately see where latency went.
The panel also includes the full usage summary (tokens, cost, admission, cache
status) alongside the trace.

chunks.title: Observability
chunks.heading: Request-level visibility
chunks.text:
Prometheus and Grafana give you aggregate throughput, latency histograms, and
scheduler pressure. For **individual requests** — who called what, when, how
long it took, and what it cost — use the control plane **Request Logs** page or
`GET /api/v1/usage/logs` on the Management API.

Each completed request (including rejections) writes one row to the ClickHouse
`usage` ledger with a timestamp, tenant/key/model, session id (when provided),
request type, tokens, TTFT, total latency, status, and frozen USD cost. The
dashboard live-tails this feed (15s refresh) with filters and keyset pagination.

Gateway-internal traffic is tagged in the same ledger and excluded from usage and
cost figures by default: health probes record `request_type = "health_probe"`,
and traffic from tenants flagged synthetic (obench fixtures, and the dashboard's
own model-test and benchmark runs) records `request_type = "benchmark"`. Pass
`include_internal=true` to include it.

See [Control Plane — Request Logs](/docs/guides/control-plane#request-logs) and
[Management API — Request logs](/docs/reference/management-api#request-logs).

chunks.title: Observability
chunks.heading: Spans
chunks.text:
Each request produces a `proxy_request` span with child spans for the pipeline
phases:

- `auth_resolve` — API key resolution (moka → Redis)
- `cache_lookup` — response cache check
- `reserve_budget` — atomic tenant token-budget reservation
- `reserve_key_budget` — the same, for the key's own budget
- `upstream_request` — the call to the inference backend

MCP gateway calls produce an `mcp_request` span tagged with the server name.

Each request's spans also carry a **`session.id`** attribute (with
`session.id.source` = `client` or `derived`), so a whole conversation's spans can
be grouped in your tracing backend rather than viewed one turn at a time. The
same id is recorded on the usage row. See
[Conversations & Sessions](/docs/guides/conversations-and-sessions).

chunks.title: Observability
chunks.heading: What is recorded
chunks.text:
When `tracing_enabled` is set, each request writes its spans to the ClickHouse
`spans` table via the same non-blocking telemetry sink used for usage rows.
Unlike usage rows, spans are not spilled to the WAL: spans produced while
ClickHouse is unreachable are discarded.
Spans recorded per request:

| Span | Parent | Description |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `proxy_request` | — | Root span; total request duration |
| `auth_resolve` | `proxy_request` | API key + tenant resolution (moka → Redis) |
| `auto_route` | `proxy_request` | Auto-router model selection (when active) |
| `admission` | `proxy_request` | Fairshare semaphore acquisition |
| `cache_lookup` | `proxy_request` | Response cache check |
| `boon:vision` | `proxy_request` | Vision boon image-injection time |
| `boon:knowledge` | `proxy_request` | [Knowledge](/docs/guides/knowledge-base) retrieval; attributes include the outcome and the chunks injected |
| `boon:image_generation` | `boon:tool_loop` | Gateway-executed `generate_image` tool call; attributes include the image count, size, and model |
| `boon:tool_loop` | `proxy_request` | Gateway MCP tool loop; attributes include `turns` and `tools` used |
| `boon:tool_loop:iter:{n}` | `boon:tool_loop` | Per-turn breakdown: `tool_ms` (MCP execution) and `model_ms` (re-dispatch) |
| `boon:image_generation` | `boon:tool_loop` | One gateway-executed `generate_image` call; attributes include the images produced |
| `boon:compression` | `proxy_request` | All compression passes; `jso

chunks.title: Scaling
chunks.heading: ClickHouse scaling
chunks.text:
ClickHouse is append-only for obleth and handles high insert rates natively. A
single ClickHouse instance handles tens of thousands of rows per second without
tuning.

For high-traffic or large-history deployments:

- Use a replicated ClickHouse cluster (2–3 replicas with ZooKeeper or ClickHouse
  Keeper).
- Control disk growth with the gateway's usage retention window
  (`OBLETH_USAGE_RETENTION_DAYS`, or Settings → Data). The permanent
  `usage_daily` rollup is never pruned.

chunks.title: Scaling
chunks.heading: Concurrency model
chunks.text:
Each gateway process admits requests into **one pool per model**:

- A model's pool size is its `max_in_flight`, or
  `OBLETH_DEFAULT_MODEL_MAX_IN_FLIGHT` (default `32`) when unset.
- `OBLETH_GLOBAL_MAX_IN_FLIGHT` (default `1024`) is a total ceiling across all
  pools in that process. It is a safety guard, not a fairness input: keep it
  above the sum of your pool sizes. When it is lower, the gateway logs a warning
  at start-up and the ceiling binds before the pools do.

Pools, weights, and the admission formula are described in
[Fairshare Engine](/docs/concepts/fairshare-engine).

chunks.title: Scaling
chunks.heading: Docker Compose
chunks.text:
The shipped Compose stack runs one gateway container, and
`docker compose up --scale obleth=N` is not supported:

- The `obleth` service publishes a fixed host port (`8088:8080`), so a second
  container fails with a host-port conflict.
- The bundled `haproxy.cfg` declares a single `server obleth1 obleth:8080` entry.
  Its Docker DNS resolver re-resolves that name, so a recreated container is
  picked up without restarting HAProxy, but it does not balance across several
  gateway containers.

Use Kubernetes to run multiple gateway replicas.

chunks.title: Scaling
chunks.heading: Horizontal scaling
chunks.text:
Each obleth pod runs independently with its own:

- In-process caches for keys, models, and MCP servers (5-minute TTL, evicted
  immediately by the `obleth:invalidate` pub/sub channel)
- Fairshare scheduler and model pools (per pod, not global)
- In-flight ceiling (`OBLETH_GLOBAL_MAX_IN_FLIGHT` per pod)
- Fairshare activity history for the dashboard chart (per process, reset on
  restart)

The aggregate concurrency reaching an upstream is therefore
`replicas × pool size` for each model, and at most
`replicas × OBLETH_GLOBAL_MAX_IN_FLIGHT` in total. HAProxy or your ingress
distributes requests across pods.

chunks.title: Scaling
chunks.heading: Kubernetes HPA
chunks.text:
The chart ships an HPA that is **off by default**:

```yaml
hpa:
  enabled: false
  minReplicas: 1
  maxReplicas: 20
  targetCPUUtilizationPercentage: 70
```

It is off because pools and the ceiling are per replica: an autoscaled replica
count moves the aggregate concurrency reaching your upstreams with no config
change — scaling 2 → 8 pods raises it fourfold. If you enable it, size the pools
so that `maxReplicas × pool size` stays within what each upstream can absorb, and
accept that the upstream is under-subscribed below full scale-out.

obleth is CPU-light for most workloads (it proxies bytes rather than computing).
A better signal for scaling is admission queue depth. With Prometheus Adapter you
can write a custom HPA metric:

```yaml
# Scale when average queue depth exceeds 20 per pod
metrics:
  - type: Pods
    pods:
      metric:
        name: obleth_queue_depth
      target:
        type: AverageValue
        averageValue: 20
```

chunks.title: Scaling
chunks.heading: Monitoring capacity signals
chunks.text:
| Metric | What it tells you |
| --- | --- |
| `obleth_in_flight` | Current concurrent requests per pod |
| `obleth_queue_depth` | Requests waiting for admission (should be near 0 at steady state) |
| `obleth_requests_total{admission="queued"}` | Requests that had to wait for a slot — sustained growth means the pools are at capacity |
| `obleth_requests_total{admission="fast"}` | Requests admitted immediately — a good signal of headroom |

The dashboard's **Fairshare** page shows occupancy and waiting tenants per model
pool. Queued requests that wait longer than `OBLETH_ADMISSION_TIMEOUT_SECS`
(default `60`) return `503`; see
[Saturation Behavior](/docs/concepts/saturation-behavior).

chunks.title: Scaling
chunks.heading: One replica by default
chunks.text:
The Helm chart defaults to a **single** gateway replica so the configured pool
sizes are the ones that reach your upstreams:

```yaml
obleth:
  replicas: 1
  globalMaxInFlight: 1024
  defaultModelMaxInFlight: 32
```

For redundancy, set `replicas: N` and divide each model's `max_in_flight` (and
`defaultModelMaxInFlight`) by N. The aggregate then holds, but replicas cannot
lend each other idle capacity: a quiet pod's share goes unused, so utilization is
lower than one pod running the full pools. Within a single pod, idle
fairshare-group capacity *is* redistributed — see
[Fairshare Engine](/docs/concepts/fairshare-engine).

To keep a single node failure from taking the whole data plane down, spread
replicas with the chart's `affinity.antiAffinity` value (`soft`, the default,
prefers distinct nodes; `hard` requires them; `""` disables). A
PodDisruptionBudget with `minAvailable: 1` is rendered only when more than one
replica is guaranteed (`obleth.replicas`, or `hpa.minReplicas` with the HPA on),
because a PDB over a single pod would block node drains.

Rolling updates and scale-downs drain each pod before it exits; see
[Shutdown & Timeouts](/docs/operations/graceful-shutdown-and-timeouts).

chunks.title: Scaling
chunks.heading: Overview
chunks.text:
obleth keeps its shared state in Postgres and Redis and can run behind a load
balancer as multiple pods. Admission is per process, though: every replica runs
its own scheduler with its own model pools and ceiling, so replica count and pool
sizes have to be chosen together.

chunks.title: Scaling
chunks.heading: Postgres scaling
chunks.text:
Postgres handles configuration mutations (low frequency), audit log appends, the
knowledge base, and the dashboard's auth tables. It is rarely the bottleneck. Use
CloudNativePG or a managed service for HA. Read replicas are not needed for
obleth's workload.

chunks.title: Scaling
chunks.heading: Redis scaling
chunks.text:
Redis serves sub-millisecond key lookups and atomic Lua budget operations. A
single Redis primary handles the load of most deployments.

The gateway connects to **one Redis primary URL**. Cluster mode is not
supported: the budget and cache scripts operate on several keys in one call, and
the client is built without cluster support. For high availability, use a
managed Redis whose failover endpoint always presents a single primary at a
stable address.

chunks.title: Scaling
chunks.heading: Sizing the pools
chunks.text:
A model's pool size controls how many requests the gateway sends to that model at
once. Setting it too high moves queuing into the inference backend, where it is
hidden and hard to observe. Setting it too low grows obleth's visible queue.

**Target:** the number of concurrent requests the model's backend (vLLM, AIBrix,
or similar) can serve without internal queuing, divided by the gateway replica
count.

```bash
# Set a model's pool size (applies live)
curl -X PUT http://localhost:9180/api/v1/models/$MODEL_ID/capacity \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"max_in_flight": 64}'
```

Pool sizes are stored in Postgres and apply to every replica. Tune them manually
or use the auto-tune ramp probe (chat and embedding only) from the Management API
or control plane; see [Capacity Auto-tune](/docs/guides/capacity-autotune).

chunks.title: Scaling
chunks.heading: The global ceiling
chunks.text:
The ceiling can also be changed live, but only on the pod you call, and only
until that pod restarts:

```bash
# Raise this pod's ceiling
curl -X PUT http://localhost:9180/api/v1/capacity \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"max_in_flight": 2048}'

# Check it
curl http://localhost:9180/api/v1/capacity \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN"
```

To change it on every pod, set `OBLETH_GLOBAL_MAX_IN_FLIGHT` (Helm
`obleth.globalMaxInFlight`) and roll the pods. The Compose file hardcodes the
ceiling (`1024`) and the default pool size (`32`), so in Compose change pool
sizes per model.

chunks.title: Security
chunks.heading: Admin token
chunks.text:
The Management API and control plane are protected by a single bearer token (`OBLETH_ADMIN_TOKEN`). This is intentionally simple — it's a service-to-service credential, not a user-facing RBAC system. There is **no default**: the gateway refuses to start without it, and the control plane fails every Management API call until it is set. The token is compared in **constant time** to avoid timing side-channels.

**Hardening:**
- Use a randomly generated token of at least 32 characters: `openssl rand -hex 32`
- Store it in a Kubernetes Secret or a secrets manager (Vault, AWS Secrets Manager)
- Restrict access to `:9180` at the network layer (firewall, Kubernetes NetworkPolicy)
- Rotate by updating the env var and rolling the pods; the control plane config is updated simultaneously

chunks.title: Security
chunks.heading: API key storage and verification
chunks.text:
obleth never stores raw API keys. When a key is created:

1. The gateway generates a secret in the format `sk_{24 random bytes hex-encoded}`.
2. The secret is returned to the caller **once** and never stored.
3. A SHA-256 hash of the secret is stored in Postgres (`api_keys.key_hash`) and cached in Redis (`obleth:key:{hash}`).

On each request, the gateway hashes the incoming credential — `Authorization: Bearer ...` or `x-api-key: ...` — and looks up the hash. A stolen database or Redis dump does not expose valid API keys.

chunks.title: Security
chunks.heading: Attack surface summary
chunks.text:
| Surface | Exposure | Mitigations |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Data plane `:8080` | Public (via HAProxy/Ingress) | API key auth, TLS at edge, request-path traversal rejected |
| Admin API `:9180` | Internal only | Constant-time bearer token, SSRF validation, secrets never returned, network restriction |
| Metrics `:9091` | Internal only (Prometheus) | Network restriction |
| Control plane | Public (dashboard) | Login + rate limiting, nonce-based CSP, security headers, required secrets |
| Postgres | Internal only | Strong password, encryption at rest, AES-256-GCM column encryption (only when `OBLETH_ENCRYPTION_KEY` is set) |
| Redis | Internal only | Required password, network restriction |
| ClickHouse | Internal only | Strong password, network restriction |

chunks.title: Security
chunks.heading: Container hardening
chunks.text:
The published Docker images run as a **non-root** user. In Compose, the
datastores and management surfaces are published on `127.0.0.1` only: Postgres,
Redis, and ClickHouse, and also the Management API (`9180`), the metrics endpoint
(`9091`), and the bundled Prometheus and Jaeger. They are reachable from the
host, not from the network. The data plane (`8088`), the dashboard (`3002`), the
edge proxy (`80`), Grafana (`3001`), and the optional benchmark fixture backend
(`8081`) and Dex identity provider (`5556`, `sso-dev` profile) are published on
all interfaces. The Compose stack and Helm chart both **require** secrets to be
set explicitly (`${VAR:?}` / Helm `required`) rather than shipping weak
defaults, including the Redis password: the bundled Redis always runs with
`requirepass`, because the request path reads API keys from it. The data plane
and control plane images also declare container
`HEALTHCHECK`s (the data plane probes `/health`; the control plane probes its
login page) so orchestrators can detect and restart unhealthy containers.

chunks.title: Security
chunks.heading: Control plane hardening
chunks.text:
The Next.js control plane has several built-in protections:

- **Required secrets, no weak defaults.** A break-glass admin email
  (`DASHBOARD_ADMIN_EMAIL`), a password (`DASHBOARD_PASSWORD`), and
  `DASHBOARD_SESSION_SECRET` must all be supplied. The app fails closed at
  startup if the session secret is missing or shorter than 32 characters. The
  seeded password is stored hashed by the auth layer; rotate it after first
  sign-in and prefer SSO for day-to-day access.
- **Login rate limiting.** Sign-in attempts are limited per client IP
  (fixed window) to slow credential-stuffing and brute-force attempts.
- **Nonce-based Content Security Policy.** Every dashboard document is served
  with a per-request CSP carrying a fresh 128-bit nonce. Scripts run only by
  nonce (`script-src 'self' 'nonce-…' 'strict-dynamic'`); there is no
  `'unsafe-inline'` and no `'unsafe-eval'` in production, so an injected inline
  script does not execute. Development builds add `'unsafe-eval'` for React
  Refresh and source maps only. The policy also sets `default-src 'self'`,
  `frame-ancestors 'none'`, `object-src 'none'`, `base-uri 'self'`,
  `form-action 'self'`, and `connect-src 'self'`.
  Styles remain on `'unsafe-inline'`: the Next.js font loader, Recharts, and the
  shadcn primitives write style attributes a nonce cannot cover.
- **Other security headers.** Responses also set `Strict-Transport-Security`
  (HSTS), `X-Frame-Options: DENY`, `X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff`,
  `Referrer-Policy

chunks.title: Security
chunks.heading: Fail-open security tradeoff
chunks.text:
`OBLETH_FAIL_OPEN` governs the **budget** checks, not identity. Authentication never fails open:

- A key found in neither the in-process cache nor Redis is rejected with `401`.
- A Redis error during key lookup is rejected with `503` (`authentication backend unavailable`), not treated as an unknown key and never as a valid one.

With `OBLETH_FAIL_OPEN=true` (default), a Redis failure at the budget step is logged, alerted (`redis_budget_reserve_failed_open`), and the request proceeds unmetered, so an exhausted budget may be bypassed while Redis is down.

With `OBLETH_FAIL_OPEN=false`, those requests are rejected with `503` (`budget check failed` or `key budget check failed`) instead. This provides strict budget enforcement at the cost of availability during Redis outages.

Choose based on your requirements:
- **Multi-tenant deployments** where availability matters most: fail-open (availability > strict budget enforcement during outages)
- **Hard budget caps / compliance requirements**: fail-closed

chunks.title: Security
chunks.heading: Key hashing implementation
chunks.text:
```
Hash      = SHA-256(raw_key_bytes)                       # no pepper
Hash      = SHA-256(raw_key_bytes || 0x00 || pepper)     # OBLETH_API_KEY_PEPPER set
Redis key = "obleth:key:" + hex(Hash)
```

The gateway computes the hash before any Redis lookup. The raw key value never touches the network after the initial creation response.

chunks.title: Security
chunks.heading: Kubernetes restricted Pod Security Standard
chunks.text:
The Helm chart applies the Kubernetes [restricted](https://kubernetes.io/docs/concepts/security/pod-security-standards/#restricted)
Pod Security Standard to its stateless workloads (obleth data plane,
control-plane, benchmark-backend) **by default** — `runAsNonRoot`,
`seccompProfile: RuntimeDefault`, `allowPrivilegeEscalation: false`, and all
Linux capabilities dropped. UID is not pinned because the images ship distinct
non-root users (obleth `10001`, control-plane `1000`); `runAsNonRoot` enforces
non-root without hardcoding a UID. The bundled datastores are excluded on purpose
— their official images manage their own users (the Postgres entrypoint must
start as root). See [Helm Values — Security contexts](/docs/reference/helm-values#security-contexts-pod-security-standard).

chunks.title: Security
chunks.heading: Optional pepper
chunks.text: Set `OBLETH_API_KEY_PEPPER` to mix a secret server-side value into every key hash. This is defense-in-depth: even if the config database leaks, an attacker cannot pre-compute or brute-force key hashes without also knowing the pepper. Keep it secret and stable — changing it invalidates all previously issued keys. Generate with `openssl rand -hex 32`.

chunks.title: Security
chunks.heading: Outbound alert transport
chunks.text:
[Alert delivery](/docs/operations/alerting) is an outbound connection from the
gateway, and its confidentiality depends on how you configure it:

- **Slack** uses the HTTPS incoming-webhook URL you supply, validated against the
  destination policy above when saved.
- **Email** uses STARTTLS when the `starttls` setting is on (the default). With
  it off, the gateway opens a **plain, unencrypted SMTP connection** — the alert
  body and any configured SMTP username and password cross the network in the
  clear. Only disable STARTTLS for a relay on a trusted network path.

The Slack webhook URL and the SMTP password are write-only over the API and the
dashboard: reads report only whether each is set.

chunks.title: Security
chunks.heading: Pre-created Secrets and NetworkPolicy
chunks.text:
For production, the chart can reference **pre-created** Secrets
(`obleth.existingSecret` / `controlPlane.existingSecret`) so real credentials
never enter values files or `--set`/CLI history. An opt-in NetworkPolicy
(`networkPolicy.enabled: true`) admits only the obleth pods to the bundled Redis
and ClickHouse, the obleth and control-plane pods to the bundled Postgres, and
only the control-plane and provisioner pods to the Management API port (`9180`).
The data plane (`8080`) and metrics (`9091`) ports stay open so an
out-of-namespace ingress and Prometheus can reach them. The policy requires a CNI
that enforces NetworkPolicy and does not cover external datastores. When the
chart renders the obleth Secret itself, a change to it rolls the gateway and
bundled Redis pods. See the [Production](/docs/guides/self-hosting#scenario-4-production)
scenario.

chunks.title: Security
chunks.heading: Request-path traversal
chunks.text:
The upstream URL is built by joining the validated `api_base` with the inbound
request path. As defense-in-depth, the data plane rejects request paths that
contain traversal sequences — literal `..` segments, backslash separators, and
their percent-encoded forms (`%2e`, `%2f`, `%5c`) — with `400 Bad Request`
before the upstream call is made. This keeps a crafted path from escaping the
configured upstream base onto a different path on the same host. The same guard
applies to MCP gateway requests.

chunks.title: Security
chunks.heading: Revocation
chunks.text: Deleting or disabling a key, tenant, model, MCP server, or alias removes it from Redis and publishes an invalidation that evicts it from every gateway's in-process cache. If the Redis eviction fails, the Management API call returns `502` naming `POST /api/v1/resync` rather than reporting success while the old entry keeps serving; run the resync (Settings → Data → Reconcile cache) to rebuild the caches from Postgres and prune stale entries. A pod that misses the invalidation message serves its cached copy for at most the 5-minute cache TTL.

chunks.title: Security
chunks.heading: Secrets in API responses
chunks.text: The Management API never returns stored upstream secrets. Model, endpoint, and MCP server responses carry `api_key_set` / `auth_header_set` booleans; the alert settings report `slack_webhook_set` and `password_set`; the Slurm settings show only the last four characters of the JWT. Writes accept the secret. For model and endpoint `api_key` and MCP `auth_header`, omit the field to keep the stored value and send `""` to clear it. The Slack webhook and SMTP password keep their stored value when omitted or blank and are cleared only with `clear_slack_webhook` / `clear_smtp_password`; the Slurm JWT keeps its stored value when omitted or blank. The tenant portal receives an allowlisted view of models with no upstream URLs or keys.

chunks.title: Security
chunks.heading: Sensitive fields in Postgres
chunks.text:
These database fields contain credentials:

| Field | Table | What it is |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `api_key` | `models`, `model_endpoints` | Upstream API key for the inference backend |
| `auth_header` | `mcp_servers` | Auth header value for MCP server calls |
| Slurm JWT | `app_settings` (`slurm`) | Token the provisioner presents to `slurmrestd` |
| Control-plane key | `app_settings` (`control_plane_key`) | The dashboard's own data-plane key for Playground and benchmark traffic |

When `OBLETH_ENCRYPTION_KEY` is set (base64 of 32 random bytes), these values are
encrypted at rest with **AES-256-GCM** before being written to Postgres. Encrypted
values carry an `enc:v1:` prefix followed by a per-value 12-byte nonce; the
gateway transparently decrypts them when resolving routes. Generate a key with:

```bash
openssl rand -base64 32
```

If `OBLETH_ENCRYPTION_KEY` is **unset**, the cipher is disabled: these columns are
stored in **plaintext**, and a warning is logged at startup. Nothing else changes
— the gateway starts and serves normally — so treat setting the key as a
deliberate production step, not something the gateway will force on you.

Decryption is prefix-driven: a value carrying `enc:v1:` is decrypted, and an
untagged value is passed through as-is. That is what makes migration painless
(legacy plaintext rows keep working once you enable a key, and are re-encrypted
on their next write), and it is also why enabling a key does **not** retroactively
protect rows you never wri

chunks.title: Security
chunks.heading: TLS architecture
chunks.text:
obleth itself does not terminate TLS. TLS should be terminated at the edge by HAProxy or your Ingress controller.

```
Internet
  |  HTTPS (TLS)
  v
HAProxy / Ingress
  |  HTTP (internal only)
  v
obleth :8080
```

**Never expose obleth's data plane or admin port directly to the internet.** They are HTTP-only.

For internal service-to-service communication (e.g., control plane to Management API within a cluster), TLS is optional and typically omitted for pods within the same Kubernetes namespace.

chunks.title: Security
chunks.heading: Upstream URL validation (SSRF)
chunks.text:
Admin-registered upstream URLs — a model's `api_base` and an MCP server's
`upstream_url` — are validated when created or updated. obleth is built for
self-hosted, local-first deployments where the upstreams you register usually
live on the same private network (another cluster node, a LAN VM, a model server
on `localhost`). So **by default, private/RFC1918, loopback, CGNAT
(`100.64.0.0/10`), and IPv6 unique-local targets are allowed** — these are the
addresses a local operator legitimately needs to reach.

What is **always blocked** is the genuinely dangerous class with no legitimate
local-upstream use: link-local and the cloud metadata endpoints
(`169.254.0.0/16`, including `169.254.169.254`; `fe80::/10`; AWS's IPv6 IMDS
address `fd00:ec2::254`; and Alibaba Cloud's `100.100.100.200`), the unspecified
address, and broadcast/documentation ranges. IPv4 addresses written in IPv6 form —
IPv4-mapped (`::ffff:a.b.c.d`), IPv4-compatible (`::a.b.c.d`), and the NAT64
prefix (`64:ff9b::a.b.c.d`) — are checked as the IPv4 address they embed. Hostnames are resolved first, so a public name that maps to a blocked
address is still rejected. This keeps a compromised or careless admin token from
turning the gateway into a server-side request forgery (SSRF) pivot at cloud
metadata.

This class is checked **before** the allowlist, so a broad
`OBLETH_ALLOWED_PRIVATE_CIDRS` entry (say `0.0.0.0/0` or `169.254.0.0/16`) cannot
reopen it.

The same policy covers every admin-supplied destination the g

chunks.title: Troubleshooting
chunks.heading: 403 "model is disabled"
chunks.text:
The model is registered but disabled. Re-enable it in **Models**, or update the
route with `"enabled": true`. A model under a maintenance window or marked
unhealthy is also excluded from auto-routing; see
[Model Health](/docs/guides/model-health).

chunks.title: Troubleshooting
chunks.heading: 404 `{"detail":"Not Found"}` from a non-chat route
chunks.text:
If embeddings, audio, or image requests return `{"detail":"Not Found"}` (note:
`{"detail":...}` is the **upstream**'s error shape, not obleth's
`{"error":...}`), the model's `api_base` is almost certainly a full endpoint URL
instead of the provider base.

obleth appends the client's request path to `api_base`. A route configured with
`api_base: https://provider.example/v1/embeddings` plus a client call to
`/v1/embeddings` yields a doubled path the upstream can't resolve.

```bash
# Inspect the route's api_base
curl http://localhost:9180/api/v1/models \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" | jq '.[] | {name: .model_name, type: .model_type, api_base}'

# Fix: set api_base to the provider base ending in /v1
curl -X PUT http://localhost:9180/api/v1/models/$MODEL_ID \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{..., "api_base": "https://provider.example/v1"}'
```

See [Multi-modal Models](/docs/guides/multi-modal-models#the-api_base-convention).

chunks.title: Troubleshooting
chunks.heading: 404 on a model
chunks.text:
```bash
# List models
curl http://localhost:9180/api/v1/models \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" | jq '.[] | {name: .model_name, aliases, enabled}'
```

The `model` field in the request must match a registered `model_name` or one of
its aliases. On chat completions, completions, embeddings, Responses, audio, and
image routes, an unknown model gets the gateway's own `404` `model '' is
not registered`. On other recognised API paths, a request that names no
registered model is forwarded to the default upstream
(`OBLETH_UPSTREAM_BASE_URL`), so a `404` there usually comes from that upstream.
A request that names no registered model on a path the gateway does not
recognise gets `404` `unknown endpoint`. A model that is registered but has
`enabled=false` returns `403` `model is disabled`, not `404`; re-enable it.

chunks.title: Troubleshooting
chunks.heading: 413 "request body too large"
chunks.text:
The request body exceeds the gateway's limit: 64 MiB for most routes, 32 MiB for
`/v1/messages`, and 16 MiB for the MCP gateway. `/v1/responses` has a 32 MiB
limit too, but reports it as `400` `request body too large or unreadable`. Large
multimodal payloads (images, audio) are the usual cause; send them by URL where
the upstream supports it, or reduce their size.

chunks.title: Troubleshooting
chunks.heading: 429 quota exceeded
chunks.text:
```bash
# Check tenant quota and current budget
curl http://localhost:9180/api/v1/tenants/$TENANT_ID \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" | jq '{tpm: .tokens_per_minute, group: .fairshare_group}'

# Increase quota
curl -X PUT http://localhost:9180/api/v1/tenants/$TENANT_ID/quota \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"tokens_per_minute": 200000}'
```

The budget is a token bucket, not a fixed window: it refills continuously at `tokens_per_minute / 60000` tokens per millisecond, up to a burst ceiling equal to `tokens_per_minute`. If a tenant is consistently hitting 429, either increase their quota or check for a runaway workload. Setting `tokens_per_minute` to `0` removes the per-minute cap entirely.

chunks.title: Troubleshooting
chunks.heading: 502 when deleting or disabling
chunks.text:
Deleting or disabling a key, tenant, model, MCP server, or alias returns `502`
when the gateway could not remove the entry from Redis. The change is saved in
Postgres, but the old entry could still be serving, so the call reports failure
instead of success. Once Redis is healthy, rebuild the caches:

```bash
curl -X POST http://localhost:9180/api/v1/resync \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN"
```

The same action is **Settings → Data → Reconcile cache**. It republishes keys,
models, and MCP servers from Postgres and removes entries that no longer exist.

chunks.title: Troubleshooting
chunks.heading: 503 "authentication backend unavailable"
chunks.text:
The gateway could not read the key from Redis: the command failed or took longer
than `OBLETH_REDIS_RESPONSE_TIMEOUT_MS` (default `250`). Authentication never
fails open, so these requests are rejected rather than served. A
`redis_key_lookup_failed` alert accompanies them. See
[Redis connectivity issues](#redis-connectivity-issues).

chunks.title: Troubleshooting
chunks.heading: 503 "timed out waiting for model capacity"
chunks.text:
The request waited in the model's fairshare queue for longer than
`OBLETH_ADMISSION_TIMEOUT_SECS` (default `60`). The response carries
`Retry-After: 5`. The model's pool is saturated: see
[Requests piling up in the queue](#requests-piling-up-in-the-queue).

chunks.title: Troubleshooting
chunks.heading: Anthropic clients get `not_found_error`
chunks.text:
Claude Code and Anthropic SDKs send the model name their own configuration
names, which is often not a model the gateway has registered. When the requested
model does not resolve, the gateway uses the **Default model for Anthropic
clients** (Settings → Routing); when that is unset, it returns `404` with type
`not_found_error`. Set the default model, or register the requested name as an
alias. See [Claude Code & Anthropic SDKs](/docs/guides/anthropic-messages-api).

chunks.title: Troubleshooting
chunks.heading: Auth failures (401/403)
chunks.text:
```bash
# 1. Confirm the key exists
curl http://localhost:9180/api/v1/keys \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" | jq '.[] | select(.key_prefix == "sk_abc1")'

# 2. Confirm it's not disabled
# If "disabled": true, re-enable:
curl -X PUT http://localhost:9180/api/v1/keys/$KEY_ID/disabled \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"disabled": false}'

# 3. Check the key format: it must be the full secret (sk_...), not the prefix
```

Key resolution flow: the gateway hashes the full key with SHA-256 (mixing in
`OBLETH_API_KEY_PEPPER` when set), checks its in-process cache, then
`obleth:key:{hash}` in Redis. Postgres is **not** consulted on the hot path.
Redis is populated from Postgres at start-up, on every config write, every
`OBLETH_REDIS_REWARM_SECS` (default `300`), and after every pub/sub reconnect. If
both caches miss, the request is rejected with `401`.

A key you just deleted or disabled that still works on one replica is a stale
in-process entry: the `obleth:invalidate` pub/sub message normally evicts it
immediately, and otherwise it expires within the 5-minute cache TTL. A key that
authenticates nowhere after a Redis flush heals on the next rewarm; to fix it
immediately, run `POST /api/v1/resync` (Settings → Data → Reconcile cache).

chunks.title: Troubleshooting
chunks.heading: ClickHouse connectivity issues
chunks.text:
```
WARN obleth_telemetry: clickhouse insert failed
```

This is non-fatal — requests continue, and usage rows spill to the local WAL.
The gateway also boots without ClickHouse, logging
`telemetry started in spill mode; ClickHouse schema deferred until reachable`.
Check:

```bash
curl http://$CLICKHOUSE_HOST:8123/ping
# Expected: Ok.
```

Common causes: wrong `OBLETH_CLICKHOUSE_URL`, wrong credentials, ClickHouse not
started. After connectivity is restored, obleth applies the schema if needed and
replays the spilled segments automatically, in checkpointed batches.

chunks.title: Troubleshooting
chunks.heading: `column "…" does not exist` after an upgrade
chunks.text:
The gateway applies its schema itself: the numbered files under
`schema/postgres/` are embedded in the binary and run in order on every boot,
serialized across replicas by a Postgres advisory lock. Every statement is
idempotent and additive, so re-running them is safe. A startup that reaches
`postgres connected + schema applied` has a current schema; a migration failure
is fatal and the process exits.

So a missing-column error at runtime means the schema was never applied, not that
you need to patch it by hand. Check, in order:

1. The gateway actually started — look for `postgres connected + schema applied`
   in its logs, and for a migration error just before an exit.
2. `OBLETH_DATABASE_URL` points at the database you are inspecting.
3. The database user can run DDL (`CREATE TABLE`, `ALTER TABLE`) — a read-only or
   restricted role fails the migration.
4. Nothing else holds the advisory lock indefinitely (a stuck earlier boot).

Restarting the gateway re-runs the migrations. Do **not** reach for
`docker compose down -v`: it destroys the volume and every tenant, key, and model
in it.

chunks.title: Troubleshooting
chunks.heading: Enable debug logging
chunks.text:
```bash
RUST_LOG=obleth=debug
```

This adds verbose output for request routing, cache hits/misses, Redis operations, and fairshare decisions.

chunks.title: Troubleshooting
chunks.heading: Fresh Helm install (empty registry)
chunks.text:
A new Kubernetes install starts with **zero models**. `helm install` does not run
model registration — you must `POST /api/v1/models` (or import via the
dashboard) before inference traffic can succeed. See
[Installation — post-install steps](/docs/getting-started/installation#post-install-steps-kubernetes).

chunks.title: Troubleshooting
chunks.heading: Health check
chunks.text:
Both listeners expose a plain liveness probe that returns the literal string `ok`:

```bash
curl http://localhost:8080/health      # data plane
curl http://localhost:9180/api/v1/health   # Management API
```

It proves the process is up and serving; it does **not** check Redis, Postgres,
or ClickHouse. Check dependency health from the logs, from the Prometheus
metrics, or by connecting to each datastore directly.

Build identity is separate: `GET /api/v1/version` returns the running gateway's
version and, for released images, the commit and build timestamp.

chunks.title: Troubleshooting
chunks.heading: HTTP error reference
chunks.text:
Gateway errors use the body `{"error": {"message": "<message>", "type": "obleth_gateway_error"}}`. The
Anthropic Messages API returns the same conditions in Anthropic's error envelope;
see [Claude Code & Anthropic SDKs](/docs/guides/anthropic-messages-api). The full
table is in [Data-Plane Routes](/docs/reference/data-plane-routes).

| Status | Message | Common cause |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `400` | `invalid JSON body`, `model is required`, `invalid request path` | Malformed request, or a path containing traversal sequences |
| `401` | `missing bearer token` | No `Authorization: Bearer` or `x-api-key` header |
| `401` | `invalid api key` / `invalid token` | The key is not in the registry, or an identity token failed verification |
| `403` | `api key disabled` | The key was disabled |
| `403` | `tenant is not active`, or an access-window or schedule reason | The tenant is suspended, expired, or outside its access window |
| `403` | `model is disabled` | The model exists but is disabled |
| `403` | `model not permitted for tenant` | The tenant has a model allowlist that excludes the model |
| `403` | `tenant term budget exhausted` / `api key term budget exhausted` | A cumulative term budget is used up |
| `404` | `unknown endpoint` | The path is not a recognised API path and the request named no registered model |
| `413` | `request body too large` | The body exceeds 64 MiB (32 MiB for `/v1/messages`, 16 MiB for `/mcp/*`). `/v1/responses` over 32 MiB returns `400` `request body

chunks.title: Troubleshooting
chunks.heading: Identity tokens rejected (401 `invalid token`)
chunks.text:
A `401` whose body is `invalid token` rather than `invalid api key` means the
credential was verified as a JWT and failed. The response is deliberately the
same for every cause, so read the reason from metrics:

```bash
curl -s http://127.0.0.1:9091/metrics | grep obleth_jwt
```

`obleth_jwt_verify_total{result}` names the failed check —
[Identity Tokens](/docs/guides/identity-tokens#troubleshooting) maps each label
to its cause.

If no `obleth_jwt*` metric exists at all, the feature is off: `OBLETH_JWT_ISSUERS`
is unset or empty, so every bearer credential is looked up as an API key and JWTs
fail as unknown keys. Confirm with the boot log, which prints
`jwt bearer auth enabled` when the issuer list parsed and `jwks loaded` per
issuer. The variable is read only at startup, so restart the gateway after
setting it.

`obleth_jwks_refresh_total{issuer_index,result="error"}` climbing means the key
document is unreachable or not valid JWKS. Fetch the configured `jwks_url` from
inside the gateway container: a reverse proxy returning HTML or a `500` for an
unmatched path is a common cause, and it looks identical to an outage from the
gateway's side. Until a fetch succeeds, verification uses the last good snapshot,
or rejects everything if none was ever loaded.

chunks.title: Troubleshooting
chunks.heading: Model registration rejected (400, SSRF)
chunks.text:
Symptom: `POST /api/v1/models` or a dashboard import fails with a blocked-host
message when `api_base` points at an internal Service.

By default, private/LAN addresses are allowed, so `*.svc.cluster.local` hostnames
that resolve to RFC1918 IPs should register cleanly. Failures usually mean:

1. **Strict SSRF is on** (`OBLETH_BLOCK_PRIVATE_NETWORKS=1`) and the pod CIDR is
   not in `OBLETH_ALLOWED_PRIVATE_CIDRS` — add e.g. `10.0.0.0/8` in Helm
   `obleth.allowedPrivateCidrs` or the equivalent env var.
2. **The host resolves to a blocked range** — link-local / cloud metadata
   (`169.254.x.x`) is always rejected.

```bash
# Confirm current models and api_base values
curl http://localhost:9180/api/v1/models \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" | jq '.[] | {name: .model_name, api_base}'
```

See [Security — SSRF](/docs/operations/security#upstream-url-validation-ssrf).

chunks.title: Troubleshooting
chunks.heading: NOAUTH or WRONGPASS after an upgrade
chunks.text:
Redis requires a password. `NOAUTH` in the gateway's Redis errors means it
connected without one; `WRONGPASS` means the password does not match the one
Redis was started with. Put the same value in `REDIS_PASSWORD` and in the
password part of `OBLETH_REDIS_URL` (`redis://:PASSWORD@host:6379`). In Compose
both come from `REDIS_PASSWORD` in `deploy/docker/.env`; in Helm, from
`redis.password` or your `existingSecret`. See
[Upgrades](/docs/operations/upgrades).

chunks.title: Troubleshooting
chunks.heading: "prompt is too long: N tokens > W maximum"
chunks.text:
On `/v1/messages`, the gateway clamps `max_tokens` to the served model's context
window. When the prompt alone meets or exceeds the window, it returns `400` with
this message, using Anthropic's exact wording so that Claude Code compacts its
context automatically. A context-length error from the upstream is rewritten to
the same `prompt is too long:` prefix. If it appears for prompts that should fit,
check the model's `context_window` in the registry.

chunks.title: Troubleshooting
chunks.heading: Redis connectivity issues
chunks.text:
When Redis is unreachable or slow, key lookups that miss the in-process cache
fail with `503` `authentication backend unavailable`, and budget checks follow
`OBLETH_FAIL_OPEN`: admitted unmetered (default) or rejected with `503`. Typical
log lines:

```
WARN obleth_proxy: redis key lookup failed
WARN obleth_proxy: budget reserve failed; failing open
```

Check:

```bash
docker compose -f deploy/docker/docker-compose.yml logs redis
redis-cli -h $REDIS_HOST -a "$REDIS_PASSWORD" --no-auth-warning ping
```

When Redis reconnects, the gateway re-pushes its configuration from Postgres and
resumes normal operation. Check that `OBLETH_REDIS_URL` is correct. The scheme
must be `redis://` (not `rediss://` unless TLS is configured).

chunks.title: Troubleshooting
chunks.heading: Replica state is frozen (Slurm)
chunks.text:
If a model's Replicas panel shows a warning with a failure reason, its state
badges are grayed out with a `?`, or Settings → Slurm reads "running but failing
since X", the provisioner process is alive but its reconcile ticks are failing —
so every replica state shown is the last value it managed to reconcile, not live
truth. The usual cause is `slurmrestd` being unreachable or rejecting the
gateway's JWT.

After 10 minutes without a successful tick (and only while Slurm provisioning is
enabled), a `slurm_reconcile_held` alert fires, with a recovery notice when it
clears. See [Slurm Provisioning](/docs/guides/slurm-provisioning).

chunks.title: Troubleshooting
chunks.heading: Requests piling up in the queue
chunks.text:
Each model has its own admission pool. When a pool is full, new requests for that
model wait in its fairshare queue until a slot frees up, for at most
`OBLETH_ADMISSION_TIMEOUT_SECS` (default `60`), after which they get `503`.
Persistent queue growth means the model's pool is too small for the offered load.
Check:

```bash
# Live stats
curl http://localhost:9180/api/v1/stats -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN"
# Look at: in_flight, queued, max_in_flight (the sum of the enabled models' pools)

# Prometheus
curl http://localhost:9091/metrics | grep 'obleth_queue_depth\|obleth_in_flight'
```

The dashboard's **Fairshare** page shows occupancy and waiting tenants per model.

Options:
1. Raise the model's `max_in_flight` (only if its backend can handle more concurrency)
2. Add capacity behind the model (more endpoints or replicas)
3. Review tenant and key weights so high-priority traffic keeps advancing while the queue is deep

chunks.title: Troubleshooting
chunks.heading: Start-up warning: ceiling below the pool sum
chunks.text:
```
OBLETH_GLOBAL_MAX_IN_FLIGHT is below the sum of the enabled models' pool sizes;
the ceiling will bind first and pools will be served round-robin
```

The total ceiling is lower than the pools it covers, so it caps the gateway
before the pools do. Raise `OBLETH_GLOBAL_MAX_IN_FLIGHT` (Helm
`obleth.globalMaxInFlight`) above the pool sum. See
[Scaling](/docs/operations/scaling).

chunks.title: Troubleshooting
chunks.heading: Streams that end early (502 in the request log)
chunks.text:
When an upstream stream breaks before its final chunk, the gateway aborts the
response to the client (so a truncated body is never mistaken for a complete one)
and records the request as `502`. It bills the usage the upstream reported, or
the prompt estimate plus the streamed text when it reported none. A stream that
goes silent for longer than `OBLETH_UPSTREAM_READ_TIMEOUT_SECS` ends the same way.
An `upstream_stream_error` alert accompanies it. Check the backend's logs around
the request time; restarts, out-of-memory kills, and idle timeouts on proxies in
front of the backend are common causes. See
[Shutdown & Timeouts](/docs/operations/graceful-shutdown-and-timeouts).

chunks.title: Troubleshooting
chunks.heading: The spill is bounded: watch for dropped rows
chunks.text:
Spill is capped at **256 MiB** total and **1,024 segments** (segments live in
`<OBLETH_WAL_PATH>.segments/`). Past either limit, new spill is refused rather
than older accounting being evicted, and the batch is dropped:

```
ERROR obleth_telemetry: telemetry WAL spill failed; records dropped
```

`obleth_telemetry_dropped` counts records that were never persisted. Any
non-zero value means usage rows are gone for good. If a ClickHouse outage is
going to outlast the spill budget, restore ClickHouse (or point
`OBLETH_CLICKHOUSE_URL` at a reachable instance) before the cap is hit. The spill
path must also be writable by the gateway's non-root user.

A growing spill directory with ClickHouse healthy points at replay failing rather
than insertion — look for `telemetry WAL read failed` or
`telemetry WAL checkpoint failed` in the logs.

chunks.title: Troubleshooting
chunks.heading: Usage or cost numbers look too low
chunks.text:
Usage, cost, and report reads exclude gateway-internal traffic by default: health
probes (`request_type = 'health_probe'`) and traffic from tenants flagged
**synthetic** (`request_type = 'benchmark'`), which covers obench fixture tenants
and the dashboard's own model-test and benchmark runs. Pass
`include_internal=true` on the usage/cost endpoints — or the equivalent dashboard
toggle — to see it.

Benchmark traffic is also never written into the permanent `usage_daily` rollup,
so historical reports will not show it even with the flag set.

chunks.title: Upgrades
chunks.heading: 1. Redis requires a password
chunks.text:
Every supported deployment now runs Redis with authentication, and the gateway
connects with a password-bearing URL (`redis://:PASSWORD@host:6379`). The
password is embedded in that URL, so it must be URL-safe: a hex value is
simplest.

**Helm.** Supply `redis.password` on the upgrade. The chart fails to render
without it (`redis.password is required when redis.enabled=true`), and also
fails if the value contains `@`, `:`, `/`, `?`, `#`, `%`, or whitespace.

```bash
helm upgrade obleth \
  oci://ghcr.io/thediymaker/charts/obleth \
  --version 1.3.0 \
  --namespace obleth \
  --reset-then-reuse-values \
  --set redis.password=$(openssl rand -hex 16) \
  --wait
```

The value is kept by `--reset-then-reuse-values` on later upgrades, so pass it
once. The gateway now reads `OBLETH_REDIS_URL` from the obleth Secret instead of
a plain environment value. The bundled Redis restarts with the password when the
Secret changes, so expect a short interruption while Redis and the gateway pods
roll.

The chart's bundled Redis also gets a 512Mi memory limit with `maxmemory 400mb`
and the `volatile-lru` policy; the Compose Redis sets no `maxmemory`. Under that
policy only keys with a TTL (response cache, compression originals, per-minute
buckets, term-budget counters) are evicted; when Redis is full it refuses writes
to keys without a TTL rather than evicting API keys or model routes.

**Helm with `obleth.existingSecret`.** The chart no longer renders its own
Secret in this mode, so add these

chunks.title: Upgrades
chunks.heading: 2. Upstream secrets are no longer returned by the Management API
chunks.text:
Model, endpoint, and MCP server responses carry `api_key_set` /
`auth_header_set` booleans instead of the secret itself. Writes are unchanged:
omit the field to keep the stored value, or send `""` to clear it. Any client or script
that read `api_key` or `auth_header` from a response must be updated. See
[Management API](/docs/reference/management-api).

chunks.title: Upgrades
chunks.heading: 3. Response cache and compression store are scoped per tenant
chunks.text:
The response-cache key now includes the tenant, as does the compression
originals store. Entries written by earlier versions are not reused: expect one
cache miss per distinct request until the cache repopulates.

A model cache TTL of `0` now means **do not cache**: no lookup and no write.
Earlier versions treated `0` as "never expire", and entries they wrote that way
have no TTL, so they are never evicted and stay in Redis until removed. To remove
only those entries, run this where `REDIS_PASSWORD` is set (for example inside
the Redis container):

```bash
redis-cli -a "$REDIS_PASSWORD" --no-auth-warning --scan --pattern 'obleth:cache:*' |
while read -r key; do
  if [ "$(redis-cli -a "$REDIS_PASSWORD" --no-auth-warning ttl "$key")" = "-1" ]; then
    redis-cli -a "$REDIS_PASSWORD" --no-auth-warning del "$key" > /dev/null
  fi
done
```

Every entry written by v1.3.0 carries a TTL, so the loop never removes current
entries. See [Response Cache](/docs/guides/response-cache).

chunks.title: Upgrades
chunks.heading: 4. `POST /v1/messages` is translated, not passed through
chunks.text:
The gateway now serves the Anthropic Messages API itself and translates it onto
the chat pipeline. Earlier versions forwarded `POST /v1/messages` to the upstream
unchanged; a deployment that relied on that pass-through must route those
requests another way. See
[Claude Code & Anthropic SDKs](/docs/guides/anthropic-messages-api).

chunks.title: Upgrades
chunks.heading: 5. Size the in-flight ceiling above the model pools
